facts: THREAT: Powerful Catholic bishops inherited from Mary held key positions.
THREAT: Much of English population had never left Catholicism.
THREAT: Many Catholics viewed Elizabeth as illegitimate.
THREAT: Mary Queen of Scots had Catholic claim - alternative monarch existed.
THREAT: Catholic gentry could afford recusancy fines - sustained Catholic worship privately.
THREAT: Church Papists attended both services - faith persisted under cover of conformity.
NO THREAT: For first decade there was 'limited overt Catholic challenge'.
NO THREAT: Elizabeth's tolerance defused tensions - heresy laws repealed.
NO THREAT: Manageable fine of 1 shilling for Catholic gentry.
NO THREAT: Northern JPs allowed to avoid implementing fines - flexible enforcement.
NO THREAT: Philip of Spain persuaded Pope NOT to excommunicate Elizabeth in 1563.
NO THREAT: Habsburg-Valois rivalry prevented united Catholic action.
NO THREAT: Catholicism was 'dying out naturally without trained priests to sustain it'.

subheadings.label: Mary's arrival and why she was dangerous
facts: Mary returned to Scotland in 1561 but was forced to abdicate in 1567 following her suspected involvement in the assassination of her second husband Lord Darnley. In 1568 she fled to northern England seeking Elizabeth's support.

Mary was a real danger to Elizabeth as she was Elizabeth's cousin and next in line to the throne. If Mary succeeded as Queen she would likely restore Catholicism to England. More concerningly, many of Elizabeth's Catholic subjects already viewed Mary as the true Queen of England.

Mary's arrival in the highly Catholic North of England in 1568 provided a figurehead around which Catholic plots would ferment. Even under house arrest, where Elizabeth placed her, Mary acted as a 'lightning rod' for Catholic opposition.

subheadings.label: Elizabeth's response and Mary's impact
facts: Elizabeth placed Mary under house arrest — Mary was too dangerous to release (a Catholic claimant to the English throne) but too politically sensitive to execute or return to Scotland. This solution satisfied nobody and left the problem unresolved for nearly 20 years.

Mary's presence meant that every Catholic plot from 1568 onwards had a potential Catholic successor ready to take the throne — making the plots far more dangerous than anything Elizabeth had faced in the first decade of her reign.

1570: Pope Pius V issued Regnans in Excelsis, excommunicating Elizabeth and absolving Catholics of loyalty to her — transforming the Catholic threat from passive non-conformity into active potential treachery. After 1570 every English Catholic was theoretically required to choose between loyalty to the Pope and loyalty to the Queen.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was Mary Queen of Scots a serious threat?
facts: SERIOUS: Mary was 'a real danger' as Elizabeth's cousin and next in line to the throne.
SERIOUS: Many Catholic subjects viewed Mary as 'true Queen of England' - direct challenge.
SERIOUS: Mary acted as 'lightning rod for Catholic opposition' - centre of plots.
SERIOUS: Every Catholic plot from 1568 had a potential successor - dramatically increased threat.
SERIOUS: If Mary succeeded she would 'likely restore Catholicism to England'.
SERIOUS: Plots became 'far more dangerous than anything Elizabeth had faced'.
SERIOUS: Required execution in 1587 to remove the threat - extreme measure.
NOT SERIOUS: Mary placed under house arrest - threat contained for nearly 20 years.
NOT SERIOUS: Mary forced to abdicate in Scotland - already discredited as ruler.
NOT SERIOUS: Suspected involvement in Darnley's assassination undermined her legitimacy.
NOT SERIOUS: All plots based around her were uncovered before action.
NOT SERIOUS: After her execution in 1587, Catholic plots 'became far less dangerous'.

subheadings.label: The plot and the rebellion
facts: A plot emerged to marry Mary Queen of Scots to the powerful Duke of Norfolk to strengthen her claim to the English throne — uncovered by Cecil in 1569.

In desperation, the Catholic northern Earls of Northumberland and Westmoreland launched an uprising. The rebels captured Durham and held Catholic Latin mass in the Cathedral. A summons was issued to other Catholic nobility and gentry — none answered the call.

subheadings.label: Suppression and consequences
facts: A royal army led by the Earl of Sussex marched north and the rebels fled without fighting a major battle. Mary was moved to Coventry, away from the Catholic North. Elizabeth resisted calls from her Privy Council to execute the Duke of Norfolk — but did execute 450 rebels.

In 1570 Pope Pius V issued his Papal Bull Regnans in Excelsis, excommunicating Elizabeth. Catholics were now absolved of any loyalty to Elizabeth — transforming the Catholic threat from passive non-conformity to active potential treachery. The government responded with the Treason Act 1571: it became treason to possess or distribute a copy of the Papal Bull.

subheadings.label: Significance
facts: The Rising was the largest armed challenge to Elizabeth's authority and showed the danger that Mary's presence posed as a Catholic figurehead. However the failure of other Catholic nobles to answer the summons showed how limited active Catholic opposition actually was.
The Rising, combined with the Papal Bull, directly accelerated the government's anti-Catholic legislation and marked a decisive hardening of Elizabeth's religious policy.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was the Rising of the North a serious threat?
facts: SERIOUS: 'Largest armed challenge to Elizabeth's authority' of her reign.
SERIOUS: Captured Durham and held Catholic Latin mass in the Cathedral - religious defiance.
SERIOUS: Triggered Pope's excommunication of Elizabeth (1570) - escalated threat to active treachery.
SERIOUS: Northumberland and Westmoreland launched armed uprising.
SERIOUS: 450 rebels executed - significant repression.
SERIOUS: Plot to marry Mary to Norfolk - aristocratic conspiracy against the queen.
SERIOUS: Showed danger of Mary's presence as Catholic figurehead.
NOT SERIOUS: No other Catholic nobles answered the summons - showed limited support.
NOT SERIOUS: Rebels fled without fighting major battle - little real military commitment.
NOT SERIOUS: Active Catholic opposition was 'limited' even at peak.
NOT SERIOUS: Elizabeth refused to execute Duke of Norfolk despite Council pressure - regime confident.
NOT SERIOUS: Most Catholic nobility remained loyal to Elizabeth rather than joining the rising.

subheadings.label: The plots 1571–86
facts: Ridolfi Plot (1571): following Elizabeth's excommunication, Catholic banker Ridolfi plotted with the Pope, Philip II and the Duke of Norfolk to marry Mary to Norfolk and provoke a Catholic uprising. Discovered by Cecil. Norfolk was executed in 1572 but Elizabeth resisted calls to execute Mary.

Throckmorton Plot (1583): plot to liberate Mary and overthrow Elizabeth. Involved Mary's cousin the Duke of Guise, Philip II, the Pope and William Allen's seminary priests. Uncovered by Walsingham's spy network. Throckmorton was executed.

Babington Plot (1586): plot involving Elizabeth's assassination and invasion by Spanish and French forces. Walsingham discovered evidence directly implicating Mary herself. Parliament put Mary on trial and found her guilty of treason.

subheadings.label: Counter-measures
facts: 1584: Bond of Association agreed by the Privy Council — anyone who benefited from the assassination of Elizabeth would be executed at any cost.
1584: Treaty of Joinville — Spanish and French Catholics joined together against Protestantism, raising fears of co-ordinated international action against Elizabeth.

subheadings.label: Mary's execution (1587)
facts: Parliament repeatedly pushed for Mary's execution in 1572, 1585 and 1586. Elizabeth consistently resisted executing her cousin and fellow monarch — concerned about the precedent of executing an anointed sovereign.

The combined pressure of the Lords, Commons and Privy Council, combined with the evidence from the Babington Plot directly implicating Mary, finally forced Elizabeth's hand. Mary was executed on 8 February 1587.
Mary's execution removed the key Catholic figurehead. After 1587, Catholic plots became far less dangerous — they had lost their potential monarch.

subheadings.label: Debate: Were the Catholic plots serious?
facts: SERIOUS: Series of major plots (Ridolfi 1571, Throckmorton 1583, Babington 1586) - persistent threat.
SERIOUS: Involved foreign Catholic powers (Pope, Philip II, France, Duke of Guise).
SERIOUS: 1584 Treaty of Joinville unified Spanish and French Catholics.
SERIOUS: Required Bond of Association (1584) - extreme measure.
SERIOUS: Required Mary's execution to resolve - drastic action.
SERIOUS: Parliament pushed for execution three times - sustained pressure.
SERIOUS: Babington Plot involved Elizabeth's assassination AND foreign invasion.
SERIOUS: Norfolk executed in 1572 for involvement in Ridolfi - lethal threat.
NOT SERIOUS: All major plots were discovered before execution (Cecil/Walsingham).
NOT SERIOUS: Plots never materialised into successful action - just plots.
NOT SERIOUS: After Mary's execution in 1587, plots 'became far less dangerous'.
NOT SERIOUS: Elizabeth survived all plots - government remained in control.
NOT SERIOUS: Walsingham's intelligence service effectively neutralised the threat.
NOT SERIOUS: Ridolfi himself was Italian banker, not a powerful figure - amateur plotting.

subheadings.label: Seminary priests — origins and scale
facts: Elizabeth's hope that the lack of trained Catholic priests would lead to Catholicism dying out was countered by William Allen's 'English College' at Douai in France, founded in 1568. Allen trained seminary priests specifically to return to England and minister secretly to English Catholics.
The first Seminary Priests arrived in 1574. By 1585, 279 Seminary Priests had travelled to England, sheltered by Catholic gentry in priest holes.

Cuthbert Mayne was the first seminary priest to be executed — caught in Cornwall in 1577 and hanged, drawn and quartered. His execution signalled that the government viewed the mission as treasonous from the outset.

subheadings.label: The Jesuits
facts: From the 1580s the Jesuits also arrived — the Society of Jesus was a more militant, highly trained Catholic order. In total around 650 Jesuits or seminary priests were active in England across the reign.
The most famous Jesuit was Edmund Campion, who arrived in 1580. He was captured in 1581, tortured and executed — his death became a cause célèbre among English Catholics.

Robert Parsons was another leading Jesuit who escaped to the Continent and continued organising the mission. The 1570 excommunication had transformed the Jesuits' mission — their presence was politically as well as spiritually charged.

subheadings.label: Government response and executions
facts: Government response escalated specifically in response to the priests: 1581 — recusancy fines raised to £20 a month; converting someone to Catholicism made treason. 1585 — all Catholic priests expelled from England; harbouring a priest punishable by death.

133 seminary priests and Jesuits were executed under the 1585 legislation. The arrival of priests revitalised English Catholicism — but also gave the government justification for treating all Catholics as potential traitors.

subheadings.label: Debate: Were seminary priests/Jesuits a serious threat?
facts: SERIOUS: 279 Seminary Priests had reached England by 1585 — massive influx.
SERIOUS: 650 Jesuits/seminary priests active across the reign — sustained mission.
SERIOUS: Revitalised English Catholicism — countered Elizabeth's strategy of letting it die out.
SERIOUS: Required major legislative response (1581, 1585) — escalating threat.
SERIOUS: 133 executed under 1585 legislation — scale of response shows scale of threat.
SERIOUS: Sheltered by Catholic gentry in priest holes — networked underground.
SERIOUS: Campion's death became a 'cause célèbre' — inspired Catholic resistance.
NOT SERIOUS: Cuthbert Mayne caught immediately in 1577 — government detection was effective.
NOT SERIOUS: Campion captured and executed within a year of arrival — early decapitation of the mission.
NOT SERIOUS: Legislation gave justification for treating Catholics as traitors — turned threat to advantage.
NOT SERIOUS: The mission could not overturn the Settlement — English Catholicism remained underground.

subheadings.label: Elizabeth's initial tolerance
facts: Elizabeth's Religious Settlement was pragmatic and relatively tolerant in the early period. She promised she 'would not open windows unto men's souls' — only outward conformity was demanded.
Catholic Mass was made illegal under the 1559 Settlement and recusancy fines imposed, but the initial fine was just 1 shilling — a manageable sum for the Catholic gentry.
Elizabeth even allowed northern JPs to avoid implementing recusancy fines. Church Papists — who attended Anglican services but also maintained private Catholic worship — were tacitly tolerated.

subheadings.label: Obstacles to full Catholic restoration
facts: The Habsburg-Valois rivalry between Spain and France prevented joint Catholic action against England throughout the 1560s. Spain was fighting the expensive Dutch Revolt (from 1566). Philip persuaded Pope Pius IV not to excommunicate Elizabeth in 1563.

The excommunication of 1570 came too late — after eleven years during which England had accommodated to the Settlement, and after the Northern Rising had already been crushed. It transformed Catholics into potential traitors rather than non-conformists.

Elizabeth's longevity was the ultimate obstacle. Both Edward VI (six years) and Mary I (five years) had been unable to cement religious change. Elizabeth's 45-year reign allowed a whole generation to grow up under the Settlement.

subheadings.label: Escalating persecution
facts: 1571: treason to possess or distribute a copy of the Papal Bull. 1581: recusancy fines raised to £20 a month; converting someone to Catholicism made treason. 1585: all Catholic priests expelled; harbouring a priest punishable by death.
133 seminary priests and Jesuits were executed under the 1585 legislation.
After Mary Queen of Scots's execution in 1587, Catholic plots became far less dangerous — they had lost their potential Catholic monarch.
By 1589 the Catholic cause in England was effectively defeated. Catholicism survived only underground, sustained by a network of Catholic gentry families in the north.

subheadings.label: Debate: How serious or difficult were the changes Catholics faced?
facts: SERIOUS/DIFFICULT: Excommunication of 1570 transformed Catholics from non-conformists into potential traitors.
SERIOUS/DIFFICULT: 1571 legislation made it treason to possess or distribute Papal Bull.
SERIOUS/DIFFICULT: 1581 legislation increased recusancy fines to £20 a month - a massive sum.
SERIOUS/DIFFICULT: 1581 made converting someone to Catholicism treason.
SERIOUS/DIFFICULT: 1585 expelled all Catholic priests and made harbouring a priest punishable by death.
SERIOUS/DIFFICULT: 133 seminary priests and Jesuits executed under 1585 legislation.
SERIOUS/DIFFICULT: Mary's execution in 1587 removed their potential Catholic successor.
SERIOUS/DIFFICULT: 1588 Armada defeat ended their hope of external Catholic rescue.
SERIOUS/DIFFICULT: Elizabeth's 45-year reign outlasted the Marian Catholic establishment.
SERIOUS/DIFFICULT: New generation grew up under Settlement - lost the next generation.
SERIOUS/DIFFICULT: By 1589 'Catholic cause in England was effectively defeated'.
NOT SO DIFFICULT: Elizabeth's tolerance was 'genuine in the early period' - heresy laws repealed.
NOT SO DIFFICULT: Initial recusancy fine was just 1 shilling - manageable for gentry.
NOT SO DIFFICULT: Northern JPs allowed to avoid implementing fines - flexible enforcement.
NOT SO DIFFICULT: Church Papists tolerated - could outwardly conform whilst remaining Catholic.
NOT SO DIFFICULT: Elizabeth promised 'would not open windows unto men's souls'.
NOT SO DIFFICULT: Seminary priests/Jesuits revitalised English Catholicism - 650 priests active.
NOT SO DIFFICULT: Catholic gentry sheltered priests in priest holes - networked underground.
NOT SO DIFFICULT: Habsburg-Valois rivalry meant no foreign action - Catholics had hope of rescue.
NOT SO DIFFICULT: Excommunication came 'too little too late' - already bedded in.
NOT SO DIFFICULT: Catholic worship survived underground - faith preserved if not public.

subheadings.label: The monarch's powers and the Royal Prerogative
facts: The monarch was believed to derive their power directly from God. All legislation had to receive the monarch's Royal Assent. The monarch could issue Royal proclamations expected to be followed, and had the power to call, prorogue and dissolve Parliament at will.

The Royal Prerogative were issues only the monarch had the right to decide: religion, the succession and foreign policy. Parliament could not legislate on prerogative matters without the monarch's consent — a source of recurring conflict under Elizabeth.

subheadings.label: The Privy Council
facts: The Privy Council was the council of the monarch's most important advisors — maximum of 20 members, meeting several times a week. Key figures included the Secretary of State and Lord Treasurer.

The Council managed Parliament by setting the parliamentary agenda, influencing the election of the Speaker and promoting supporters as MPs. Dominated for most of Elizabeth's reign by William Cecil, who held the post of Secretary of State (until 1572) then Lord Treasurer (to 1598).

subheadings.label: Parliament
facts: Parliament could pass legislation more permanent and enforceable than a proclamation. The monarch needed Parliamentary approval to gain taxation — Parliament could withhold grants until grievances were addressed.

Called ten times during Elizabeth's reign over thirteen sessions. MPs in the House of Commons tended to be members of the gentry. The House of Lords included the Lords Temporal (nobility) and Lords Spiritual (bishops). Legislation had to be approved by both houses before receiving Royal Assent.

subheadings.label: Debate: Effective or issues?
facts: EFFECTIVE: Monarch derived power 'directly from God' - clear legitimacy.
EFFECTIVE: Royal Assent gave veto power over legislation.
EFFECTIVE: Privy Council of max 20 members met several times a week with key experienced figures.
EFFECTIVE: William Cecil dominated for most of the reign - continuity and skill.
EFFECTIVE: Parliament only called 10 times in 45 years - controlled access.
EFFECTIVE: Royal Prerogative kept key issues (religion, succession, foreign policy) for monarch.
EFFECTIVE: Power to call, prorogue and dissolve Parliament at will.
ISSUES: Required parliamentary approval for taxation - weakness in finance.
ISSUES: Legislation needed both houses' approval - potential blocking.
ISSUES: System depended heavily on a few individuals (especially Cecil).
ISSUES: Parliament increasingly assertive over key issues (religion, succession).
ISSUES: Only 20 members on Privy Council - limited representation of nobility.

subheadings.label: Why gender was a problem
facts: Elizabeth was only the second woman to rule England in her own right. Mary I's reign had been associated with religious persecution and military failure, creating negative views of female rule. Many believed women were intellectually and emotionally unfit to rule.

John Knox wrote 'The First Blast of the Trumpet against the Monstrous Regiment of Women' (1558), comparing female rulers to 'the blind leading those who can see'. Parliament and the Privy Council assumed a queen would need a king to govern effectively. Elizabeth could not be called Supreme Head — theologically objectionable for a woman — so 'Supreme Governor' was used instead.

subheadings.label: How Elizabeth managed and exploited gender
facts: Elizabeth's response was to construct a carefully managed public image that transcended gender. At Tilbury she declared 'I know I have the body of a weak, feeble woman; but I have the heart and stomach of a king, and of a king of England too.' She presented herself simultaneously as the Virgin Queen and as Gloriana.

She used her femininity deliberately as a political tool — courtiers competed for her personal affection, making loyalty partly emotional. Leicester, Essex, Hatton and Raleigh all sought to be her favourite. Marriage ambiguity became a tool of foreign policy throughout the 1560s and 1570s.

The 'Supreme Governor' compromise actually made the Settlement more acceptable to Catholics who could not accept a woman as Head of the Church. Gender, while a challenge, also gave Elizabeth unique tools that male monarchs lacked.

subheadings.label: Debate: Did Elizabeth's gender have serious impact?
facts: SERIOUS IMPACT: Only second woman to rule England in her own right - unprecedented position.
SERIOUS IMPACT: Mary I's reign created negative views of female rule (persecution, military failure).
SERIOUS IMPACT: Many believed women 'intellectually and emotionally unfit to rule'.
SERIOUS IMPACT: Pressure to marry/produce heir framed as uniquely female failing.
SERIOUS IMPACT: Couldn't be 'Supreme Head' - theologically objectionable for woman.
SERIOUS IMPACT: Marriage alliances dominated diplomacy for 20 years.
SERIOUS IMPACT: Parliament and Privy Council 'assumed a queen needed a king to govern effectively'.
NO SERIOUS IMPACT: Tilbury speech transcended gender ('heart and stomach of a king').
NO SERIOUS IMPACT: Virgin Queen and Gloriana image used effectively.
NO SERIOUS IMPACT: Used femininity for faction management - courtiers competing for affection.
NO SERIOUS IMPACT: Leicester, Essex, Hatton and Raleigh all competed to be her favourite.
NO SERIOUS IMPACT: 'Supreme Governor' compromise actually made Settlement more acceptable to Catholics.
NO SERIOUS IMPACT: Marriage uncertainty became a tool of foreign policy, not just a weakness.

heading: Key figures on the Privy Council

subheadings.label: William Cecil (Lord Burghley)
facts: William Cecil (Lord Burghley from 1571): Cecil was Elizabeth's principal advisor until his death in 1598. He was Secretary of State until 1572, then Lord Treasurer. Extremely hard-working and loyal, he helped draft the Religious Settlement, managed Elizabeth's correspondence, created an intelligence service and ran the Privy Council. By nature cautious and pragmatic.

subheadings.label: Sir Francis Walsingham
facts: Sir Francis Walsingham: a protégé of Cecil with a similar loyalty to Elizabeth and equal hostility to Mary Queen of Scots. Took over the intelligence service and Secretary of State in 1573. A devout Puritan who uncovered the Throckmorton and Babington Plots.

subheadings.label: Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester
facts: Robert Dudley (Earl of Leicester from 1564): Dudley was Elizabeth's favourite — they had been imprisoned together in the Tower under Mary. Promoted more for personality than political skill — tall, handsome, charismatic. His wife Amy Robsart died in mysterious circumstances in 1560. A devout Puritan who championed military intervention to protect Protestants abroad.

subheadings.label: Thomas Howard, Duke of Norfolk
facts: Thomas Howard, Duke of Norfolk: the most senior nobleman in England and the only Duke. Raised Protestant but with strong Catholic familial links. Initially a member of the Privy Council but executed in 1572 for his involvement in the Ridolfi Plot.

subheadings.label: Robert Devereux, Earl of Essex
facts: Robert Devereux, Earl of Essex: rose to favour in the 1590s as Leicester's godson. Charming, impulsive and popular but lacking political judgement. Raised to the Privy Council in 1593 but fell from grace over Ireland in 1599. His 1601 rebellion against Cecil's dominance failed immediately — executed for treason.

subheadings.label: Sir Robert Cecil
facts: Sir Robert Cecil: son of William Cecil, rose to Secretary of State in 1596 whilst Essex was at Cadiz. Cautious and systematic like his father. From 1601 onwards dominated government unopposed and managed the smooth transition to James I in 1603.

subheadings.label: Debate: Were Elizabeth's councillors effective or limited?
facts: EFFECTIVE: William Cecil 'Elizabeth's principal advisor' for 40 years (until death 1598) - extraordinary continuity.
EFFECTIVE: Cecil 'extremely hard-working and loyal' - helped draft Religious Settlement, ran Privy Council.
EFFECTIVE: Walsingham uncovered major plots (Throckmorton, Babington) - state security.
EFFECTIVE: Walsingham took over intelligence service and Secretary of State in 1573.
EFFECTIVE: Robert Cecil rose to Secretary of State in 1596 - managed smooth transition to James I in 1603.
EFFECTIVE: Cecil dynasty (William then Robert) gave continuity across the reign.
EFFECTIVE: Most Council members served loyally and effectively for decades.
LIMITED: Leicester promoted 'more for personality than political skill' - tall, handsome, charismatic.
LIMITED: Norfolk executed in 1572 for involvement in Ridolfi Plot - factional treason.
LIMITED: Essex 'charming, impulsive and popular but lacking political judgement' - raised to Council on personality.
LIMITED: Essex executed for treason in 1601 - faction continued to lethal end.
LIMITED: Amy Robsart's mysterious 1560 death damaged Leicester's reputation.
LIMITED: Council divided on Dutch Revolt (1578-85) - Leicester/Walsingham vs Burghley.

subheadings.label: Methods
facts: Elizabeth stayed aloof of faction, and in fact encouraged such disputes to get a wider debate on certain issues. By taking her time before making decisions, Elizabeth did not show favour to any particular faction and was not easily swayed by her Councillors.
Elizabeth used her gender to manage loyalty as courtiers and Councillors would compete for her affection.

subheadings.label: Leicester vs Norfolk (1565-66)
facts: 1565-66: Leicester came into dispute with a faction led by Norfolk and his cousin the Earl of Sussex. Norfolk accused Leicester of having murdered Amy Robsart. The factions wore identifying ribbons at court and Leicester and Sussex almost fought a duel. Elizabeth ended the dispute by making it clear she would not marry Leicester.

Leicester also used factional methods against Cecil's preferred suitors. In 1567 Cecil promoted Archduke Charles of Austria — Leicester used anti-Catholic propaganda to scupper the proposal. Similarly in 1579-84, Leicester deployed anti-Catholic propaganda to whip up public opposition to Burghley's preferred match, the French Duke of Alençon.

subheadings.label: The Dutch Revolt division (1578-85)
facts: 1578-85, The Dutch Revolt divided the Council. Leicester and Walsingham, as devout Puritans, urged direct intervention to support the Dutch rebels. The more watchful Burghley urged caution for fear of risking Spanish retaliation and an expensive and threatening war.
1585: pressure following the assassination of William of Orange forced Elizabeth's hand to intervene in the Netherlands — Treaty of Nonsuch committed her to support the Dutch rebels.

subheadings.label: Council united against Elizabeth: Mary QoS
facts: Mary, Queen of Scots was an issue that united the Council against Elizabeth. Repeatedly the Council petitioned Elizabeth to execute Mary. They agreed the Bond of Association to force the matter in 1584.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was Elizabeth's management of faction effective?
facts: EFFECTIVE: Stayed aloof of faction - not swayed by particular faction.
EFFECTIVE: Encouraged disputes for wider debate - constructive use of faction.
EFFECTIVE: Used her gender to manage loyalty - unique tool male monarchs lacked.
EFFECTIVE: Successfully resolved 1565-66 Leicester-Norfolk dispute by clarifying marriage position.
EFFECTIVE: Took time before making decisions - couldn't be rushed by Council.
EFFECTIVE: Courtiers and Councillors competed for her affection - tool for managing loyalty.
NOT EFFECTIVE: Major factional disputes continued throughout her reign (1565-66, 1578-85).
NOT EFFECTIVE: Dutch Revolt issue divided Council for seven years (1578-85).
NOT EFFECTIVE: Council 'united against Elizabeth' on Mary Queen of Scots - failed to maintain unity.
NOT EFFECTIVE: Bond of Association (1584) forced her hand on Mary.
NOT EFFECTIVE: Couldn't prevent Norfolk's involvement in Ridolfi Plot - faction turned to treason.
NOT EFFECTIVE: Essex's 1601 rebellion shows faction continued to be a problem at end of reign.

subheadings.label: Dissolution
facts: If Elizabeth disapproved of a particular batch of MPs in a Parliament she could dissolve the parliament. Then when she called a new Parliament, new MPs would be elected.

subheadings.label: Prorogation
facts: Alternatively Elizabeth could prorogue parliament which would suspend the parliament for as long as she liked. During the suspension she or her Privy Council could put pressure on MPs to change their position.

subheadings.label: The Privy Council in Parliament
facts: The Privy Council were expected to promote Elizabeth's wishes in Parliament. Many Councillors were prominent politicians who dominated Parliamentary business.

subheadings.label: Speaker of the House
facts: Elizabeth and the Privy Council influenced the choice of Speaker of the House who controlled debates, chose who could speak and thus could control the Commons.

subheadings.label: Royal Veto
facts: If a bill that Elizabeth disapproved of did manage to pass both Houses of Parliament, Elizabeth could use her Royal Veto to reject the proposed law.

subheadings.label: Arrest of MPs as last resort
facts: As a last resort, Elizabeth had the ability to arrest MPs who directly challenged her prerogative as traitors. However such an aggressive use of royal power could potentially increase parliamentary opposition.

subheadings.label: Debate: Did Elizabeth manage Parliament with skill or force?
facts: SKILLFUL: Influenced choice of Speaker who controlled debates - subtle management.
SKILLFUL: Privy Council systematically promoted her wishes in Parliament - persuasion not force.
SKILLFUL: Used prorogation to suspend Parliament and pressure MPs to change positions.
SKILLFUL: Many Councillors were prominent politicians who dominated Parliamentary business.
SKILLFUL: Worked within constitutional framework - prerogative, Council, Speaker.
SKILLFUL: Only called Parliament 10 times in 45 years - controlled access without force.
FORCE: Could dissolve Parliament if she disapproved of MPs - threat of removal.
FORCE: Used Royal Veto to reject bills that passed both Houses.
FORCE: Could arrest MPs who 'directly challenged her prerogative as traitors' - extreme measure.
FORCE: Strickland barred from Parliament, Cope sent to Tower - direct coercion.
FORCE: 'Aggressive use of royal power could potentially increase parliamentary opposition'.
FORCE: Framed religion as Royal Prerogative - shut down legitimate debate by force of authority.

subheadings.label: Over religion
facts: Religion: 1571 Parliament – Strickland's Bill. Strickland was questioned by the Privy Council for infringing on the Royal Prerogative before being suspended from Parliament. 1586 Parliament – Cope's Proposals. Cope and four supporters were sent to the Tower of London and the bill was defeated.

subheadings.label: Marriage petitions: 1559 and 1563
facts: Marriage and the Succession: many MPs were concerned that if Elizabeth remained unmarried and had no heir then after Elizabeth's death the throne would fall to the Catholic Mary, Queen of Scots. 1559 and 1563 Parliaments – Elizabeth was presented with petitions that she should marry.

subheadings.label: The 1566 Parliament crisis
facts: 1566 Parliament – the issue was seen as extremely important following Elizabeth's near-fatal experience of Smallpox in 1562. William Cecil himself helped organise the delegation from Parliament to the Queen requesting she named a successor. Elizabeth reduced her subsidy request by 1/3 to appease Parliament and publicly reaffirmed that the succession was part of her Royal Prerogative but did promise to marry.

subheadings.label: Over freedom of speech
facts: Elizabeth's rigid defence of the Royal Prerogative angered some MPs who believed Parliament should have broader powers.
MPs pushed for greater freedom of speech to debate issues Elizabeth considered exclusively her domain, like religion and marriage.
Peter Wentworth notably argued for Parliament's right to free speech, directly challenging Elizabeth's authority.
These conflicts revealed the tension between expanding Parliament and Elizabeth's insistence on royal control.

subheadings.label: Over Mary Queen of Scots
facts: Parliament was vehemently hostile to Mary, QoS and pushed for her execution for many years. 1572 Parliament – following the Rising of the North and the Ridolfi Plot, the Commons and Lords argued for Mary's execution. Elizabeth vetoed the execution of Mary but agreed to execute Norfolk.

subheadings.label: The Wentworth brothers' challenges
facts: Paul Wentworth MP led the first major free speech challenge in 1566, criticising Elizabeth's denial of Parliament's right to discuss the succession. His brother Peter continued these complaints across the Parliaments of 1571, 1576, 1587 and 1593.

Peter Wentworth 1576: compared Elizabeth's interference in Parliament to 'the work of the devil'. Crucially, the House of Commons itself interrupted his speech and sent him to the Tower — without Elizabeth's involvement — showing that even most MPs preferred co-operation to confrontation.
The Wentworths' persistence demonstrated genuine constitutional tension, but Peter's isolation within the Commons shows the limits of Puritan radicalism as a parliamentary force.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was Parliament in conflict with Elizabeth or cooperating?
facts: CONFLICT: Strickland's Bill (1571) - tried to alter Book of Common Prayer; Strickland barred from Parliament.
CONFLICT: Cope's Proposals (1586) - Cope and four supporters sent to the Tower of London.
CONFLICT: 1559 and 1563 Parliaments presented petitions urging Elizabeth to marry.
CONFLICT: 1566 Parliament - issue 'extremely important' after 1562 Smallpox; pressed for succession.
CONFLICT: Wentworth challenged Elizabeth's authority on free speech, religion, marriage.
CONFLICT: Parliament 'vehemently hostile to Mary QoS' - pushed for execution for many years.
CONFLICT: 1572 Parliament argued for Mary's execution after Rising of the North and Ridolfi Plot.
COOPERATION: Cecil himself helped organise 1566 delegation - Council siding with Parliament constructively.
COOPERATION: Elizabeth reduced subsidy request by 1/3 to appease Parliament in 1566 - compromise.
COOPERATION: Elizabeth promised to marry in 1566 - showed willingness to engage.
COOPERATION: Elizabeth vetoed Mary's execution in 1572 but agreed to execute Norfolk - middle ground.
COOPERATION: Most legislation passed through both Houses - functional relationship.
COOPERATION: Parliament operated within constitutional framework - never sought to overthrow her.

subheadings.label: The problem
facts: It was expected that Elizabeth would marry and produce an heir. An unclear succession following a monarch's death had previously led to anarchy, civil war and, in Elizabeth's lifetime, the Lady Jane Grey affair.
The next in line to the throne was Elizabeth's cousin Mary, Queen of Scots. If Elizabeth did not produce her own heir she risked her Protestant settlement being undone.

subheadings.label: Elizabeth's reluctance
facts: Choice of husband was almost impossible: a foreign monarch risked entanglement in his wars (cf. Mary I and Philip); an English noble would create faction; almost all candidates were Catholic.
Personal experience coloured her view: her mother Anne Boleyn was executed; stepmother Catherine Howard executed; her sister Mary's marriage brought war and humiliation. Marriage meant danger.
Elizabeth described naming a successor as being 'buried alive' — enemies would plot around that person; ministers would desert her for the incoming monarch.

subheadings.label: Suitors
facts: Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester — Elizabeth's likely personal preference; but his father, brother and grandfather all executed as traitors. Amy Robsart's suspicious death in 1560 made him politically unmarriageable.
Habsburg candidates: Archduke Charles of Austria — insistence on practising Catholicism privately was a dealbreaker. Philip II proposed in 1559 — wildly unpopular after Mary's reign.
Francis, Duke of Alençon — the only suitor to visit Elizabeth in person (1579). Elizabeth called him her 'frog'. Died 1584 — ending the last serious marriage negotiation.

subheadings.label: Elizabeth's strategy: 'married to England'
facts: Elizabeth kept suitors hopeful but ultimately unmarried, preserving her freedom to make political alliances while avoiding marital subordination.
She framed her unmarried status as a 'marriage to England', using her single status as a unique political asset rather than a liability.

subheadings.label: Parliamentary pressure
facts: Parliament repeatedly petitioned Elizabeth to marry or name a successor. Debates over the issue led to further conflict over parliamentary privilege and freedom of speech.

Public opposition to marriage was also fierce. In 1579, Puritan MP John Stubbs wrote a pamphlet denouncing the proposed Alençon match. Elizabeth had all copies burned and had Stubbs' right hand removed as punishment. The watching crowd called Stubbs 'a true Englishman' — showing popular support for opposition to the foreign match.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was marriage/succession a source of conflict or cooperation?
facts: CONFLICT: Parliament 'repeatedly petitioned Elizabeth to marry or name a successor to no avail'.
CONFLICT: Debates over marriage led to further conflict over parliamentary privilege and freedom of speech.
CONFLICT: Elizabeth 'resented the idea of sharing her power with a man' - constitutional standoff.
CONFLICT: Wentworth brothers' persistent challenges over succession became major source of parliamentary conflict.
CONFLICT: Elizabeth described naming a successor as 'buried alive' - sharply rejected Council's wishes.
CONFLICT: 1566 Parliament organised major delegation to force the issue.
COOPERATION: Elizabeth promised to marry in 1566 - response to parliamentary pressure.
COOPERATION: Elizabeth kept suitors hopeful for diplomatic leverage - worked with Council on alliances.
COOPERATION: Marriage alliances 'dominated diplomacy' for 20 years - close coordination with Council.
COOPERATION: Cecil himself helped organise 1566 delegation - working within system.
COOPERATION: 'Marriage to England' framing turned single status into asset - Crown and Parliament eventually accepted.
COOPERATION: Eventual peaceful succession to James in 1603 - long-term cooperation worked.

subheadings.label: The danger of an unclear succession
facts: The succession question was most dangerous in 1562 when Elizabeth nearly died of Smallpox. The Privy Council could not agree on a successor — in desperation Elizabeth asked that Robert Dudley be made Protector of the Realm. There was great relief from Cecil when she recovered.

The next in line was Catholic Mary Queen of Scots. An uncertain succession threatened the Religious Settlement — if Elizabeth died without a Protestant heir, Mary would restore Catholicism just as Elizabeth had reversed Mary I's changes.

subheadings.label: Conflict with Parliament and the Bond of Association
facts: Parliament repeatedly petitioned Elizabeth to marry or name a successor. The issue fuelled conflict over parliamentary privilege and freedom of speech — Elizabeth's rigid defence of her Royal Prerogative inflamed MPs.

In 1584 the Privy Council agreed the Bond of Association — an unprecedented agreement that anyone who benefited from the assassination of Elizabeth would be executed. In effect it ensured that Mary Queen of Scots would die if any plot in her name succeeded. Elizabeth tacitly supported it.

subheadings.label: Elizabeth's management and the outcome
facts: Despite never formally naming a successor, Elizabeth's tacit acknowledgement that James VI of Scotland (Mary's Protestant son) would inherit meant the issue was manageable. Her letters to James indicated he would be King — this meant he did not aggressively oppose his mother's execution in 1587.

In 1579, John Stubbs wrote a pamphlet denouncing the Alençon match — Elizabeth had his right hand removed. The watching crowd called Stubbs 'a true Englishman', showing how deeply the succession question stirred public opinion.

The peaceful accession of James I in 1603 vindicated Elizabeth's approach — by refusing to name a successor formally she avoided creating a rival power centre, while managing the transition through secret diplomacy.

subheadings.label: Debate: Did the succession question make the realm stable or unstable?
facts: UNSTABLE: 1562 Smallpox crisis - Privy Council 'could not agree on a successor', near collapse.
UNSTABLE: If Elizabeth died, Catholic Mary QoS would 'likely restore Catholicism' - religious settlement at risk.
UNSTABLE: 'Constant urgency throughout the reign' - never resolved while Elizabeth alive.
UNSTABLE: Wentworth brothers' challenges 'became a major source of parliamentary conflict'.
UNSTABLE: 1584 Bond of Association 'unprecedented' - shows succession 'permeated political life'.
UNSTABLE: France used Mary QoS as 'potential lever over England' for 1560s-1580s.
UNSTABLE: Auld Alliance created outlet for French influence via Scotland.
UNSTABLE: Foreign powers 'constantly measured Elizabeth against potential successors'.
STABLE: Elizabeth used succession ambiguity as 'diplomatic tool' - turned threat to advantage.
STABLE: Kept foreign Catholic powers hopeful - 'manipulated international relations'.
STABLE: Maintained diplomatic leverage - 'kept potential rivals uncertain'.
STABLE: Robert Cecil's secret correspondence with James prepared smooth transition.
STABLE: Eventual peaceful succession on 24th March 1603 - succession question resolved stably.
STABLE: Elizabeth recovered from 1562 Smallpox - immediate crisis passed without disaster.

subheadings.label: James as likely heir and diplomatic management
facts: James VI of Scotland was the son of Mary Queen of Scots and Lord Darnley — Elizabeth's closest Protestant relative and the most plausible successor to the English throne. Elizabeth never formally named him as heir, but her correspondence tacitly acknowledged it.

Following Mary's execution in 1587, Cecil needed James not to react so aggressively as to provoke war with Scotland. Robert Cecil began a secret correspondence with James from the late 1590s — keeping James informed about English politics and ensuring he would be accepted smoothly when the moment came.

James's presence as the likely heir had a stabilising effect in the later years of the reign. Despite socioeconomic unrest, Essex's rebellion and Elizabeth's physical decline, there was no serious succession crisis because everyone knew who would follow.

subheadings.label: The peaceful succession (1603)
facts: James became King of England on Elizabeth's death on 24th March 1603, succeeding as James I whilst remaining James VI of Scotland. The transition was entirely peaceful — a remarkable achievement given 50 years of succession anxiety.

The peaceful succession vindicated Elizabeth's policy of managed ambiguity. By refusing to name James formally, she avoided creating a rival power centre; by managing the transition through Cecil's secret correspondence, she ensured continuity.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was James a serious issue?
facts: SERIOUS: Mary's execution in 1587 risked war with Scotland.
SERIOUS: Elizabeth refused to formally name James despite obvious need.
SERIOUS: Mary tried to disinherit James in favour of Philip II - complicated succession.
SERIOUS: Cecil's secret correspondence done 'without Elizabeth's knowledge or approval' - shows tension.
SERIOUS: Despite stability, no formal succession plan in place.
NOT SERIOUS: James 'most plausible successor' from 1580s onwards - widely understood.
NOT SERIOUS: James accepted Mary's death rather than provoking war.
NOT SERIOUS: James wanted English inheritance - would not jeopardise it.
NOT SERIOUS: Cecil's management ensured 'smooth succession'.
NOT SERIOUS: James's presence had 'stabilising effect' on politics.
NOT SERIOUS: Transition on 24th March 1603 was 'entirely peaceful' - succession worked.
NOT SERIOUS: Protestant gentry and nobility broadly accepted James.

heading: Financial situation in 1558

subheadings.label: The inherited debt
facts: When Elizabeth acceded to the throne in 1558, the English Crown had debts of £227,000 left over from Mary's involvement in the war with France. This debt was largely owed to the Antwerp Exchange and came with an interest rate of 14%.

subheadings.label: Mary's earlier reforms
facts: Mary had introduced some reforms to make financial administration more efficient; most notable the revised Book of Rates which determined customs duties. Mary gave greater import to the Exchequer which now collected roughly three-quarters of Crown revenue.

subheadings.label: Gresham's analysis of the problems
facts: Sir Thomas Gresham identified three major problems: (1) debasement of the coinage begun under Henry VIII; (2) the cost of war and the damaging loans needed to fund it; (3) the control the Hanseatic League enjoyed over the export market of English wools from their base at the Steelyard in London, which damaged English merchants' profits.

subheadings.label: Gresham's advice
facts: Gresham's primary advice to Elizabeth was to in peacetime maintain an excellent credit rating by swiftly repaying existing debt, and avoiding taking loans. In 1565 Gresham founded the Royal Exchange as a London equivalent to the Antwerp Exchange.

subheadings.label: Elizabeth's success
facts: Elizabeth quickly and effectively removed the Marian debt. By 1576 the Chancellor of the Exchequer informed parliament that the Marian debt had been removed. By 1584 Elizabeth had accrued a surplus of £300,000. She achieved this by not indulging in the excessive lifestyle of her father, avoiding lavish building projects, going on 'progress' each summer, and avoiding war at all cost.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was the financial situation serious?
facts: SERIOUS: Inherited massive £227,000 debt with 14% interest - starting position weak.
SERIOUS: Debt 'largely owed to the Antwerp Exchange' - foreign creditors held leverage.
SERIOUS: Three major underlying problems remained (debasement, war costs, Hanseatic League).
SERIOUS: Required 18 years to clear debt (1558-76) - long-term burden.
SERIOUS: Strategy depended on avoiding war - vulnerable when war came after 1585.
SERIOUS: Marian debt came with 14% interest - massive interest burden.
NOT SERIOUS: Mary had improved financial administration with revised Book of Rates.
NOT SERIOUS: Exchequer collected three-quarters of Crown revenue - efficient system inherited.
NOT SERIOUS: Gresham identified problems clearly - had skilled financial advisor.
NOT SERIOUS: Removed Marian debt by 1576 and accrued £300,000 surplus by 1584.
NOT SERIOUS: Avoided lavish lifestyle, went on 'progress' each summer to reduce costs.
NOT SERIOUS: Founded Royal Exchange (1565) - London equivalent of Antwerp.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs

heading: Methods of raising income

subheadings.label: Revenue streams
facts: Ordinary revenue came by default each year: Crown lands, Customs Duties, profits from justice and Church revenue (First Fruits and Tenths). Extraordinary revenue required exceptional measures: parliamentary subsidies, forced loans from nobles, or borrowing at high interest rates.

Crown Lands: Elizabeth increased annual revenues from £86,000 to £111,000. However, Crown lands were customarily rented on long leases, which meant the short-term rent rises employed by the nobility were not an option. Elizabeth also sold a significant portion of Crown Lands — bringing £600,000 but depleting long-term Crown income.

Customs Duties: Mary's revision of the Book of Rates in 1558 provided an immediate boost — annual revenue jumped from £29,315 to £82,797 in one year. Parliamentary taxation raised around £100,000 per subsidy and £30,000 from fifteenths and tenths.
Church revenue: Elizabeth gained income from First Fruits and Tenths, recusancy fines (increased significantly in 1581) and by keeping bishoprics vacant for extended periods.

subheadings.label: Gresham, Paulet and clearing the debt
facts: Sir Thomas Gresham: highly perceptive financier experienced in key money markets. Stopped debasement and led the recoinage of 1560–61. In 1565 he founded the Royal Exchange as a London equivalent to the Antwerp Exchange.
William Paulet was a highly effective Lord Treasurer — his excellent financial management helped Elizabeth clear the Marian debt by 1576.

By 1576 the Marian debt had been cleared entirely. By 1584 Elizabeth had accrued a surplus of £300,000 — achieved by avoiding lavish expenditure, going on summer progress at courtiers' expense, and avoiding war.

subheadings.label: Limitations
facts: The Book of Rates was not regularly revised — by the 1590s customs revenue stood at only £91,000, barely above the 1558 level of £82,797 and far below real terms value given decades of inflation.

Elizabeth hoped to increase customs by encouraging English merchants to finish wool into cloth in England rather than exporting raw wool — a more profitable trade mostly done in the Netherlands. The reluctance of the English to adopt this practice significantly limited the gains from trade.

Local gentry systematically undervalued their neighbours' lands — England's taxes were among the lowest in Europe. Elizabeth refused to fund a professional tax-collecting service and Customs Farmers led to widespread corruption.

subheadings.label: Debate: Were Elizabeth's methods of raising income effective or ineffective?
facts: EFFECTIVE: Crown lands revenue increased from £86,000 to £111,000.
EFFECTIVE: Customs revenue jumped from £29,315 to £82,797 after Book of Rates revision.
EFFECTIVE: Crown Lands sales brought income of £600,000 over the reign.
EFFECTIVE: 'Taxes in England were amongst the lowest in Europe' - light burden on subjects.
EFFECTIVE: Multiple revenue streams provided diversified income.
EFFECTIVE: Subsidies raised around £100,000 each time - significant supplementary income.
EFFECTIVE: Fifteenths and tenths raised around £30,000 - additional revenue stream.
INEFFECTIVE: Sold Crown Lands worth £600,000 - 'depleted long-term potential for Crown income'.
INEFFECTIVE: Customs corruption under Gresham's Custom Farmers - lost revenue.
INEFFECTIVE: Book of Rates 'not regularly revised' - revenue eroded over time.
INEFFECTIVE: Kept bishoprics vacant for extra revenue - distorted Church governance.
INEFFECTIVE: Forced loans on wealthy nobles - alienated political class.
INEFFECTIVE: Recusancy fines exploited religious tensions for revenue.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs

heading: Inflation

subheadings.label: Causes of inflation
facts: Although there had been a decline of inflation by the start of Elizabeth's reign, it accelerated in the 1560s. By the 1560s, average food prices were triple what they had been in the reign of Henry VII; industrial products had approximately doubled.

Three main causes: (1) Population rise — between 1547 and 1603 the population of England increased from c.2.7 million to c.4 million, outstripping resources. (2) Poor harvests — made common by the Little Ice Age. (3) Bullion — huge quantities of gold and silver arriving in Europe from the New World decreased the value of coinage.

subheadings.label: Government responses
facts: Sir Thomas Gresham attempted to tackle inflation through recoinage in 1560. By 1561 the debased coins had been called in and the base alloys removed. However prices did not go down — merchants simply set the same prices, or higher.
Elizabeth encouraged her people to limit demand by encouraging fasting during Lent and the observance of 'fish days' on Wednesdays and Fridays. The 1586 Book of Orders prohibited hoarding of grain.

subheadings.label: Assessment
facts: Ultimately, the lack of understanding of how rising population affected supply and demand meant the government could not tackle the root causes of inflation. The government's interventions (recoinage, fish days, Book of Orders) addressed symptoms, not causes.

Inflation was a Europe-wide problem driven by global forces — New World bullion and population growth — that no single government could fully resolve. Elizabeth's government managed the symptoms as well as could be expected given the economic understanding of the time.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was inflation serious or managed?
facts: SERIOUS: Food prices tripled compared to Henry VII's reign.
SERIOUS: Population increased 48% (2.7m to 4m) - massive demographic pressure.
SERIOUS: Poor harvests common due to Little Ice Age.
SERIOUS: New World bullion devalued coinage across Europe.
SERIOUS: Recoinage failed to lower prices - merchants kept prices high.
SERIOUS: Government 'lacked understanding' - couldn't tackle root causes.
SERIOUS: Inflation accelerated in the 1560s - getting worse over reign.
MANAGED: There had been a decline in inflation by the start of Elizabeth's reign.
MANAGED: Recoinage in 1560 successfully removed debased coins by 1561.
MANAGED: Government took action - fish days, fasting during Lent to limit demand.
MANAGED: 1586 Book of Orders prohibited hoarding of grain.
MANAGED: Inflation was European-wide problem - not unique to England.
MANAGED: Gresham attempted to tackle inflation directly through recoinage.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs

heading: The cost of war

subheadings.label: Causes and scale of the war's cost
facts: Even before the outbreak of war with Spain in 1585, the ongoing Dutch Revolt negatively affected English trade — a 1576 mutiny by Spanish troops in Antwerp destroyed much of that city.
The Treaty of Nonsuch (1585) committed Elizabeth to £126,000 per year to support the Dutch rebels.
In total the war cost Elizabeth £4.5 million — approximately £2 million in the Netherlands, £2 million in Ireland, £500,000 supporting Henry of Navarre and £160,000 against the Armada.
Her hard-won surplus of £300,000 was used almost entirely in the first year of war.

subheadings.label: Benefits of war
facts: The war did bring some benefits. Flemings fleeing the Netherlands in 1566 brought improved cloth-making skills to England; French Huguenots fleeing persecution similarly brought manufacturing skills and trade.

Drake's circumnavigation (1577–80) returned £400,000 from Spanish ships and ports. His 1587 raid on Cadiz brought £140,000. The capture of the Madre de Dios in 1592 brought riches worth half the Crown's usual annual income.
The common enemy of Spain helped unite Parliament and Crown, producing unprecedented levels of parliamentary taxation — a double subsidy in 1589 and a triple subsidy in 1593.

subheadings.label: Failures and financial consequences
facts: Drake's 'English Armada' of 1589 against Spain was an unmitigated disaster. English attempts to intercept the treasure fleet routinely failed.
Elizabeth was forced to resort to monopolies to reward courtiers — contributing to price rises and great dissatisfaction in Parliament.
Crown land sales accelerated in the 1590s, depleting long-term Crown income.
By the end of the reign England was effectively bankrupt; the debts were passed to James I.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was the cost of war serious?
facts: SERIOUS: Total cost of £4.5 million - massive financial burden.
SERIOUS: £300,000 surplus used almost entirely in first year of war.
SERIOUS: Treaty of Nonsuch (1585) committed Elizabeth to £126,000 per year for Dutch rebels.
SERIOUS: £2 million spent in Netherlands, £2 million in Ireland.
SERIOUS: £500,000 supporting Henry of Navarre, £160,000 against Armada.
SERIOUS: Forced sale of more Crown lands in 1590s - weakened long-term finances.
SERIOUS: Forced use of monopolies - caused dissatisfaction and inflation.
SERIOUS: Drake's 1589 'English Armada' was 'unmitigated disaster'.
SERIOUS: Treasure fleet interception 'routinely failed'.
NOT SERIOUS: Some benefits gained (Flemings' skills, Madre de Dios riches).
NOT SERIOUS: Privateering victories provided income (£140,000 from Cadiz).
NOT SERIOUS: Madre de Dios (1592) brought half Crown's annual income.
NOT SERIOUS: Parliament granted unprecedented taxation (double 1589, triple 1593).
NOT SERIOUS: 'Common enemy of Spain helped unite Parliament and Crown'.
NOT SERIOUS: England survived war and emerged victorious.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs

heading: Overseas trade

subheadings.label: The Antwerp market and its collapse
facts: Prior to Elizabeth's reign, English trade had been reliant on the export of wool to the cloth market in Antwerp. However, the Dutch Revolt and war with Spain led to the collapse of the Antwerp market as well as trade embargoes with Spain that severely hampered English trade.
The 1576 Spanish Fury — mutiny of unpaid Spanish troops — destroyed much of Antwerp. Elizabeth's seizure of the Genoese Leon 1568 led to a Spanish trade embargo until 1573.
Cloth trade constituted 75% of English exports at the start of the reign. Outbreak of open war 1585 closed Spanish and Portuguese markets entirely.

subheadings.label: New trading companies
facts: Muscovy Company (1555): traded English cloth for Russian hides. However, complicated faction at court and the unpredictable attitudes of Ivan the Terrible made trade unreliable and profit limited. Eastland Company (1579): established a depot in Poland to trade in the Baltic, less successful — struggled against the German Hanseatic League's dominance.

Levant Company (1580): founded to trade with the eastern shores of the Mediterranean, particularly the Ottoman Empire — more successful than the Eastland Company. Attempts were made to create trade links with the Persian Empire but were scuppered by the Shah's refusal to trade with non-Muslims and complicated Ottoman-Persian tensions. Barbary Pirates operating from North Africa further hampered English trade in the Mediterranean.
East India Company (1600): founded to trade with India. Vital to future empire but too early for Elizabeth to directly benefit.
New companies partially compensated for the loss of Antwerp but never fully replaced it. Drake's circumnavigation (1577-80) returned £600,000 of plunder from Spanish ships and ports.

subheadings.label: Beyond Europe — the New World and Asia
facts: Americas dominated by Spain and Portugal. Sir John Hawkins established English involvement in the Transatlantic Slave Trade (1562) — capturing slaves in Sierra Leone and selling them in the Caribbean — still dominated by Spanish and Portuguese.
Raleigh's colonisation attempts at Roanoke Island failed in the 1580s. John Dee and Martin Frobisher failed to find a north-west passage to Asia.

Elizabeth herself was involved in the development of the Slave Trade. In 1596 the Privy Council gave permission for merchants to deport the hundreds of Black people living freely in England and sell them as slaves; despite slavery being illegal in England. In the end, this deportation never actually occurred.
By end of reign, 75% of English trade still with traditional European partners — new companies had not transformed the picture.

subheadings.label: Assessment
facts: English merchants showed adaptability in diversifying, but the underlying picture was of a trade damaged by war and political disruption.
The East India Company (1600) laid foundations for future empire but Elizabeth's reign saw limited results from trade beyond Europe.
War with Spain from 1585 damaged trade severely — the financial cost of conflict outweighed privateering gains for most merchants.

subheadings.label: Debate: Did trade improve or remain limited?
facts: IMPROVED: Muscovy Company (1555), Eastland Company (1579), Levant Company (1580), East India Company (1600) - diversification.
IMPROVED: Hawkins created Triangular Slave Trade (1562) - new revenue source.
IMPROVED: New markets in Russia, Baltic, Middle East, Asia.
IMPROVED: Foundations laid for future empire (East India Company).
IMPROVED: English merchants adapted to loss of Antwerp.
LIMITED: Antwerp market collapsed - lost main traditional market.
LIMITED: Spanish trade embargoes hampered English trade.
LIMITED: Roanoke colony failed - couldn't compete with Spain/Portugal in New World.
LIMITED: Spain and Portugal still dominated New World trade.
LIMITED: New companies were small and struggled to establish themselves.
LIMITED: 1596 deportation plans show ethical limitations of trade policy.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs

heading: Causes of poverty and vagrancy

subheadings.label: Population pressure
facts: Another consequence of the growing population (rising from 2.8 million in the 1540s to around 4.1 million by Elizabeth's death) was an increase in poverty and vagrancy. A surplus population led to increasing demand for work which allowed employers to lower wages. Simultaneously, landlords could raise rents.

subheadings.label: Dissolution removed safety net
facts: Henry VIII's Dissolution of the Monasteries had removed a key source of charitable provision for the poor — monasteries had provided food, shelter and care for the destitute. This safety net was not replaced until the Poor Law legislation of Elizabeth's reign.

subheadings.label: Discharged soldiers and sailors
facts: In the later years of Elizabeth's reign this was compounded by the wars with Spain and Ireland. Soldiers and sailors were discharged from service at arbitrary locations far from their homes, often with no pay and with serious injuries, adding to the numbers of destitute vagrants.

subheadings.label: Contemporary blame: enclosure
facts: Contemporaries blamed poverty on greedy landlords and the practice of enclosure. By 1600, in some areas over 70% of available arable land had been enclosed — though this varied greatly by region.

There is evidence that enclosure actually declined during Elizabeth's reign, as the collapse of the Dutch cloth market removed the gentry's main incentive to convert arable land to sheep farming. Those who blamed enclosure did not understand the true causes — rising population and bullion-driven inflation.

subheadings.label: Fear of vagrants
facts: Elizabethans were particularly afraid of vagrants. Ordinary people viewed vagrants as spreaders of disease and criminals. The government feared they would encourage social unrest — especially after the experience of 1549.

subheadings.label: The 1595-97 crisis
facts: The death rate increased by 50% at the peak of the 1595–97 crisis, when a series of bad harvests combined with the socioeconomic pressures of war, taxation and population growth to create the most serious crisis of the reign.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was poverty caused by government policy?
facts: GOV POLICY: Henry's Dissolution of the Monasteries removed charitable safety net.
GOV POLICY: Wars with Spain and Ireland discharged unpaid, injured soldiers as vagrants.
GOV POLICY: Elizabethan war taxation added pressure on already struggling population.
GOV POLICY: Enclosure (often by gentry/landlords) was a contemporary target of blame.
GOV POLICY: Government's response was 'particularly afraid of vagrants' - punitive rather than supportive.
GOV POLICY: Failure to provide welfare in early reign worsened poverty.
NOT GOV POLICY: Population growth (2.8m to 4.1m) was structural, not government caused.
NOT GOV POLICY: 1595-97 bad harvests were climatic, not government caused.
NOT GOV POLICY: Wage suppression by employers was market response to surplus labour.
NOT GOV POLICY: Enclosure was 'actually declining' by 1600 due to Dutch market collapse.
NOT GOV POLICY: 50% increase in death rate (1595-97) was disease/harvest related.
NOT GOV POLICY: Landlords raising rents was market behaviour, not government direction.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs

heading: Government responses to poverty

subheadings.label: 1563 Statute of Artificers
facts: 1563 Statute of Artificers – attempt to increase long-term employment and prevent vagrancy. Introduced compulsory seven-year apprenticeships for craftspeople. JPs set maximum regional wages and discouraged economic migration in search of work. However, the Act proved impossible to enforce.

subheadings.label: 1563 Alms Act
facts: 1563 Alms Act – the 'deserving poor' were to be supported by a Poor Rate organised by the Church. Contributions to the Poor Rate were not enforced by the state.

subheadings.label: 1572 Vagabonds Act
facts: 1572 Vagabonds Act – contributions to the Poor Rate made compulsory. Severe penalties enacted against vagrants and the 'undeserving/idle poor' including whipping, mutilation and, ultimately, execution.

subheadings.label: 1576 Act for Relief of the Poor (shift in attitude)
facts: 1576 Act for the Relief of the Poor – 'Able-bodied' poor would be provided work, often in a House of Correction. First example of the state recognising the 'undeserving poor' also require help, not punishment.

subheadings.label: 1598 Act for Relief of the Poor
facts: 1598 Act for the Relief of the Poor – begging was forbidden. JPs now appointed materials to employ the able-bodied poor.

subheadings.label: 1601 Poor Law
facts: 1601 Poor Law – the government assumed the responsibility of providing for the Poor Rate from the Church. Provisions of the 1598 Acts became permanent. They would last until the mid-19th century.

subheadings.label: Local responses
facts: Norwich, influenced by the experience of Kett's rebellion, banned begging and instead had the wealthiest citizens regularly contribute to a fund to support the poorest. Ipswich, Exeter and Cambridge introduced similar schemes.

Wealthy individuals contributed directly: Archbishops Parker and Whitgift contributed to almshouses; the Earl of Leicester established a hospital for the poor in Warwick. However, these efforts were ultimately limited and no substitute for effective central legislation.

subheadings.label: Debate: Change or continuity in attitudes to the poor?
facts: CHANGE: 1576 Act for Relief of the Poor recognised 'undeserving poor' need help, not just punishment.
CHANGE: 1601 Poor Law made state responsible (taking over from Church).
CHANGE: 1601 provisions lasted until mid-19th century - permanent shift.
CHANGE: Local innovation (Norwich, Ipswich, Exeter, Cambridge) - new community responses.
CHANGE: Move from charity to state responsibility - constitutional shift.
CHANGE: Poor Rate contributions made compulsory in 1572 - state intervention.
CONTINUITY: 1572 Vagabonds Act still included whipping, mutilation, execution - traditional brutality.
CONTINUITY: 1563 Statute of Artificers tried to control migration - traditional control.
CONTINUITY: Distinction between 'deserving' and 'undeserving' poor remained.
CONTINUITY: Government still feared vagrants as social threat.
CONTINUITY: Wage controls and apprenticeship requirements maintained old order.
CONTINUITY: 1563 Alms Act not enforced by state - voluntary continued.

unit: Unit 6 – Financial, Economic and Social Affairs

subheadings.label: The war's scope
facts: The war was fought in several theatres: in the Netherlands Elizabeth sent a force initially led by Leicester to support the Dutch rebels; at sea Elizabeth sanctioned privateers including Drake; in France she sent support to the Protestant Henry of Navarre; in Ireland Spain backed Tyrone's Rebellion.
The total financial cost was £4.5 million, using up Elizabeth's carefully accumulated surplus of £300,000 in the first year alone.

The war also intensified political tensions at home. In 1594 Dr Lopez, a Portuguese Jewish physician and one of Elizabeth's own doctors, was accused of being in league with Spain to poison the Queen. He was executed despite the plot being almost certainly fabricated — a sign of how war sharpened xenophobia and suspicion.

subheadings.label: The Spanish Armada (1588) — events
facts: Philip II sent a fearsome invasion force of 130 ships and 57,000 men. English fireships scattered the Armada at Calais. The Battle of Gravelines inflicted significant Spanish losses. Storms then destroyed over half the remaining fleet off Scotland and Ireland.

Elizabeth's Tilbury speech was a masterpiece of performance: 'I myself will take up arms, I myself will be your general' and 'I know I have the body of a weak, feeble woman; but I have the heart and stomach of a king, and of a king of England too.' The threat was already receding when she spoke.
Elizabeth promoted a commemorative medal: 'God blew, and they were scattered' — attributing victory to divine intervention and making the Armada a major propaganda triumph.

subheadings.label: After the Armada — successes and failures
facts: At sea, failure became common after the Armada. Drake's 'English Armada' of 1589 was an unmitigated disaster. English attempts to intercept the treasure fleet routinely failed.
However, the capture of the Madre de Dios in 1592 brought riches worth half the Crown's usual annual income.
Henry of Navarre's conversion to Catholicism and unilateral peace with Spain in 1598 negated much of what England had spent £500,000 and 10,000 troops to achieve.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was war with Spain serious?
facts: SERIOUS: Spanish Armada of 130 ships and 57,000 men sent to invade.
SERIOUS: Multiple theatres (Netherlands, sea, France, Ireland).
SERIOUS: Cost £4.5 million - financial catastrophe.
SERIOUS: Used up £300,000 surplus in first year.
SERIOUS: Drake's 'English Armada' of 1589 was 'unmitigated disaster'.
SERIOUS: Required emergency military mobilization (Tilbury).
SERIOUS: Spain supported Tyrone's Rebellion in Ireland - threat to British Isles.
NOT SERIOUS: Armada defeated through fireships, Gravelines, and storms.
NOT SERIOUS: Capture of Madre de Dios (1592) brought half Crown's annual income.
NOT SERIOUS: 'God blew, and they were scattered' - English propaganda victory.
NOT SERIOUS: Spain never managed to invade England.
NOT SERIOUS: England survived and emerged victorious by 1603.
NOT SERIOUS: Tilbury speech demonstrated Elizabeth's 'strength and leadership'.

subheadings.label: Monopolies
facts: Prior to 1585 Elizabeth had managed to govern without relying heavily on Parliament for revenue. After 1585, five of her ten Parliaments were called — the war with Spain forced reliance on parliamentary subsidies.

Monopolies were a result of Elizabeth's lack of finances in her later years — she could no longer bestow lavish gifts on courtiers. Instead she granted monopolies (exclusive trading rights) to chosen courtiers, who could then overcharge consumers, creating economic hardship.
In the 1597 Parliament, MPs publicly listed monopolies granted — including salt, starch, iron and vinegar. The scale of the grievance threatened to overwhelm parliamentary goodwill.

In 1601 Elizabeth annulled the most contentious monopolies and delivered the Golden Speech, skilfully reframing the concession as a demonstration of her love for her people. MPs left the session satisfied.

subheadings.label: Purveyance
facts: Purveyance was the monarch's customary right to purchase goods at below market value for the royal household. It was criticised by MPs in the Parliaments of 1589 and 1593.
Lord Burghley defended purveyance as part of the Royal Prerogative. Elizabeth privately agreed to investigate abuses but made no major concessions — the right was maintained intact.
By the 1597 Parliament the issue had dissipated — evidence of Elizabeth's tactics of deliberate delay working.

subheadings.label: Succession debates
facts: As Elizabeth entered her 60s in the 1590s, Parliament's attention returned to the succession. Peter Wentworth MP wrote a pamphlet calling on Parliament to examine candidates. Questioned by the Privy Council in 1591; sent to the Tower in 1593 — where he stayed until his death in 1596.
War provided a common enemy around which Crown and Parliament united. Parliament granted unprecedented taxation: a double subsidy in 1589 and a triple subsidy in 1593, secured by Burghley.

subheadings.label: Debate: Conflict or cooperation with Parliament?
facts: CONFLICT: MPs protested monopolies harmed common people.
CONFLICT: MPs argued monopolies 'infringed on Parliament's role in legislation'.
CONFLICT: Purveyance 'highly contentious' - criticised in 1589 and 1593 Parliaments.
CONFLICT: Wentworth imprisoned for pamphlet on succession (1591).
CONFLICT: Elizabeth's 'Golden Speech' (1601) had to concede monopolies needed reform.
CONFLICT: Elizabeth increasingly reliant on Parliament after 1585 - shifted balance.
COOPERATION: War provided 'common enemy around which Crown and Parliament united'.
COOPERATION: 1589 double subsidy granted - exceptional cooperation.
COOPERATION: 1593 triple subsidy secured by Burghley - more cooperation.
COOPERATION: Five of ten Parliaments called after 1585 - functional working relationship.
COOPERATION: 1601 Golden Speech ended Parliament well - reconciliation.
COOPERATION: Elizabeth maintained Royal Prerogative even while accepting reform.

subheadings.label: Background
facts: The English Crown had laid claim to Ireland since the 12th century, but by the 16th century English power was only truly felt in the Pale.
The Pale was a small region around Dublin where English law operated; beyond it, Gaelic lords ruled independently and resisted English domination.
Ireland's geography, language and religion made English control difficult. Gaelic culture and Catholicism were deeply entrenched.
Ulster and Connaught (north/west): ruled by Gaelic chieftains, opposed to English culture. Munster and Leinster (south/east): ruled by Anglo-Norman families who resented London. All were Catholic.
Ireland a persistent source of unrest — Fitzgerald Rebellions 1569–73 and 1579–83. Plantations in Munster attempted to increase control → unsuccessfully.

subheadings.label: Tyrone's Rebellion
facts: Hugh O'Neill, Earl of Tyrone, was the most capable Irish leader of his generation, commanding unprecedented military resources and loyalty among Irish lords.
Tyrone built a powerful coalition uniting most of Ulster and gaining support from Gaelic lords across Ireland who resented English colonization.
Tyrone won major military victories, most notably at Yellow Ford in 1598, which demonstrated his ability to defeat English forces in pitched battle.
From 1601, Philip III of Spain sent 4,000 troops to support Tyrone, landing at Kinsale. This was the first time an Irish rebellion received substantial foreign military support.
Tyrone was dangerous because he combined military capability, widespread Irish support, AND Spanish backing—creating an unprecedented unified threat to English rule.

subheadings.label: English Response
facts: In 1599, the Earl of Essex was appointed to crush the rebellion with 16,000 troops—the largest English force ever sent to Ireland. However, he failed to engage Tyrone decisively and returned to England without fighting a pitched battle.
Essex's failure and unauthorized return led to his own rebellion against Elizabeth and eventual execution, showing the high stakes of the Irish conflict.
Lord Mountjoy replaced Essex in 1600. Unlike Essex, Mountjoy combined military strategy with political acumen—he conciliated several Irish lords, splitting Tyrone's coalition.
Mountjoy employed a strategy of controlled conquest: securing supply lines, building forts, and gradually extending English control rather than seeking a single decisive battle.
By 1603, Mountjoy's superior strategy forced Tyrone to surrender, just days after Elizabeth's death. The Tyrone rebellion was definitively crushed.
Following defeat, Tyrone and the Ulster lords fled to Europe in the 'Flight of the Earls' (1607). This allowed the English to colonize Ulster with Protestant English and Scottish settlers.
In total it cost Elizabeth £2 million to defeat Tyrone's rebellion—a massive drain on royal finances.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was Tyrone's Rebellion serious?
facts: SERIOUS: Largest and most unified Irish rebellion combining military strength, widespread support, and foreign backing.
SERIOUS: Required England's largest military deployment to Ireland (16,000 under Essex).
SERIOUS: Cost £2 million - massive drain on Elizabeth's finances.
SERIOUS: Threatened to establish permanent Spanish presence in Ireland.
SERIOUS: Tyrone won at Yellow Ford 1598 - defeated English in pitched battle.
SERIOUS: First time Irish rebellion received substantial foreign support (4,000 Spanish troops).
SERIOUS: Essex's failure led to his own rebellion - destabilised English politics.
NOT SERIOUS: Tyrone never attempted to invade England itself.
NOT SERIOUS: Spanish intervention limited (4,000 troops) and late (1601).
NOT SERIOUS: Irish coalition fractured under English political pressure - Mountjoy peeled away lords.
NOT SERIOUS: England had superior military organization, supply lines, resources.
NOT SERIOUS: Once proper strategy applied, rebellion defeated in a few years.
NOT SERIOUS: Tyrone forced to surrender by 1603 - decisive English victory.

subheadings.label: Essex's rise
facts: Robert Devereux, Earl of Essex, rose to Elizabeth's court as the godson of Leicester and through his marriage to Walsingham's daughter. His wit, eloquence and dashing personality made him a favourite of the ageing Elizabeth in the 1590s.

In 1587 it was scandalously reported: 'at night my lord [Essex] is at cards or one game or another with her, that he cometh not to his own lodgings until the birds sing in the morning.' Many believed Essex reminded the ageing Elizabeth of the young Leicester.
Raised to the Privy Council in 1593 more for personality than political skill. His arrogance clashed repeatedly with the more pragmatic Robert Cecil.

subheadings.label: Rivalry with the Cecils
facts: On the Privy Council, Essex's flamboyant arrogance often clashed with the more pragmatic and capable Lord Burghley and his son, Robert Cecil.

In the 1590s, following Leicester's death and due to Burghley's dotage, both Essex and Robert Cecil competed to be the principal figure on the Privy Council. In 1596, during Essex's expedition to Cadiz, Robert Cecil became Elizabeth's Secretary of State, thus securing control over the government.

The war exacerbated faction between the conservative, reactive councillors led by Burghley and Robert Cecil and the younger, more hawkish councillors led by Essex which created a lack of coherent policy.

subheadings.label: Unilateral actions
facts: Essex frequently acted without authorisation: he joined Drake's English Armada against Elizabeth's direct orders in 1589; disobeyed orders in France in 1592.
His burning of Cadiz in 1596 made him enormously popular across England — giving him an independent power base that made him harder to manage.

subheadings.label: Disgrace in Ireland (1599)
facts: In the 1590s, Essex was jealous of loss of power. Initially refused to go to Ireland on Elizabeth's orders before being slapped — and half drawing his sword.
In Ireland 1599, led 16,000 men but never fought a battle; returned to London without permission. Defiant return enraged Elizabeth → placed under house arrest.
Under house arrest, Essex lost his monopoly over sweet wines. Mountjoy's success in crushing the Tyrone Rebellion further disgraced him.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was Essex managed or not managed?
facts: MANAGED: Robert Cecil outmaneuvered Essex - became Secretary of State while Essex at Cadiz.
