MANAGED: Elizabeth tolerated Essex's behaviour - kept him in favour as long as useful.
MANAGED: Cecil faction ultimately controlled government 'unopposed' after 1601.
MANAGED: Essex's unilateral actions didn't fundamentally change policy.
MANAGED: Essex remained a courtier despite challenges - integrated in system.
NOT MANAGED: 'Lack of coherent policy' due to faction between Cecil and Essex.
NOT MANAGED: Essex acted unilaterally multiple times against Elizabeth's orders.
NOT MANAGED: 1589 joining Drake's Armada against direct orders.
NOT MANAGED: 1592 disobeyed orders re Henry IV.
NOT MANAGED: Essex's popularity gave him independent power base.
NOT MANAGED: Faction ultimately ended in Essex's rebellion - failure of management.

subheadings.label: Essex's fall from grace
facts: During discussions over dealing with Tyrone's Rebellion, Essex reacted angrily to suggestions about who should command. He was sent to Ireland in 1599, led 16,000 men but never fought a battle, and returned to London without permission. His defiant return enraged Elizabeth and he was placed under house arrest.

Whilst in house arrest, Essex lost his monopoly over sweet wines — his main source of income. He controversially commissioned a performance of Shakespeare's Richard II, which ends with a childless monarch being deposed by a noble. He also made contact with James VI of Scotland, attempting to become James's key advisor following Elizabeth's planned deposition.

subheadings.label: The rebellion and aftermath
facts: In desperation to reclaim his former position, on 8 February 1601 Essex led a band of supporters including the Earl of Southampton into the City of London attempting to raise a popular rebellion. Most of his supporters got cold feet and did not materialise. The rebellion was quickly and easily defeated.
Essex and just five supporters were executed for treason in 1601. From then on, Robert Cecil's faction controlled government unopposed — managing the smooth transition to James I in 1603.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was Essex's rebellion serious?
facts: SERIOUS: An armed rebellion against the regime in 1601.
SERIOUS: Involved senior nobility (Earl of Southampton).
SERIOUS: Commissioned Richard II performance - openly suggesting deposition.
SERIOUS: Essex compared himself to Richard II - planned regime change.
SERIOUS: Resulted in executions of leading figures including Essex himself.
SERIOUS: Showed how courtly favourites could turn into rebels.
NOT SERIOUS: 'Almost immediately defeated' - lasted hours, not days.
NOT SERIOUS: Most supporters 'got cold feet' - lacked broad support.
NOT SERIOUS: Essex and just five supporters executed - small scale.
NOT SERIOUS: Acted in 'desperation' rather than from strength.
NOT SERIOUS: Cecil faction emerged stronger - confirmed existing power balance.
NOT SERIOUS: Cecil managed smooth transition to James VI in 1603 - government continued.

subheadings.label: Persistent inflation and bad harvests
facts: Despite efforts to manage the problem earlier in her reign, inflation persisted into the end of Elizabeth's reign. A series of bad harvests from 1594–98 led to the average price of wheat doubling. Cheaper grains like oats and rye increased in price at an even faster rate. At the peak of the crisis in 1595–97 the death rate increased by 50%.

subheadings.label: War taxation pressures
facts: During the war with Spain, Parliament approved unprecedented levels of taxation in 1589 and 1593. Tax collectors found it increasingly difficult to collect the full amount as the population was unable to pay. Elizabeth's granting of monopolies to her favourites often increased prices on staple goods.

subheadings.label: Food riots and unrest
facts: Food shortages and poverty led to widespread unrest. Between 1595–98 there were food riots in Kent, Sussex, Somerset and Norfolk. Bands of roving unemployed men, many of them discharged soldiers, further threatened order.

subheadings.label: The Oxfordshire Rising (1596)
facts: The most notable example was the Oxfordshire Rising of 1596 — ostensibly a protest against enclosure, it came at the peak of the food crisis. The plot was discovered and the five ringleaders were publicly tried and executed as traitors. In the end only four people actually turned up — suggesting the threat of unrest was greater than the actual unrest.

subheadings.label: Government legislation
facts: Government action: the 1597 Tillage Act was passed to reverse any enclosure carried out since 1588. The 1598 Acts for the Relief of the Poor and Punishment of Rogues codified the distinction between deserving and undeserving poor. The 1601 Poor Law made these provisions permanent.

Books of Orders were issued to attempt localised quarantines when plague spread alongside the food crisis in 1596-97. These were often ignored or not understood by local authorities — a sign of central government's limited reach.

subheadings.label: Local responses
facts: Local responses were often more innovative than central government — Norwich, influenced by the experience of Kett's rebellion, had banned begging and created a community fund. The contrast between effective local action and sluggish central response revealed the structural limits of Elizabethan government.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was socioeconomic unrest of the 1590s serious?
facts: SERIOUS: Wheat prices doubled, oats and rye even faster.
SERIOUS: Death rate increased 50% at peak (1595-97).
SERIOUS: Food riots in multiple counties (Kent, Sussex, Somerset, Norfolk).
SERIOUS: Bands of roving unemployed men, including discharged soldiers, threatened order.
SERIOUS: Oxfordshire Rising 1596 - ringleaders executed as traitors.
SERIOUS: Inflation 'persisted into end of reign' despite earlier efforts.
SERIOUS: Required major legislation (1597 Tillage Act, 1598 Acts, 1601 Poor Law).
NOT SERIOUS: Oxfordshire Rising only had 'four people actually turn up' - threat greater than reality.
NOT SERIOUS: Government effectively suppressed unrest (executions, legislation).
NOT SERIOUS: No national rebellion emerged - localized riots only.
NOT SERIOUS: 1601 Poor Law provided lasting solution to the poverty problem.
NOT SERIOUS: Regime survived crisis - no threat to Elizabeth's rule.

subheadings.label: Managing her image
facts: As with other monarchs, Elizabeth's power relied on her image. It was important that Elizabeth seemed strong and divinely ordained. Annual Accession Day celebrations reinforced this.
In 1596 the Privy Council ordered the destruction of any 'unseemly and improper' portraits of Elizabeth — all had to be based on an agreed, flattering Mask of Youth template.

Portraits like the Rainbow Portrait used heavy symbolism to enhance Elizabeth's image — she holds a rainbow (symbol of peace and divine favour); on her sleeve a serpent (wisdom); her cloak covered in eyes and ears (omniscience).

subheadings.label: Challenges to her image
facts: As Elizabeth entered her 60s, her looks diminished. Her fondness for sugar had blackened her teeth; her grey hair was hidden by a bright red wig; her face was caked in white lead make-up. The cracks in the Mask of Youth were starting to show.

A series of scandals undermined Elizabeth's image at court. Walter Raleigh's disgrace for making Bess Throckmorton pregnant damaged the courtly image. Essex's defiance and ultimate rebellion further damaged the regime in its final years.

subheadings.label: Popular criticism and the Golden Speech
facts: The socioeconomic unrest of the 1590s led to increased popular criticism — some commented 'We shall never have a merry world while the queen liveth'. The contrast between official image and reality became impossible to sustain for those who saw her in person on progress.

In her final parliament of 1601, Elizabeth made her famous Golden Speech, annulling the most contentious monopolies and framing the concession as a demonstration of her love for her people. Many MPs were reduced to tears. It was seen as a glorious end of an era.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was Elizabeth's reputation managed or dangerous?
facts: MANAGED: Annual Accession Day celebrations reinforced divine ordination.
MANAGED: 1596 Privy Council order destroyed 'unseemly' portraits - controlled image.
MANAGED: Mask of Youth template ensured consistent flattering image.
MANAGED: Rainbow Portrait used sophisticated symbolism (peace, wisdom, omniscience).
MANAGED: Image of strength carefully cultivated despite ageing.
MANAGED: Smooth succession to James in 1603 - image lasted beyond death.
DANGEROUS: Looks diminished in 60s - 'cracks in Mask of Youth' showing.
DANGEROUS: Blackened teeth, grey hair hidden by wig, white lead make-up.
DANGEROUS: Raleigh scandal (Bess Throckmorton) damaged courtly image.
DANGEROUS: Essex's defiance and rebellion damaged regime in final years.
DANGEROUS: Popular criticism - 'We shall never have a merry world while the queen liveth'.
DANGEROUS: Contrast between managed image and 1590s suffering undermined popularity.

heading: Ideological differences and attitudes by 1941

subheadings.label: The Bolshevik Revolution and Russian Civil War
facts: The Bolshevik Revolution of October 1917 led to civil war in Russia between the 'reds' and the 'whites'. The revolutionary government sought peace, alienating Britain, the USA, France and Japan, who had been Russia's allies. These powers were hostile to the aims and ideology of the new Russian regime led by Lenin.
The Russian Civil War created bitterness and the new Union of Soviet Socialist Republics was deeply divided from the Western powers.

subheadings.label: Ideology — Marxism
facts: Lenin and the Bolsheviks were inspired by Karl Marx (1818–83), who believed that more advanced industrial countries would experience revolution and that the collapse of capitalism was inevitable.

Just as the new industrial middle class had replaced the aristocracy, so they in turn would be replaced by the industrial workers (proletariat). First a working-class dictatorship would be established; then the state would wither away and there would be a community of equals, an ideal classless society.

subheadings.label: Capitalism versus communism
facts: Marx saw capitalism as a system of exploitation. Money was invested in businesses (capital), with bosses and investors needing profits to invest more, possible only by exploiting workers.

Defenders of capitalism pointed out that invested money created jobs, social and economic opportunities, prosperity and healthy competition, which helped consumers. They also linked the economic freedom to invest with political freedom.

subheadings.label: Western intervention in the Civil War
facts: Western powers continued to see Communist Russia as an enemy. They had been shocked by the murder of the Tsar and his family, and by the Bolshevik hopes of world revolution promoted by the Comintern, an international organisation founded to promote Communism.
Britain, USA, France and Japan all intervened in the Russian Civil War (1917–22) on the side of the Whites — a direct military invasion that Stalin never forgot.
Comintern (1919) confirmed Western fears the USSR sought to export revolution. Stalin's 1930s show trials reinforced the Western image of a brutal dictatorship.
Munich (1938) convinced Stalin the West wanted Germany and the USSR to destroy each other — explaining the Nazi-Soviet Pact (1939) as a defensive move.

subheadings.label: The interwar years
facts: The rise of fascism in Germany and Italy led to a big political divide in Europe. The USSR remained isolated. Stalin pursued dramatic industrialisation policies accompanied by severe repression of the Russian people and purges of the Communist party. This seemed dangerous to many in the West.

Stalin's attempt to unite all left-wing groups against Nazism by creating a Popular Front only worried conservative opinion. His support for the Spanish Communists during the Civil War in Spain (1936–39) led to fears.
Driven by a need to protect the USSR, Stalin signed a pact with Hitler in August 1939 — the Nazi-Soviet Pact. This seemed to show that communism had more in common with fascism than democracy.

subheadings.label: The situation by 1941
facts: When WW2 broke out in 1939, Stalin regained lost lands in the Baltic states and Poland, subjecting them to tyrannous repression. The West sympathised with Finland, which resisted occupation in the Winter War of 1939–40. Indeed Britain seriously contemplated declaring war on both the USSR and Germany.

By 1941 hostility between USSR and the West was well established: deep ideological differences; the West feared Russian influence; the USSR resented exclusion from 1930s diplomacy; the West despised the Nazi-Soviet Pact and Russian expansion in Eastern Europe.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was ideology or security the main cause of long-term tensions?
facts: IDEOLOGY: Marxism-Leninism explicitly sought to overthrow capitalism — a permanent existential threat to the West.
IDEOLOGY: Comintern (1919) promoted world revolution — confirmed Western states were targets, not just rivals.
IDEOLOGY: West intervened in Russian Civil War 1917–22 on side of the Whites — the hostility was ideological from the start.
IDEOLOGY: Nazi-Soviet Pact 1939 — showing communism and fascism had more in common than democracy — a profound ideological shock.
IDEOLOGY: Stalin's purges and show trials reinforced Western image of USSR as a brutal ideological dictatorship.
SECURITY: USSR sought a buffer zone — invaded Poland in 1939 as a security move, not an ideological one.
SECURITY: Stalin only joined the Grand Alliance against Hitler — shared security interests overrode ideology.
SECURITY: Western alliance with Stalin 1941–45 showed security could trump ideological hostility.
SECURITY: Munich 1938 convinced Stalin the West wanted Germany and the USSR to destroy each other.
SECURITY: All Soviet actions in Eastern Europe after 1945 were framed in terms of security buffer against invasion.

unit: Chapter 1 – Origins of the Cold War to 1945

heading: Wartime tensions in the Grand Alliance

subheadings.label: The unexpected alliance
facts: The Grand Alliance comprised Britain, the USA and the USSR, against the Axis powers (Germany, Italy, Japan). Britain stood alone against Germany and Italy from 1940 to 1941. In June 1941, German forces invaded the USSR. Putting all ideological differences aside, Churchill offered support.
The alliance was joined by the USA after Japan attacked Pearl Harbor in December 1941. The events of war brought about an unexpected alliance between communist Russia and the capitalist West.

The USA and Britain had pledged their support for democracy in the Atlantic Charter (August 1941) — affirming self-determination, political freedom and freedom of speech. The USSR endorsed it but played no part in drafting it. Stalin resented being presented with Western liberal values as a condition of alliance, demonstrating the fundamental incompatibility of Western and Soviet war aims from the outset.

subheadings.label: The second front dispute
facts: The German invasion of 1941 took the USSR by surprise, with millions of casualties. Only a determined effort stopped the Germans taking Moscow and Leningrad (St Petersburg). In 1942 the USSR faced a further threat at Stalingrad.

Stalin looked to a British and US invasion of northern France for relief. German defences were not yet strong in northern France and the war in Russia took huge German resources. Invading and creating a second front would threaten Hitler with war on two fronts.

Yet, despite Russian pleas and the support of leading US commanders, no second front was created until June 1944. British leaders believed it would be too risky after the Dieppe failure in 1942. Instead British and US efforts focused first on North Africa, then on Sicily and Italy in 1943.

Soviet Foreign Minister Gromyko later argued the Cold War began as a 'secret Cold War' when the Allies delayed the second front. The suspicion in the USSR was that the capitalist West wanted the dictatorships to fight each other to a standstill.

subheadings.label: The Russian advance, 1943–45
facts: After the German failure at Stalingrad in February 1943, the Russians went on the offensive. This opened up the possibility of Russian expansion in Eastern Europe.
Stalin's decision not to support a Polish uprising in Warsaw in 1944 — allowing the Germans to destroy resistance before Russia moved in to take the city — alarmed the West.

It seemed that Stalin was happy to see German forces destroy Polish patriots because this would make future Soviet control of Poland easier. This followed revelations of a Soviet massacre of influential Polish officers and leaders in Katyn Forest in 1940.

subheadings.label: Limits of military cooperation
facts: Britain and the USA collaborated closely in the war, the high point being D-Day, the joint invasion of France in June 1944. Though supplies and aid had gone to Russia, there were no similar joint military operations.

Britain and the USA did not share the key military secret of the war — the development of atomic weapons — with the USSR. For its part, the USSR did not until the very end of the war join in the struggle against Japan.

Relations between alliance members remained strained: the USA disliked the idea of a war that strengthened the British Empire. Churchill feared Russian expansion. Stalin felt the West did not understand the scale of Russian losses.

subheadings.label: Debate: Which caused more tension — the second front dispute or the liberation of Eastern Europe?
facts: SECOND FRONT: Stalin felt the USSR was fighting the bulk of the war alone — 25 million Soviet dead compared to ~400,000 American.
SECOND FRONT: Delay from 1942 to 1944 — Gromyko said the Cold War began as a 'secret Cold War when the Allies delayed the second front'.
SECOND FRONT: Churchill preferred Balkans invasion — Stalin believed this was deliberate to limit Soviet influence.
SECOND FRONT: Dieppe failure 1942 (Allies) used to justify delay — Soviet view: cowardice and bad faith.
LIBERATION: Liberation of Eastern Europe was irreversible — Soviet annexation of 470,000 sq km, 90 million people.
LIBERATION: Second front dispute was resolved by D-Day 1944. Liberation of Eastern Europe created permanent Cold War division.
LIBERATION: Stalin's refusal to support Warsaw Uprising 1944 showed deliberate strategy, not just defensive security.
LIBERATION: Annexation of Baltic states, Poland, Romania contradicted the Atlantic Charter — permanent breach.
LIBERATION: The difference in 'liberation' methods between East and West was the most significant factor in long-term Cold War hostility.
LIBERATION: Western intervention in Greece showed the West also had double standards — but at far smaller scale.

unit: Chapter 1 – Origins of the Cold War to 1945

heading: Tensions at the Tehran Conference 1943

subheadings.label: The first Big Three meeting
facts: Churchill, Stalin and Roosevelt met together for the first time at Tehran, from 28 November to 1 December 1943.
By this time, the tide had turned after British victories in the Mediterranean and Russian advances following the German defeat at Stalingrad.
The Tehran Conference was a major turning point in the re-emergence of Russia as a major world power.

subheadings.label: The United Nations
facts: Roosevelt and Stalin discussed how the new UN would work, with the key roles of the 'four policemen' — Britain, the USA, the USSR and China — ensuring peace.
This gave the USSR an importance in the new organisation that it had never had in the old League of Nations.

subheadings.label: Poland and the Baltic
facts: Agreed that post-war Poland would be redrawn so that the boundary would be the Oder-Neisse Rivers. This involved moving the boundaries westwards, giving Russia the territories in eastern Poland it had occupied in 1939–40.
This was a sign that Russia would keep the lands it had taken and that the older boundaries of pre-1917 Russia would be restored.

Russia would also keep the Baltic states of Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia, made independent after World War I. This was hugely significant as Britain had gone to war in 1939 in defence of Poland but now was accepting a major change in its boundaries.

subheadings.label: Japan, France and Germany
facts: Roosevelt secured Stalin's agreement to declare war on Japan at a future date in return for territories — South Sakhalin, the Kurile Islands and access to Port Arthur.

The invasion of northern France by Britain and the USA was agreed for May 1944. Churchill would have preferred an invasion of the Balkans but the pressure was now irresistible. Stalin agreed to mount a major attack at the same time to distract German forces. This met Stalin's demand for a second front.
The conference discussed the future partition of Germany, which would be raised at the Moscow Conference (December 1945).

subheadings.label: Winners and losers
facts: Roosevelt had gained Russian support against Japan and had taken Britain away from a Balkan invasion to the policy favoured by the USA, of an invasion of northern France. He had established good personal relations with Stalin.

Stalin's military victories in 1943 gave him prestige. He gained the Allies' acceptance of expansion into Eastern Europe and an agreement for a second front in northern Europe. The USSR was set to play a much greater part in international affairs in the future United Nations. He had also divided Roosevelt and Churchill — their personal relations at Tehran were much less close than they had been.

Churchill felt slighted by private meetings during the conference between Roosevelt and Stalin and by Roosevelt's coolness towards him. Britain was committed to a second front despite Churchill's grave misgivings. Large areas of Poland were to be given to Russia, which was a blow to Britain's prestige as it had gone to war in 1939 specifically to defend Polish independence against Germany.

subheadings.label: The Percentages Agreement (October 1944)
facts: October 1944: Churchill brokered a secret deal with Stalin dividing Eastern Europe — Romania 90% Soviet, Greece 90% British, Hungary and Yugoslavia 50/50.
Churchill scribbled the percentages on a piece of paper and pushed it to Stalin, who ticked it. Churchill called it a 'naughty document'.
Never formally enacted — USA would not have agreed. Revealed Churchill and Stalin were already dividing Europe, undermining Western claims to be fighting for self-determination.

subheadings.label: Debate: How significant was Tehran for the development of the Cold War?
facts: VERY SIGNIFICANT: Accepted Soviet expansion into Eastern Europe — set precedent for post-war settlement.
VERY SIGNIFICANT: Agreed Poland would be moved westward — Britain had gone to war in 1939 specifically to defend Polish independence.
VERY SIGNIFICANT: Re-established Russia as a major world power — restored pre-1917 territories (Baltic states, eastern Poland).
VERY SIGNIFICANT: Created tensions between Roosevelt and Churchill that weakened Western unity.
VERY SIGNIFICANT: Set UN framework giving USSR a role it had never had in the League of Nations.
LIMITED: Most cooperative of the three wartime conferences — common enemy still dominated.
LIMITED: Vague agreements — real disputes about Poland, Germany and reparations only emerged at Yalta and Potsdam.
LIMITED: No formal division of Europe agreed — Percentages Agreement (Oct 1944) was separate, secret and never enacted.
LIMITED: Yalta and Potsdam more significant — they dealt with the actual post-war settlement.
LIMITED: Stalin's promises at Tehran (free elections, Japan) seemed credible — breakdown came later.

unit: Chapter 1 – Origins of the Cold War to 1945

heading: Tensions at Yalta and Potsdam 1945

subheadings.label: Yalta context (4–11 February 1945)
facts: By the time the Yalta Conference took place there were more tensions between East and West. Churchill was concerned about the growing power of the USSR as its forces controlled Eastern Europe.
Stalin wanted the West to accept that Russian future security needed a broad zone of Eastern Europe that the USSR could control as a barrier against invasion.

subheadings.label: Poland at Yalta
facts: Stalin saw the pro-Soviet Lublin Committee as the true representatives of Poland. Churchill feared these Stalinists would exclude the democratic Polish representatives in London.
It was agreed to enlarge the Lublin government and hold free elections. There was little to guarantee, however, that Stalin would actually allow this.

subheadings.label: Germany at Yalta
facts: Stalin wanted to take German machinery, food and goods. Churchill and the USA disagreed, doubting the wisdom of millions of poor and starving people at the heart of Europe.

Germany would be divided into four zones of occupation. Churchill had insisted France have a zone, as the USA would withdraw after the war and leave Britain alone to face the USSR. Stalin initially refused to give France a say in running occupied Germany, but did finally agree.

$20 billion in reparations agreed overall — half to the USSR. However the 15% agreement (whereby the West would send 15% of its reparations to the Soviet zone in exchange for food and raw materials) broke down immediately at Potsdam.

subheadings.label: United Nations and Japan at Yalta
facts: Stalin wanted greater representation by the individual republics of the USSR, fearful the UN would become anti-Soviet. Roosevelt saw the UN as the hope for the future, but Stalin feared it might become anti-communist.
Stalin agreed to declare war on Japan but demanded more than at Tehran, including railway rights in Chinese Manchuria and access to the Chinese port of Darien. Roosevelt was forced to agree.

subheadings.label: The Potsdam Conference (July–August 1945)
facts: With 10 million Soviet troops deployed in Europe, there was little to be done if Stalin imposed his will on Eastern Europe. Yalta had shown weaknesses on the part of Britain and the USA in meeting Russian demands and this resulted in a more difficult summit at Potsdam.
The new president Harry S Truman was more suspicious of Stalin and the USSR's ambitions.
Churchill had been voted out of office mid-conference. Labour PM Attlee lacked Churchill's rapport with Stalin, and his foreign secretary Ernest Bevin was hostile to communism.
Aid to the USSR under the Lend-Lease scheme was cut off by the USA on 8 May and restored until September only after Russian protests.
It was clear Stalin did not intend to share power in Poland. The arrest of 16 non-communists who had gone back to Warsaw hoping to take part in free elections was worrying.
There was also the issue of the atomic bomb, which Truman mentioned to Stalin — though the Russians were already aware of the new weapon's development through espionage.

subheadings.label: Germany at Potsdam
facts: There would be an Allied Control Commission made up of military commanders of the four zones. The Soviets, however, insisted on complete control of their own zone. There was little overall government for Germany.

Reparations were agreed on, but the policies were very different in each zone. An agreement that 15% of reparations from the West would go to the Russian zone in return for food and raw materials did not work.

subheadings.label: Eastern Europe at Potsdam
facts: There was no firm agreement on the western frontier and this was left for a future peace conference.
The Western powers supported elections in Soviet-held territory in Poland, Hungary, Romania and Bulgaria — but there was no means of enforcing this.
There was agreement but many issues were unresolved and Potsdam did not result in any general peace settlement.

subheadings.label: Debate: Did Yalta or Potsdam do more to cause the Cold War?
facts: YALTA MORE RESPONSIBLE: Set vague framework on 'free elections' and 'sphere of influence' — ambiguity allowed Soviet takeover.
YALTA MORE RESPONSIBLE: Roosevelt accepted Russian domination of Eastern Europe — too eager to secure Soviet entry against Japan.
YALTA MORE RESPONSIBLE: Vague language on Poland gave Stalin cover for breaking agreements.
YALTA MORE RESPONSIBLE: $20 billion reparations agreement created the conflicting economic frameworks that poisoned German occupation.
YALTA MORE RESPONSIBLE: 'Sphere of influence' terminology legitimised Soviet domination — Western leaders gave it away.
POTSDAM MORE RESPONSIBLE: Truman/Attlee/Bevin — new leaders with no rapport with Stalin, more confrontational tone.
POTSDAM MORE RESPONSIBLE: Stalin had already installed communist government in Poland — breaking Yalta promises before Potsdam.
POTSDAM MORE RESPONSIBLE: Atomic bomb raised by Truman — fundamentally changed power dynamic.
POTSDAM MORE RESPONSIBLE: No general peace settlement — failure to resolve key issues guaranteed ongoing conflict.
POTSDAM MORE RESPONSIBLE: 15% reparations agreement broke down immediately — practical cooperation impossible.

unit: Chapter 1 – Origins of the Cold War to 1945

heading: The liberation of Europe in East and West

subheadings.label: Soviet motives for domination
facts: The suffering of the USSR had been considerably greater during the war than that of the USA and Britain. When the Red Army moved into Eastern Europe, it was to impose Russian domination and to take revenge on its enemies.
This was partly a result of the brutalisation brought by the regime and partly in pursuit of restoring traditional Russian spheres of influence and ensuring future Russian security.
The difference in ideologies between East and West also made it seem that the expansion was motivated by a desire to export Marxism-Leninism.

subheadings.label: Western liberation
facts: The first area to be liberated was Italy. The removal of Mussolini in 1943 helped the Allies see Italy as an ally rather than as an enemy, and Italian opponents of fascism assisted the Allied advance.
The Allied forces in France, the Low Countries and Denmark were seen as liberators. They brought much-needed supplies to areas short of food.
There was clearly no thought of annexing territory or imposing an ideology in these areas.
The situation was more complex in Greece, where Britain supported the royalists in a civil war from 1944 to prevent a communist state.
The invasion of Germany by Western forces saw hard-fought conflict but not a war of revenge or reprisal. Once fighting stopped, aid was given to German civilians.

subheadings.label: Eastern liberation — revenge
facts: The experience in Eastern Europe was very different. The larger Soviet forces inflicted a much harsher retribution on Germany and its allies.
There were terrible reprisals against civilians and the Soviet army was guilty of indiscriminate sexual assaults on females. There was also plunder and removal of goods and machinery.
There was also deportation of prisoners for work in the USSR and the forced removal of ethnic Germans from annexed territories.

subheadings.label: Annexation in Eastern Europe
facts: Pre-1918 Russian territories were restored to Russian control and opposition suppressed. The Baltic states and eastern Poland, taken illegally in 1939–40, returned to Russian control.

The presence of the Red Army in Eastern Europe had quite different significance to that of the armies of Britain and the USA in the West. It led to direct annexation of territory in Poland, Finland, the Baltic states, Germany, Czechoslovakia and Romania.
Russia regained an area of 470,000 square km and 24 million people. This had no parallel in the West.

subheadings.label: Political influence
facts: As well as direct annexation, there was the spread of Russian political domination in nations that were nominally independent but in practice dominated by the USSR. This was on a large scale — over 1 million square km and 90 million people.

Soviet forces supported a coup in Romania in 1945, forcing the king to appoint a communist government. They installed a coalition in Hungary, which included communists who would later take over the state.

Soviet forces controlled Bulgaria in a special Allied Control Council. In Poland, Soviet forces established a National Liberation Committee, which had communist influence out of all proportion to the support the communist parties enjoyed in Poland.
In Czechoslovakia, negotiations between the communists and other groups were strengthened by the Soviet military presence. In Germany, the Soviet forces created a new left-wing party, the SED.

There was widespread political repression and control; 47,000 anti-communist Poles were arrested in 1944–45. There was also much less direct aid given to the peoples of Eastern Europe than was the case in the West.

subheadings.label: Debate: Who bears more responsibility for the Cold War — Soviet actions in Eastern Europe or Western counter-measures?
facts: USSR MORE RESPONSIBLE: Annexed 470,000 sq km and 90m more people under political domination — no parallel in Western liberation.
USSR MORE RESPONSIBLE: 47,000 anti-communist Poles arrested 1944–45 before any Western counter-measure.
USSR MORE RESPONSIBLE: Red Army rape, plunder and deportation in Eastern Europe had no equivalent in Western zones.
USSR MORE RESPONSIBLE: Romanian elections rigged to deliver 80% for communists — direct violation of Atlantic Charter.
USSR MORE RESPONSIBLE: Poland's communist government installed before Potsdam — broke Yalta promises immediately.
WEST MORE RESPONSIBLE: Truman Doctrine (1947) committed USA to opposing communism globally — provocative overreach.
WEST MORE RESPONSIBLE: Marshall Aid was 'dollar diplomacy' — designed to peel satellite states away from the USSR.
WEST MORE RESPONSIBLE: Western counter-measures forced Stalin to consolidate control he might otherwise have relaxed.
WEST MORE RESPONSIBLE: NATO (1949) was a military alliance that justified Soviet fears of encirclement.
WEST MORE RESPONSIBLE: Churchill's Percentages Agreement (1944) showed West also willing to divide Europe into spheres.

unit: Chapter 1 – Origins of the Cold War to 1945

heading: Relations between Stalin, Churchill and Roosevelt (and later Truman and Attlee)

subheadings.label: Churchill and Roosevelt
facts: Churchill and Roosevelt became personally close 1941–43. Churchill was anxious to keep on good terms with the USA and travelled to Canada to meet Roosevelt, even agreeing to an Atlantic Charter of shared democratic principles, which Britain did not apply to its overseas empire.

When Hitler declared war on the USA, Churchill was quick to reinforce their friendship and gain US commitment to the war in Europe, and to persuade the USA that the British strategy was the right one.

By 1943, however, despite the apparent warmth, the USA was having doubts about the way Britain was fighting the war and its focus on North Africa and the Mediterranean. Roosevelt was afraid the USA would be fighting a war for the British Empire that restricted US trade opportunities and ran counter to its beliefs in freedom.
The US influence on the conduct of the war increased and the USA dominated the D-Day invasion and the war in northern France and Germany 1944–45.

subheadings.label: Churchill and Stalin
facts: Churchill was anxious to establish good relations with the USSR once the Germans invaded Russia in 1941. In his dealings with Stalin there was a remarkable amount of mutual respect and even goodwill.

Years of past hostility to communism and underlying fears that Russia would dominate Europe made the relationship strained. Churchill was unwilling to agree to Stalin's demands for a second front and was increasingly alarmed about the advance of Russian forces after 1943.
Britain had gone to war to defend Poland and yet by 1944 was having to accept its domination by the USSR.

In October 1944 Churchill went to Moscow to try and broker a deal and secured the so-called Percentages Agreement, that Eastern Europe would be divided between Russia and the West into spheres of influence. This showed the contempt both leaders had for the wishes of the people of Eastern Europe. It was never put into practice, as the USA would not have agreed.

subheadings.label: Roosevelt and Stalin
facts: Roosevelt was less concerned with the possible domination of Eastern Europe. He believed that he could get deals with Stalin over elections in Russian-occupied territories and needed Russia to enter the war against Japan, which was taking an increasingly heavy toll on US forces.

By 1945 Roosevelt had accepted Russian domination of Eastern Europe; the division of Germany was agreed, as was a new United Nations organisation for peace, but with safeguards against any possible condemnation of Russian actions.
Churchill had realised that Britain could no longer exert the major influence on world affairs.

subheadings.label: New leaders — Truman and Attlee
facts: The changes in leadership after Yalta brought new leaders. Roosevelt died in April 1945 and Churchill lost the election of 1945. The new leaders were Labour PM Clement Attlee and US vice president Harry S Truman.
Attlee and Truman had little experience of foreign affairs, and the strong personal relations between the 'big three' could no longer guide international affairs.
Truman had less inclination to make concessions to Stalin, and Attlee's foreign minister, Bevin, was a tough negotiator who disliked communism.

The realities of Russian influence in the East were hitting home and at the Potsdam Conference it was harder to bring about decisive solutions. No general peace settlement ended the war, and Truman and Stalin were poised for the confrontations of the Cold War.

subheadings.label: Debate: Were new leaders (Truman/Attlee) or Stalin's actions more responsible for the breakdown in relations?
facts: NEW LEADERS: Truman more suspicious of Stalin — less inclined to make concessions than Roosevelt.
NEW LEADERS: Bevin (Attlee's foreign secretary) was a tough negotiator who disliked communism — hardened British position.
NEW LEADERS: Roosevelt's death removed the one Western leader with personal rapport with Stalin.
NEW LEADERS: Lend-Lease cut-off on 8 May 1945 sent a hostile signal before Potsdam even met.
NEW LEADERS: Truman's revelation of the atomic bomb at Potsdam transformed the power dynamic.
STALIN'S ACTIONS: Stalin had already installed communist government in Poland before Potsdam — broke Yalta promises.
STALIN'S ACTIONS: Arrest of 16 Polish non-communists hoping for free elections showed bad faith.
STALIN'S ACTIONS: Soviet actions in Eastern Europe would have produced the same Western response regardless of leadership.
STALIN'S ACTIONS: Churchill (not Truman) first raised alarm — Iron Curtain speech March 1946.
STALIN'S ACTIONS: The Percentages Agreement showed Churchill himself was willing to divide Europe — Stalin's tactics, not personality, drove the conflict.

unit: Chapter 1 – Origins of the Cold War to 1945

heading: The Iron Curtain speech and the origins of containment thinking

subheadings.label: The Fulton speech (March 1946)
facts: In opposition, Churchill was freer to give his views on the international situation. He was increasingly concerned that Britain and the USA had allowed the USSR to dominate Eastern Europe, and that the USA might withdraw from Europe and retreat into isolation, not understanding what he saw as the threat from communism.

In March 1946 Churchill made a speech at Westminster College, Fulton, Missouri, which he called 'The Sinews of Peace'. The speech was not all hostile to Stalin, but it used a phrase that became famous: 'From Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic, an iron curtain has descended across the continent.'

Churchill referred to the great capitals of Eastern Europe — Warsaw, Berlin, Prague, Vienna, Budapest, Belgrade, Bucharest and Sofia — being behind that curtain in the Soviet sphere. He referred to the 'indefinite expansion of its power and doctrines'.
He saw Stalin as admiring strength and despising weakness and urged a settlement with him 'supported by the whole strength of the English-speaking world'.

subheadings.label: Key ideas in the speech
facts: Europe was firmly divided. The USSR controlled all the Eastern European countries equally. The West needed to negotiate from a position of strength. The USSR wanted to expand without limit. The USSR wanted to expand not only its power but the doctrine of communism.

Goebbels, the Nazi propaganda minister, had used the key phrase 'iron curtain'. That did not stop it becoming highly influential, and the term 'Iron Curtain Countries' became widespread for the 'Soviet bloc' or Eastern Europe in general.

subheadings.label: Reactions to the speech
facts: Stalin reacted by arguing that the USSR, having lost so many people in the war, had a right to take measures to ensure its security and had only peaceful ambitions to ensure neighbouring states were loyal. He accused Churchill of being 'a firebrand of war'.
Many in the USA thought the speech was irresponsible and one newspaper described it as 'poisonous'. Truman did not immediately signify his approval.
Though the phrase 'iron curtain' was influential, the speech did not in itself change US policy, which was moving towards the idea of opposing any expansion of communism.

subheadings.label: Kennan and the Long Telegram (February 1946)
facts: George F. Kennan, US ambassador in Moscow, had sent his 8,000-word 'Long Telegram' just weeks before Churchill's speech. It warned of traditional Russian ambitions and the desire for expansion and of the need to oppose these.
Kennan argued the USSR sought the destruction of capitalism but was not suicidal and would back down under firm pressure. This became the intellectual basis for containment.

By 1946 the mood in the USA was shifting away from possible isolationism to meeting the dangers of communist expansion. Churchill's speech did more to confirm changing views than to create them. Churchill's speech was much less important than the views of influential foreign policy experts like Kennan.

subheadings.label: Novikov Telegram (September 1946)
facts: The Soviet equivalent: Nikolai Novikov, Soviet ambassador in Washington, reported back to Moscow that the USA planned to dominate the world using its overwhelming military and economic might.
Argued cooperation since Roosevelt's death had become impossible — the Truman administration was hostile to Soviet interests.
Together with Kennan's Long Telegram, these documents confirmed to each side that the other was their enemy — formalising Cold War thinking at the highest level.

subheadings.label: Accuracy and limits of the Iron Curtain image
facts: The content of the speech was flawed. The rigid demarcation of West and East did not amount to an iron curtain in 1946 and Soviet influence was not as uniform as Churchill made out.

Berlin was not under total Soviet control, nor was Vienna. In Belgrade, the capital of Yugoslavia, it was not as strong as in other capitals. Total Soviet domination was not yet established in Prague.

The speech showed little awareness of Soviet security needs and concerns and made assumptions about 'indefinite expansionism' and respect for sheer force. Stalin, for example, had not attempted to intervene in Greece.
The vivid image of the speech, however, helped to encourage anti-Russian sentiment — and provoked equally strong rhetoric from the USSR, ramping up tension and verbal conflict.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was the Iron Curtain speech or Kennan's Long Telegram more significant for Western policy?
facts: IRON CURTAIN SPEECH: Term entered common usage — shaped popular understanding of Cold War for decades.
IRON CURTAIN SPEECH: Provoked strong Soviet response, escalating rhetoric and confirming mutual hostility.
IRON CURTAIN SPEECH: Shifted US public mood from potential isolationism to engagement.
IRON CURTAIN SPEECH: Churchill's prestige as wartime leader gave the speech weight beyond his opposition status.
IRON CURTAIN SPEECH: Factually inaccurate (Berlin, Vienna not fully Soviet) — but politically powerful.
LONG TELEGRAM MORE SIGNIFICANT: Kennan's analysis directly shaped US containment policy as an official diplomatic document.
LONG TELEGRAM MORE SIGNIFICANT: Provided the intellectual framework — the USSR would back down under firm pressure.
LONG TELEGRAM MORE SIGNIFICANT: Led directly to NSC-68 and the Truman Doctrine — Churchill's speech had no policy output.
LONG TELEGRAM MORE SIGNIFICANT: Kennan was the 'father of containment' — the doctrine that shaped US foreign policy for 45 years.
LONG TELEGRAM MORE SIGNIFICANT: Truman did not immediately approve Churchill's speech — Kennan's analysis was taken seriously by policymakers immediately.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955

heading: Soviet control of Eastern Europe — salami tactics

subheadings.label: Failure of the Declaration on Liberated Europe
facts: At Yalta in February 1945, Roosevelt had persuaded Stalin and Churchill to accept the Declaration on Liberated Europe. This emphasised the right of all peoples to choose the form of government under which to live.
By 1948 it was apparent that this had not been upheld in Eastern Europe. In lands annexed by the USSR, there was no choice for the inhabitants.

subheadings.label: Poland
facts: Soviet forces had set up a new Provisional Government in June 1945 that was dominated by the Polish communists, who had little support in the country.
It was obvious when the Polish government in exile in London joined that there would not be free elections. The non-communist Peasant Party representatives resigned in protest.

subheadings.label: Romania
facts: A new government was imposed on the king by the USSR in December 1945. Stalin created a new communist-dominated National Democratic Front in 1946.
By violence and pressure, this won 80% of the vote in the election of November 1946.
In December 1947, the king was forced to abdicate and a Communist People's Republic was formed in April 1948.

subheadings.label: The Soviet zone of Germany
facts: The socialist SPD was forced to merge with the communists to form a Socialist Unity Party (SED) after large numbers of arrests of SPD members.
This new party would be the basis of government when an independent East Germany was established in 1949.

subheadings.label: Bulgaria
facts: Stalin at first insisted that the communists who dominated the government accept non-communist members and accept the election results of October 1946, which gave a third of the votes to non-communist parties.
By 1947, however, Stalin allowed the communists to repress all opposition, with the backing of the Russian army.

subheadings.label: Hungary
facts: In Hungary, Stalin did allow free elections in November 1945. In 1947 the leading opposition leader was arrested and increasing Soviet control was subsequently established.
In March 1948, the socialists were forced to merge with the Hungarian communists and this new Independent Front was the only party.

subheadings.label: Czechoslovakia
facts: The elections of March 1946 gave the Czech communists 38% of the vote, and were genuinely free. The Czech leader, Beneš, had been able to work with the Czech communists, but in 1947 there was more pressure for communist domination.
The USSR was determined to prevent the Czechs from accepting US Marshall Aid and in February 1948 a communist coup with Soviet support took place.

The February 1948 Czech coup shocked the West — foreign minister Jan Masaryk was defenestrated. Czech communists had won only 38% in genuinely free 1946 elections. The coup played on Western guilt over 1938–39 and directly accelerated NATO's formation. The term 'salami tactics' was coined by Hungarian communist Mátyás Rákosi — the communists' own description of their strategy.

subheadings.label: Elements of Soviet domination ('salami tactics')
facts: The Russians and their allies used 'salami tactics' — they entered into pacts with other political parties, then when the time was right had 'sliced them' out of the coalition governments.
The USSR had also used forced mergers with socialist parties to strengthen its position.
Elections were carefully controlled by violence and intimidation. There was extensive propaganda and the establishment of political police.
By 1948, unrepresentative pro-Moscow communist leaders had been established and opposition destroyed by arrests, intimidation and murder.

Western suspicion of Russian ambitions in Eastern Europe led to counter-measures in the form of the policy of containment in 1947. This in turn led to greater Russian control being imposed, so Cold War tensions escalated.
Stalin did not intervene everywhere — he did not intervene in the civil war in Greece and did not attempt to control Finland. This showed security, not ideology, set the limits of Soviet expansion.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was Soviet control of Eastern Europe driven more by ideology or security?
facts: IDEOLOGY: Marxism-Leninism required exporting communism — a neutral Eastern Europe was ideologically impossible.
IDEOLOGY: Salami tactics followed identical pattern across all countries — planned, not improvised in response to security threats.
IDEOLOGY: Term 'salami tactics' was coined by Hungarian communist Rákosi — a deliberate ideological strategy.
IDEOLOGY: Czech coup 1948 — communists had won only 38% in free elections. Takeover was ideological, not defensive.
IDEOLOGY: Cominform (1947) coordinated all European communist parties — explicitly ideological organisation.
SECURITY: USSR lost 25 million dead in WW2 — need for buffer states was a genuine and proportionate response.
SECURITY: Three times invaded via Eastern Europe in one century (1914, 1918 intervention, 1941).
SECURITY: Initially tolerated coalitions (Czechoslovakia 1946, Hungary 1945) — only tightened after Western counter-measures.
SECURITY: Stalin did not intervene in Greece — showed security, not ideology, set the limits.
SECURITY: Truman Doctrine (March 1947) and Marshall Aid forced Stalin to consolidate — Western pressure accelerated the takeover.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955

heading: The Truman Doctrine and Marshall Aid

subheadings.label: Truman's appeal to Congress (March 1947)
facts: On 12 March 1947, Truman appealed for Congress to strengthen non-communist forces in areas thought to be vulnerable to possible communist domination.

He set out his view of competing ways of life. The first had free institutions, representative government, free elections, guarantees of individual liberty, freedom of speech and religion, and freedom from oppression. The second was based on the will of a minority forcibly imposed on the majority, using terror and oppression.
It was the policy of the USA to support free peoples who resist attempted 'subjugation by armed minorities or outside pressures'.
It recognised that political extremism and dictatorship had its origins in misery and want; its seeds 'grow in the evil soil of poverty'.

subheadings.label: Why these policies were adopted
facts: The USA could no longer rely on Britain, which had economic problems and overstretched forces, to guarantee that Greece and Turkey would remain free from communism.
More fighting had broken out in Greece in September 1946 and Stalin had allowed communist forces from other Balkan countries to assist the Greek communists, contrary to his earlier policy.
By 1947 it was clear that Stalin was not keeping to the agreement made at Yalta about elections in Eastern Europe.
There were large communist parties in Italy and Germany, and communist forces were fighting against US-backed nationalists in China.
The expansion of communism was not only against US ideology but also a threat to its economic interests.
Key US advisers had accepted the model of a dynamic and expansionist communism that threatened US interests.

subheadings.label: The Marshall Plan (June 1947)
facts: The follow-up was the Marshall Plan of June 1947, in which the secretary of state George Marshall offered an aid package to Europe.
No distinction was made between 'free' and 'unfree' countries. Stalin, however, forbade the Soviet-dominated nations to attend a meeting in Paris, attended by 16 nations.

Congress approved the policy in 1948. An Organisation for European Economic Development was set up to promote common growth policies, but the aid was deployed by US representatives and the individual Western European governments with limited overall planning.

subheadings.label: Results
facts: The USA was committed to an active foreign policy of containment and to use its economic and military power to intervene in European and then in world affairs. This was in marked contrast to the isolationism that followed WW1.
The policy confirmed the emergence of mutually hostile blocs. It strengthened anti-communist feeling in the USA and the so-called Red Scare.
It also strengthened the hostility in the communist bloc, which saw only US attempts to use 'dollar diplomacy' to exercise power and bolster its existing allies.

Aid went to 17 countries, but mostly to the UK and West Germany (which were not in danger of becoming communist), France and Italy. Most of the $12.7 billion in aid was used to purchase goods and raw materials from the USA, and considerable amounts went into defence spending.
It supported the re-industrialisation of West Germany, which promoted its political stability after 1949.
There was a long-term commitment to aid, which continued after 1951 with $7 billion a year going to Europe under the Mutual Security Plan.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was the Truman Doctrine or Marshall Aid the more significant turning point?
facts: TRUMAN DOCTRINE MORE SIGNIFICANT: First formal commitment of the USA to containment — ended American isolationism permanently.
TRUMAN DOCTRINE MORE SIGNIFICANT: Committed $400m to Greece and Turkey — first direct Cold War intervention.
TRUMAN DOCTRINE MORE SIGNIFICANT: Framed the Cold War in global ideological terms — 'free peoples' vs communism.
TRUMAN DOCTRINE MORE SIGNIFICANT: Provoked Soviet counter-measures (Cominform Sept 1947) that hardened the division.
TRUMAN DOCTRINE MORE SIGNIFICANT: Set the intellectual framework that justified all subsequent US Cold War actions.
MARSHALL AID MORE SIGNIFICANT: $12.7 billion in aid — tangible economic commitment rather than rhetoric.
MARSHALL AID MORE SIGNIFICANT: Rebuilt West Germany — the most strategically significant outcome of the whole policy.
MARSHALL AID MORE SIGNIFICANT: Prevented communist takeovers in France and Italy by addressing the economic desperation.
MARSHALL AID MORE SIGNIFICANT: Stalin's refusal forced him into creating Cominform and Comecon — completing the division of Europe.
MARSHALL AID MORE SIGNIFICANT: Long-term commitment continued after 1951 — $7bn/year under Mutual Security Plan.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955

heading: Cominform and Comecon

subheadings.label: Origins
facts: Stalin sent his foreign minister Molotov to meet representatives from France and Britain to discuss Marshall Aid proposals, but feared Western interference with economic policy in the East.

Stalin banned Soviet bloc governments from accepting aid, and called a conference in Poland of all European communist parties, including those in France and Italy. From that, the Communist Information Bureau (Cominform) emerged in September 1947.
The other communist organisation formed as a reaction to US policies was the Council of Mutual Economic Assistance (Comecon) in 1949.

subheadings.label: Cominform (1947–56)
facts: The Polish Conference was held to resolve disagreements in Eastern Europe about rejecting much-needed aid.

From 1919 to 1943 there had been a central organisation to coordinate communist parties — the Comintern or the Third International. This had been dominated by the USSR. Cominform was intended as propaganda to prevent any communist party being lured by US 'dollar diplomacy'.

The most enthusiastic party was the Yugoslav and its first headquarters was in Belgrade. Its aims were to provide information to strengthen 'the anti-imperialist and democratic camp, the principal aim of which is to undermine imperialism, strengthen democracy and liquidate the remnants of fascism'.

After the rift between the Yugoslav communist leader Tito and Stalin and the expulsion of Yugoslavia in 1948 Cominform moved to Bucharest, though the dominant influence was the USSR. The propaganda aimed to undermine the Truman Doctrine and the Marshall Plan in France and Italy, and to maintain socialist unity in the East. It was abolished in 1956.

subheadings.label: Comecon (1949–1991)
facts: Politically, Stalin had established greater control in Eastern Europe, and the formation of the Comecon in 1949 was to create an economic alliance. Just as the Marshall Plan saw a link between economic prosperity and political stability, so did Stalin.

The initial members were the USSR, Albania (left in 1961), Bulgaria, Romania, Hungary, Poland and Czechoslovakia. The DDR (East Germany) joined in 1950. In 1962 Mongolia joined, with Cuba in 1972 and Vietnam joining in 1978. Yugoslavia had links with Comecon. Unlike Cominform, Comecon lasted into the 1990s.

During the Stalin era there was direct economic aid to Eastern Europe, but Comecon did not develop much in the way of regional cooperation between members. Economic life was dominated by relations between Comecon members and the USSR. In this it paralleled the operation of Marshall Aid.

The Eastern bloc provided an outlet for Soviet manufacturers and a supply of raw materials. There was also a focus on developing industries to avoid the need for imports from outside the bloc. After 1956 more ambitious regional policies were attempted.

The principle of socialist economic planning was applied, ensuring that the different countries did not replicate industrial production but specialised on key products. It also promoted infrastructure development, like the international railway and electric power grid. Just as the USA supplied fuel, the USSR provided oil exports and later finance from a development bank (1963).

subheadings.label: Significance
facts: Marshall Aid would have required a convertible currency and trade with the West. Stalin's control of Eastern Europe would have been threatened if Poland, Hungary and Czechoslovakia had accepted it. It forced Stalin into creating a division between East and West, represented by Cominform and Comecon.
Cominform emphasised Moscow's control of 'information' and the ideology of other communist parties. This strengthened the view in the West of a solid bloc of communism that had to be opposed.
Comecon helped divide Europe into two competing economic blocs. It boosted the USSR's control of its satellites.

Cominform and Comecon were part of a reaction against US policies, which also included Stalin approving the communist takeover of Czechoslovakia, tightening of control over Eastern Europe and blockading East Berlin.

subheadings.label: Yugoslavia and the Cominform split
facts: Tito's Yugoslavia was expelled from Cominform in 1948 for refusing to follow Moscow's line — the only communist country to break from Stalin successfully. Cominform HQ moved from Belgrade to Bucharest.
Yugoslavia's expulsion showed that Soviet control of the Eastern bloc depended ultimately on geography and the Red Army's presence — states Stalin could not physically dominate could resist him.

subheadings.label: Debate: Were Cominform and Comecon more significant as causes or consequences of the Cold War?
facts: CAUSES: Cominform's aim to undermine the Truman Doctrine in France and Italy was active interference — escalated tensions.
CAUSES: Cominform coordinated Czech coup 1948 — Soviet domination of Eastern Europe accelerated.
CAUSES: Comecon permanently split Europe into two competing economic blocs.
CAUSES: Both created lasting institutional structures that perpetuated Cold War confrontation.
CAUSES: Strengthened view of monolithic communist bloc in the West — made diplomatic nuance impossible.
CONSEQUENCES: Both were direct responses to the Truman Doctrine and Marshall Aid — consequences, not initiators.
CONSEQUENCES: Stalin only created Cominform after Marshall Aid threatened to peel away satellite states.
CONSEQUENCES: Comecon mirrored OEEC — both were consequences of the division Marshall Aid created.
CONSEQUENCES: Yugoslavia's expulsion from Cominform 1948 showed Stalin was reacting to circumstances, not following a plan.
CONSEQUENCES: Without the Truman Doctrine and Marshall Aid, Stalin might have allowed Eastern Europe more economic autonomy.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955

heading: The Berlin Blockade and Airlift 1948–49

subheadings.label: The fundamental conflict over Germany
facts: The creation of four occupation zones as a result of the wartime conferences and a joint Control Commission gave rise to conflicts about running Germany. A special problem was the division of Berlin, which lay in the USSR's zone, into Western and Eastern zones. As the two sides had very different views about how to treat occupied Germany, conflicts arose.

Initially, the USA favoured a decentralised and deindustrialised Germany as in the Morgenthau Plan. But this was impractical and US policy changed. At Potsdam there had been agreement that Germany would be treated as a single economic unit, but the USSR's heavy reparations and failure to conform to the agreements made about exchange of goods and raw materials went against that.

subheadings.label: Bizonia and the London Conference
facts: In January 1947 Bizonia was created from the US and British zones. In 1948 Bizonia ceased reparations and a policy of re-establishing a German industrial base began. There were also moves towards more German local self-government in the zone.

In February 1948 a conference was held in London at which the USA, Britain, France and the Benelux countries met to discuss establishing a separate West German nation. In June 1948 Germans in the West were allowed to create a democratic constitution and a new currency.
The key Russian aim was to prevent the creation of a West German state. Stalin chose to put pressure on the West's weakest point — West Berlin.

subheadings.label: Currency reform and the blockade
facts: The decision to create a separate currency, the Deutschmark, for the West was a key turning point. The USSR had not been consulted and responded by creating its own currency for the East, the Ostmark.
In retaliation for the Deutschmark, Stalin imposed a blockade on all road and rail links to West Berlin on 23 June 1948 and cut off its electricity.

The Allies supplied the city by air. Each day 2,000 tonnes of supplies were flown in and, as a threat, 60 B29 bombers were stationed in eastern England. The airlift was extended, reaching 8,000 tonnes a day by February 1949. The blockade and airlift ended in May 1949.

subheadings.label: Who was more to blame?
facts: The USSR could not afford to allow Germany to exercise political freedom, and the damage done to the USSR in the German invasion of 1941 seemed to justify reparations.
The context of increasing Soviet control of Eastern Europe worried the West and the practical needs of restoring the German economy seemed to override possible dangers.

Negotiating with the Russians in the Allied Control Commission had been difficult and there was little prospect of agreement over Bizonia or the currency issue, so unilateral decisions were taken that nevertheless seemed to be threatening, especially in the context of the Truman Doctrine and containment.

subheadings.label: Consequences
facts: The blockade was a propaganda disaster for the USSR — confirming the view of Soviet aggression in Western minds.
It accelerated the formation of NATO in April 1949.
It directly led to the creation of two separate German states: the Federal Republic of Germany (West, May 1949) and the German Democratic Republic (East, October 1949).

The ability of the West to supply its zone in Berlin forced Stalin to back down, but also added to tensions as he had little option but to create a communist East Germany as a counterweight to the FRG.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was the Berlin Blockade the most important turning point in the early Cold War?
facts: YES — TURNING POINT: Directly created NATO (April 1949) — the permanent US military commitment to Europe.
YES — TURNING POINT: Directly created two separate German states — the defining division of the Cold War.
YES — TURNING POINT: Proved the West would stand firm under Soviet pressure — established the credibility of containment.
YES — TURNING POINT: First direct military confrontation between superpowers — proved MAD logic worked.
YES — TURNING POINT: Propaganda disaster for USSR — shifted Western public opinion permanently against Soviet aggression.
NOT THE MOST IMPORTANT: Truman Doctrine (1947) was more significant — committed USA to containment globally, not just in Germany.
NOT THE MOST IMPORTANT: Marshall Aid (1947) had deeper long-term consequences — rebuilt Western Europe.
NOT THE MOST IMPORTANT: Salami tactics in Eastern Europe (1945–48) had already created the division the Blockade confirmed.
NOT THE MOST IMPORTANT: Soviet atomic bomb (1949) was more consequential — created MAD and transformed military balance.
NOT THE MOST IMPORTANT: Czech coup (February 1948) had already provided the decisive impetus for NATO.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955

heading: The creation of East and West Germany

subheadings.label: Separate development, 1948–49
facts: When France agreed to join Bizonia, this became Trizonia in April 1949. It was clear that separate states would emerge in East and West. Both sides had found political leaders with whom they could work. The experience of the blockade crisis had brought about increased division.

The West approved the Basic Law, the constitution for the new West German state, in spring 1949, and elections took place in August. Adenauer became the new Chancellor but there was control of key areas of policy concerning foreign policy, defence and economic matters from a High Commission of the former occupying powers.
The new republic was known as the Federal Republic of Germany and the pre-1933 political system re-emerged, with power being shared with the individual states. Bonn became the new capital.

subheadings.label: East Germany (DDR)
facts: In the East, there was more reluctance on Stalin's part to opt for an independent East German state. This would leave the richer and more industrial part of Germany, especially the Ruhr, in the hands of the West.
The official line of the now-dominant SED — a coalition between the former socialists and communists, in practice dominated by pro-Moscow Marxists — was that they stood for national unity.

The events of the blockade made national unity unlikely and in May 1949 the People's Council approved a constitution. The elections offered the people of the Soviet zone a choice of candidates from the SED only. The People's Republic was a one-party state backed by a security apparatus more developed even than that of its Nazi predecessor.

Stalin delayed approving the formation of a new German Democratic Republic government until October 1949. A Soviet Control Commission mirrored the West's High Commission and exerted a great deal of control over the new state, although Russian occupying forces were withdrawn.

subheadings.label: Berlin
facts: Fear and dislike of the SED led to the establishment of a West Berlin city government and elected assembly in November 1948. Officially the four-power Control Commission ran the city, but West Berlin sent representatives to the Bonn parliament though they had no voting rights.
East Berlin became the capital of the new Democratic Republic.

subheadings.label: Stalin's Peace Note (March 1952)
facts: In March 1952, Stalin proposed a unified, democratic and neutral Germany — free elections, all occupation forces withdrawn, no alliance obligations.
Timed to derail West German rearmament and NATO integration. Adenauer, whose strategy depended entirely on Western alignment, opposed reunification on these terms.
The West rejected it — they feared a reunified Germany would drift Soviet, and doubted Stalin would deliver genuine free elections.
Historians remain divided: Loth argues the offer was genuine; others see it as a propaganda move. One of the Cold War's great 'what-ifs' — reunification may have been achievable in 1952.

subheadings.label: Results of the division
facts: France and the USSR were unhappy about the creation of independent states. The USA and Britain, however, were deeply committed to promoting West Germany as a prosperous and stable ally.

East Germany became one of the most closely controlled, both economically and politically, and ideologically committed of all the satellite states. Its leadership was unhesitatingly supportive of Moscow.

West Germany and West Berlin seemed to be a model of capitalist development and the great success story of the Allies — the Nazi past was put aside, there was an economic miracle and stable, conservative politics.
East Germany and East Berlin remained impoverished, battle-scarred and drab. Unification was increasingly unlikely.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was the division of Germany the most significant development in the Cold War 1945–55?
facts: MOST SIGNIFICANT: Division of Germany was the physical embodiment of the Cold War — its most visible and enduring symbol.
MOST SIGNIFICANT: West Germany's economic miracle (Wirtschaftswunder) made it the most powerful argument against communism.
MOST SIGNIFICANT: Berlin remained a permanent flashpoint — three crises (1948–49, 1958–61, 1961) emanating from German division.
MOST SIGNIFICANT: West Germany's rearmament and NATO entry (1955) triggered the Warsaw Pact — militarised the division.
MOST SIGNIFICANT: Stalin's Peace Note (1952) showed even Stalin recognised Germany's centrality — willing to sacrifice the DDR.
NOT MOST SIGNIFICANT: Soviet control of Eastern Europe (salami tactics 1945–48) preceded and shaped German division.
NOT MOST SIGNIFICANT: The nuclear arms race was more globally significant — affected all states, not just Germany.
NOT MOST SIGNIFICANT: Truman Doctrine and Marshall Aid created the broader framework within which German division occurred.
NOT MOST SIGNIFICANT: Korea (1950–53) showed Cold War was a global confrontation, not purely a German one.
NOT MOST SIGNIFICANT: NATO was the more enduring institutional creation — German division ended in 1990, NATO continues.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955

heading: NATO and the Warsaw Pact

subheadings.label: Origins of NATO
facts: In March 1947 France and Britain signed the Treaty of Dunkirk, pledging mutual support in the event of a war against Germany. By 1948, however, fears about Germany had given way to greater fears about the expansion of the USSR after the seizure of power by the communists in Czechoslovakia in February of that year.

In March 1948 the Brussels Pact bound Belgium, Britain, France, Luxemburg and the Netherlands into a pact for mutual defence against an aggressor, unnamed but obviously the USSR. There were agreements about broader cultural and social cooperation. The aim, however, was to get US support, and secret talks were held between Britain, Canada and the USA.
The result was the North Atlantic Treaty of 4 April 1949.

subheadings.label: Nature of NATO
facts: This was partly a traditional treaty for mutual defence. There was an ideological element, however, as it was to defend not merely national security but 'freedom, common heritage and civilisation'.

The actual commitment was limited by the phrasing that each state could seek assistance in the event of an attack 'as it deems necessary' and the scope of action would be 'the area north of the Tropic of Cancer'.
There was to be 'continuous and effective' mutual aid to support countries' defensive capacity, however, and a Council with regular meetings.

NATO was like a wartime alliance. It also had distinct political aims. It was not a response to a similar organisation in the East — and indeed a parallel pact, the Warsaw Pact, was not created until 1955.

subheadings.label: NATO expansion
facts: In September 1949, it was learnt that Stalin had atomic weapons. In Asia, the communists took power in China in 1949. Then, in 1950, communist North Korea invaded the non-communist South.
NATO countries joined the Korean War to expel the North Korean invaders in 1950–53. There was the development of military agreements to standardise weapons and signalling.

In 1952 the Lisbon Conference set up a permanent HQ in Paris under a Secretary General and a permanent military force of 35 divisions. The first major exercise was held in September 1952 and defence planning expanded.

subheadings.label: The Warsaw Pact (May 1955)
facts: The Warsaw Pact was signed on 14 May 1955 by the USSR and most of its Eastern European satellites (the DDR signed in 1956). Unlike NATO, it was not an agreement between independent states but a policy move by the USSR.
It was a response to the entry of the German Federal Republic into NATO. It promised consultation on issues of mutual interest and assistance in the event of an attack on any one member country.

Like NATO, it led to military exercises and planning. If 'a general European treaty of Collective Security' were signed — i.e. the reunification of a neutral Germany — it would lapse, indicating it was more a political than a defensive move.
Though it seemed that the pact divided Europe into armed camps, little had changed; Moscow already controlled the foreign and defence policies of its Eastern European allies.

However, it did mean that if any of the satellites defected then the defence of the USSR would be threatened, so it strengthened the determination of Russian leaders to prevent any sign of criticism. It also meant that suppression of discontent would be by 'the Warsaw Pact' rather than by the USSR alone — a convenient fiction.

subheadings.label: Debate: Did NATO or the Warsaw Pact do more to prolong the Cold War?
facts: NATO PROLONGED IT: Permanent US military commitment to Europe made Soviet withdrawal from Eastern Europe impossible.
NATO PROLONGED IT: West German rearmament and NATO entry (1955) directly triggered the Warsaw Pact.
NATO PROLONGED IT: Article 5 collective defence made any Soviet move against a member state an act of war against America.
NATO PROLONGED IT: NATO expansion gave the USSR legitimate security concerns throughout the Cold War.
NATO PROLONGED IT: US nuclear umbrella in Europe gave Western Europe security without requiring negotiation.
WARSAW PACT PROLONGED IT: Gave legal framework for Soviet troops to remain in Eastern Europe permanently.
WARSAW PACT PROLONGED IT: Made suppression of dissent (Hungary 1956, Czechoslovakia 1968) a multilateral 'Warsaw Pact action'.
WARSAW PACT PROLONGED IT: Clause about lapsing if German reunification occurred shows it was designed to prevent that outcome.
WARSAW PACT PROLONGED IT: Institutionalised the Soviet bloc — made gradual reform impossible without threatening the whole structure.
BOTH EQUALLY: Both institutionalised the division of Europe — once created, neither side could dissolve them without strategic surrender.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955

heading: The Arms Race and atomic weapons 1946–55

subheadings.label: The US atomic monopoly
facts: The successful testing of an atomic weapon by the USA on 16 July 1945 and the destruction of two Japanese cities, Hiroshima and Nagasaki, on 6 and 9 August 1945 were significant for the Cold War.
The USA and Britain had not shared atomic secrets with Stalin. The USSR was therefore vulnerable to pressure as the West had vastly more destructive capacity.

Not until September 1949 did the Russians successfully test their own atomic weapons, which led to an arms race and the possibility of Mutually Assured Destruction if the Cold War developed into an unlimited war.

The potential to put pressure on the USSR was not taken advantage of. The USA was aware that espionage meant the USSR would catch up and develop its own atomic weapons. Official US policy was to work for international control of atomic energy, and in November 1945 it called for a UN commission to set down rules for control of weapons and to develop atomic energy for peaceful means.
The USSR was suspicious, however, vetoing US plans for control and instead demanding an end to all weapons in December 1946.

subheadings.label: The arms race
facts: In practice, the USA went on developing atomic weapons. The USSR had the capacity and was helped by espionage, which provided Western secrets. On 29 August 1949, an atomic weapon that was a virtual copy of one of the 1945 US bombs was successfully tested in Kazakhstan.

The arms race intensified with the development of a hydrogen bomb by the USA. This produced a weapon in 1954 with the capacity of an explosion equivalent to 10 million tonnes of TNT (the Hiroshima explosion had been 12,500 tons). The Russians tested their own thermonuclear bomb in 1953 and had a weapon equivalent to that of the USA by 1955.

subheadings.label: Espionage
facts: The revelations that the Soviets had benefited from spies like the scientist Klaus Fuchs passing on atomic secrets increased tensions and also suspicions of communist infiltration.
It led to the execution of two of those involved, Julius and Ethel Rosenberg, in 1953 and fuelled the anti-communist hysteria stirred up by US senator Joseph McCarthy.

subheadings.label: Doctrine of Massive Retaliation (1954)
facts: In January 1954, US secretary of state Dulles proclaimed what came to be known as the doctrine of Massive Retaliation. He argued that local defences would not be enough to prevent a communist invasion and that given 'the mighty land power' of the USSR, only a 'further deterrent of massive retaliatory power' would be sufficient for defence. In other words, the USSR should be aware that nuclear weapons would be used.
Part of Eisenhower's 'New Look' policy — nuclear weapons were cheaper than maintaining large conventional armies: 'more bang for the buck'.

This intensified the Cold War. The idea encouraged the development of missiles, however, and also the idea of a pre-emptive strike, and so increased the dangers from a possible conflict. It also encouraged the idea that war would result in Mutually Assured Destruction.

Whether the arms race intensified the Cold War and endangered peace or whether it in fact prevented a war from breaking out directly between the USSR and the West because the dangers were too great, is open to discussion.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was the nuclear arms race the most destabilising factor in the Cold War 1946–55?
facts: MOST DESTABILISING: Soviet atomic bomb 1949 — transformed a US monopoly into mutual vulnerability overnight.
MOST DESTABILISING: Massive Retaliation (1954) — lowered threshold for nuclear use; made any crisis potentially existential.
MOST DESTABILISING: H-bomb 1952/1953 — 10 million tonnes TNT, 800x Hiroshima; annihilation of Europe now feasible.
MOST DESTABILISING: Rosenberg executions and McCarthyism — domestic paranoia that poisoned diplomatic flexibility.
MOST DESTABILISING: Soviet espionage access to US atomic secrets destroyed trust at the most fundamental level.
NOT MOST DESTABILISING: Korean War (1950–53) was the actual armed conflict — more destabilising than theoretical weapons.
NOT MOST DESTABILISING: Soviet takeover of Eastern Europe (1945–48) created the underlying division the arms race built on.
