NOT MOST DESTABILISING: Both sides' possession of atomic weapons actually imposed restraint — neither could start a war.
NOT MOST DESTABILISING: Berlin Blockade (1948) was a direct confrontation; nuclear weapons remained theoretical.
NOT MOST DESTABILISING: The arms race created MAD — which, paradoxically, made the Cold War cold rather than hot.

unit: Chapter 2 – Development of the Cold War 1946–1955

heading: Revolts in the Eastern bloc 1956: De-Stalinisation, Poland and Hungary

subheadings.label: Death of Stalin and hopes for change
facts: The death of Stalin in March 1953 encouraged hopes for change in Eastern Europe. Communism had shallow roots in largely agrarian societies, and the imposition of Soviet economic policies of collectivisation, and those of forced industrialisation and state controls that favoured the USSR, had caused deep resentment.
Khrushchev emerged as the dominant figure in the Soviet leadership by 1955–56, outmanoeuvring Malenkov and Beria.

subheadings.label: The Secret Speech (February 1956)
facts: In February 1956 Khrushchev gave his 'secret speech' at the 20th Party Congress denouncing Stalin's crimes — the purges, show trials, cult of personality and abuse of power.
Not intended to be made public but quickly leaked across the Communist world.

This 'de-Stalinisation' radically changed the official narrative. It unleashed expectations for reform that Khrushchev could not fully satisfy — directly contributing to the Polish October and Hungarian Uprising of 1956.

subheadings.label: Poland — the Polish October
facts: In Poland, there had been hopes that the so-called new course after 1953 might bring reform, better living standards and more political freedom.
Poland's large Catholic population was unhappy about many aspects of communism; workers' wages and conditions were poor and farmers resented controls.

The party itself was divided and after the death of the Moscow-dominated leader Bierut, the more liberal wing asserted itself and refused to accept Russia's nominee, Marshal Rokossowski, as defence minister. Hardliners could no longer count on the police and the army, and pent-up discontents emerged, with mass meetings and demonstrations and student publications calling for change.

In October, party support went to Wladyslaw Gomulka, a communist leader who had been imprisoned from 1949 to 1954 for 'deviationist' activities. Khrushchev accepted Gomulka rather than launching a massive invasion into Poland.
Gomulka proved to be a limited reformer, loyal to the USSR and to the Warsaw Pact. The unrest in Poland was a major factor in similar, more serious unrest in Hungary.

subheadings.label: Hungary — the revolt
facts: Hungary also resented Stalinist policies and the domination of a Stalinist leader, Rakosi, who was heavily dependent on repression. The condemnation of Stalinism in Russia weakened the leadership.

Political rallies spread and on 23 October 1956 the police fired on protestors, leading to workers joining students and intellectuals in protesting. As in Poland, a previously disgraced liberal communist, Imre Nagy, took power. But Nagy went further than Gomulka, allowing non-communists into government and talking of leaving the Warsaw Pact and Hungary becoming a neutral non-aligned country.

The USSR invaded with the sheer size of the military force — over a thousand tanks deployed — making resistance impossible. Janos Kadar was appointed leader and — after seeming to be liberal — imposed Moscow's rule brutally. Nagy was executed and some 180,000 Hungarians fled to the West.

subheadings.label: Why revolts had limited effect on the Cold War
facts: The attention of the world was diverted by the British and French invasion of Suez in 1956 after the Egyptian leader nationalised the key routeway of the Suez Canal.
The USA disapproved of the action of Britain and France, meaning that the West was divided at a crucial time.
The scenes of repression by Soviet tanks shocked many, but as the USSR had accepted change in Poland there was still room for some hope for change.
In the UN, most Asian and Middle East states abstained in a resolution calling for the Soviet withdrawal of troops from Hungary, so the West could not count on international support for any measures.
The West had accepted the brutal control of the USSR over Eastern Europe and that had become part of an accepted view of the 'iron curtain'.

Kadar made concessions after the repression that strengthened the regime. The failure of the USA to intervene revealed the limitations of containment. NATO was a defensive alliance and the West had already accepted that Hungary was part of the Soviet bloc.
The East German Rising of June 1953 had already shown the pattern: ~400,000 participants, ~55 killed, Soviet tanks deployed. The West did not intervene then either — setting the precedent for 1956.

subheadings.label: Debate: Did the Secret Speech or the Hungarian Uprising matter more for the Cold War?
facts: SECRET SPEECH MORE SIGNIFICANT: Directly unleashed expectations for reform across the entire Eastern bloc.
SECRET SPEECH MORE SIGNIFICANT: By delegitimising Stalin, it delegitimised the entire Soviet model — long-term corrosive effect.
SECRET SPEECH MORE SIGNIFICANT: Without the Secret Speech, neither the Polish October nor Hungarian Uprising would have occurred.
SECRET SPEECH MORE SIGNIFICANT: Its ideas could not be contained — leaked across the Communist world immediately.
SECRET SPEECH MORE SIGNIFICANT: Created the ideological contradiction that Gorbachev's generation inherited and was forced to resolve.
HUNGARIAN UPRISING MORE SIGNIFICANT: Showed the military reality — USSR would use 1,000 tanks to maintain control.
HUNGARIAN UPRISING MORE SIGNIFICANT: 180,000 refugees demonstrated scale of Eastern bloc's failure to attract loyalty.
HUNGARIAN UPRISING MORE SIGNIFICANT: Proved the limits of containment — West would not intervene in the Soviet sphere.
HUNGARIAN UPRISING MORE SIGNIFICANT: Confirmed the Iron Curtain as a military reality the West accepted.
HUNGARIAN UPRISING MORE SIGNIFICANT: Soviet tanks in Budapest did more damage to global communist credibility than any Western propaganda.

heading: West German rearmament and NATO entry

subheadings.label: The East German Rising (June 1953)
facts: After Stalin's death in March 1953, the Ulbricht regime in the DDR increased work norms by 10% while cutting wages. Workers in East Berlin took to the streets on 16 June 1953, with strikes spreading across the country.
Soviet troops and tanks moved in to suppress the uprising in June. Ulbricht's authority was reinforced and there was no repeat of the resistance to Russian domination in the 1950s and 1960s.

The USSR responded to West German rearmament concerns by offering to support German reunification and the creation of a neutral Germany that would not join the EDC or NATO. Little came of this, however, and Ulbricht was allowed to begin a more doctrinaire socialist policy in the DDR.

subheadings.label: The dilemma of German rearmament
facts: The division of Germany raised issues about the role of West Germany in Europe. Was it to be a semi-occupied satellite state of the victor powers or a truly independent sovereign state? If so, should it have its own armed forces and should it be part of NATO?

The general view developed that the German people had been victims of Nazism as much as those Europeans whom the Nazis had occupied and terrorised. As the Cold War developed it was seen as necessary to have the cooperation of West Germany.

The Korean War was worrying for the United States and Britain. The East German leader, Ulbricht, supported North Korea and suggested that a similar action might be taken by the East. As the Federal Republic had no armed forces, it was highly vulnerable. On the other hand, the East had built up a paramilitary police force of 60,000. Adenauer asked the Allied High Commissioners to be allowed to build a defence force.

subheadings.label: The EDC debate
facts: A European Defence Community with a European army was suggested in 1950 by the French premier, Pleven. This seemed impractical, but a compromise was agreed that NATO would create a force in Europe that would include German armed units.

The idea of Germany re-arming was highly controversial: it reinforced the idea that Germany would become permanently divided and was opposed by many in the Federal Republic. It alarmed opinion in France, which feared future German revenge for defeat.

From 1951 to 1952 there were negotiations, driven by the USA, to establish a new relationship with West Germany that would make it an independent state and to begin re-armament. In May 1952 a General Treaty replaced the Occupation Statute and removed the High Commission, paving the way for Germany to create armed forces.
The French, however, rejected the idea of the EDC in 1954.
Spofford Compromise (1951–52): an interim measure of limited West German troops under Allied command while the EDC debate continued.

subheadings.label: Resolution and entry into NATO (1955)
facts: Germany could not remain defenceless, however, and in October 1954 France was persuaded to agree to a limited West German army and German entry into NATO, which took place in 1955.
Germany was not to have nuclear weapons and British forces would remain there as a safeguard.
Adenauer won the elections of September 1953 and the General Treaty was accepted by both the German and French parliaments in 1954.
West German re-armament strengthened the division of Germany and also contributed to the creation of the Warsaw Pact (see page 38).
The East German rising of June 1953 led to greater support for an independent West Germany — Adenauer's case for Western alignment was confirmed.
Hallstein Doctrine (1955): the FRG would break off diplomatic relations with any state that officially recognised the DDR — effective until Brandt's Ostpolitik from 1969.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was West German rearmament or the Soviet atomic bomb more significant for Cold War tensions?
facts: WEST GERMAN REARMAMENT MORE SIGNIFICANT: Directly triggered the Warsaw Pact (14 May 1955 — one week after NATO entry).
WEST GERMAN REARMAMENT MORE SIGNIFICANT: Ended any prospect of German reunification for a generation.
WEST GERMAN REARMAMENT MORE SIGNIFICANT: Hallstein Doctrine (1955) further polarised European diplomacy.
WEST GERMAN REARMAMENT MORE SIGNIFICANT: Created permanent conventional ground forces that gave NATO credibility.
WEST GERMAN REARMAMENT MORE SIGNIFICANT: Made West Germany the keystone of Western Europe — 'Wirtschaftswunder' was the most powerful argument against communism.
SOVIET ATOMIC BOMB MORE SIGNIFICANT: Transformed the entire strategic balance — from US monopoly to mutual vulnerability.
SOVIET ATOMIC BOMB MORE SIGNIFICANT: Created MAD — the fundamental logic that governed Cold War from 1949.
SOVIET ATOMIC BOMB MORE SIGNIFICANT: Led directly to H-bomb race, then ICBM race — spiralling global danger.
SOVIET ATOMIC BOMB MORE SIGNIFICANT: Made any direct military conflict between superpowers potentially nuclear — constrained all subsequent Cold War crises.
SOVIET ATOMIC BOMB MORE SIGNIFICANT: Espionage needed to accelerate it (Fuchs, Rosenbergs) permanently poisoned US-Soviet trust.

heading: The Berlin Wall: causes and consequences

subheadings.label: The brain drain problem
facts: The division of Germany produced, not the 'iron curtain' of Churchill's imagining, but a relatively open front between the Soviet zone and later the DDR and the West.

The steady flow of those leaving the East by 1950 had reached 187,000. In 1952, after appeals from the East German leadership, Stalin agreed to close the border, but a loophole remained in Berlin and emigrants used the city as a route to the West. In 1955 the USSR gave control of the border to the East German authorities.

The problem was that the steady flow of emigrants — 3.5 million by 1961 — was causing long-term economic damage to the DDR. In all, 20% of its people had left — including some of the best educated and trained, who looked to find better conditions in the West. In July and early August 1961 alone, 36,000 left via Berlin.

subheadings.label: Khrushchev's ultimatum (November 1958)
facts: From 1958 the East German leadership was considering greater controls. Khrushchev issued the Berlin Ultimatum — the West had six months to leave West Berlin or he would hand control to East Germany.
The USA, UK and France refused to abandon West Berlin — Western prestige and security in Europe was at stake.

Khrushchev needed to show the world — and the critical Chinese communists — that Soviet economic policies worked; and yet in East Germany they were obviously failing. Loss of skilled labour could not continue.

subheadings.label: Failed summits
facts: The Paris Summit (1960) collapsed when a U-2 spy plane was shot down over the USSR and Eisenhower refused to apologise.
The Vienna Summit (1961) failed when Khrushchev tried to bully Kennedy. Kennedy left believing Khrushchev would test him — and ordered a significant increase in US military spending.

subheadings.label: Building the Wall (August 1961)
facts: Ulbricht and his colleagues may have taken the decision on 12 August 1961. The frontier was closed that night and barriers erected, which then led to the building of a wall on 17 August.

This divided the three zones of the Western allies in Berlin from the Eastern zone. A second, inner wall was constructed in 1962 with a 'zone of death' between; this wall was strengthened right up to 1980. Some 5,000 managed to escape up to 1989 and there were possibly 136 deaths among those attempting to escape.
Kennedy did not intervene militarily — 'A wall is a hell of a lot better than a war.'

subheadings.label: Significance of the Wall
facts: The Wall was, in the view of the US secretary of state Dean Rusk, 'a monument to communist failure'. Its purpose was not to separate East from West but merely to keep East Germans from defecting.

It led to a show of determination by the USA not to abandon West Berlin — US President Kennedy increased troop numbers and made a famous speech in Berlin in June 1963, pledging support and associating himself with the people of Berlin by declaring 'Ich bin ein Berliner'.
It was a propaganda opportunity for the West as a symbol of oppression. It stepped up tensions between the USSR and the West.
It confirmed the existing status quo in Europe and ended any hopes that détente or resolving tensions might lead to fundamental change.
It showed that the communist leaders were now wedded to defence of a failing system rather than to resolving problems by expansion.
Solved the immediate crisis: stopped the brain drain and stabilised the DDR.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was the Berlin Crisis of 1958–61 or the Cuban Missile Crisis more significant for the Cold War?
facts: BERLIN MORE SIGNIFICANT: Wall became the defining symbol of the Cold War — physical embodiment of the Iron Curtain for 28 years.
BERLIN MORE SIGNIFICANT: Kennedy's acceptance of the Wall tacitly acknowledged permanent German division.
BERLIN MORE SIGNIFICANT: 3.5 million refugees showed failure of communist system — propaganda disaster.
BERLIN MORE SIGNIFICANT: Berlin remained the most dangerous flashpoint in Europe throughout the Cold War.
BERLIN MORE SIGNIFICANT: 'Ich bin ein Berliner' (1963) made West Berlin the symbol of Western values.
CUBA MORE SIGNIFICANT: Came closest to actual nuclear war — 13 days in October 1962 risked annihilation.
CUBA MORE SIGNIFICANT: Led directly to Moscow-Washington hotline (1963) and Partial Test Ban Treaty (1963).
CUBA MORE SIGNIFICANT: Demonstrated both sides' willingness to compromise — Khrushchev withdrew, Kennedy pledged no Cuba invasion.
CUBA MORE SIGNIFICANT: Khrushchev's humiliation contributed to his removal (1964) — changed Soviet leadership.
CUBA MORE SIGNIFICANT: First time nuclear war was genuinely imminent — shaped all subsequent Cold War crisis management.

subheadings.label: Origins
facts: Cuba had a revolution in 1959 in which Fidel Castro overthrew the Batista government. Cuba became communist and began receiving Soviet aid. Khrushchev saw Cuba as an opportunity to establish a Soviet presence in the Western hemisphere.
In April 1961 the USA backed a CIA-trained invasion at the Bay of Pigs — a humiliating failure that exposed Kennedy's inexperience. In Vienna (1961) Khrushchev bullied Kennedy — seeing him as weak.

In 1962 Soviet missile sites were secretly constructed in Cuba, giving the USSR the ability to strike US cities with little warning. US U-2 spy plane photographs revealed the sites on 14 October 1962.

subheadings.label: The thirteen days (October 1962)
facts: Kennedy rejected air strikes on the missile sites (which might have killed Soviet technicians and triggered war) and instead imposed a naval blockade — a 'quarantine' — of Cuba on 22 October 1962.
Soviet ships carrying further missiles turned back as they approached the quarantine line.

Khrushchev offered to remove the missiles if the USA pledged not to invade Cuba. A secret additional deal was struck — the USA would also remove its Jupiter missiles from Turkey (which threatened Soviet cities) within six months.

subheadings.label: Resolution and significance
facts: The crisis ended on 28 October 1962 when Khrushchev accepted the public deal (Cuba non-invasion pledge), keeping the Turkish withdrawal secret.
A Moscow–Washington hotline was installed in 1963 to allow direct communication between leaders in future crises.
The Partial Test Ban Treaty was signed in August 1963, banning atmospheric nuclear tests.
Khrushchev appeared to have backed down publicly — his humiliation contributed to his removal in 1964.
The crisis was the closest the Cold War came to direct nuclear confrontation. It demonstrated that both sides recognised the catastrophic risks of escalation and accelerated moves towards détente.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was the Cuban Missile Crisis primarily a turning point towards détente or evidence the Cold War was unmanageable?
facts: TURNING POINT TO DÉTENTE: Led directly to Moscow-Washington hotline (1963) — crisis communication now possible.
TURNING POINT TO DÉTENTE: Partial Test Ban Treaty 1963 — first arms control agreement of the nuclear age.
TURNING POINT TO DÉTENTE: Both sides recognised they had come terrifyingly close to nuclear war — chose caution.
TURNING POINT TO DÉTENTE: Kennedy-Khrushchev back-channel diplomacy showed leaders could compromise.
TURNING POINT TO DÉTENTE: Set the template for crisis management that prevented escalation in subsequent confrontations.
UNMANAGEABLE: Both sides made dangerous miscalculations — Khrushchev underestimated Kennedy's resolve; Kennedy's blockade risked Soviet military response.
UNMANAGEABLE: A Soviet submarine nearly launched a nuclear torpedo — averted only by one officer's veto.
UNMANAGEABLE: The 'resolution' rested on a secret deal — publically Kennedy appeared to have 'won', Khrushchev appeared to have backed down.
UNMANAGEABLE: Khrushchev's removal 1964 showed domestic costs of crisis management — lesson: don't compromise.
UNMANAGEABLE: Arms race continued — MIRV warheads, SDI, SS-20s showed neither side truly learnt to limit the race.

subheadings.label: The second arms race — missiles
facts: The first arms race had centred on building ever more powerful bombs. From the mid-1950s, the development of missiles led to a second and more deadly arms race.

The USA led the way in missile technology but by 1957 the Russians had caught up. In August 1957, the USSR tested a successful ICBM (intercontinental ballistic missile). This and the launch of its Sputnik satellite showed that Soviet technology was no longer lagging behind.

Missiles transformed the nuclear threat. A successful missile strike could neutralise the launch of an enemy counter-attack and meant there would be little warning of an attack or any chance of stopping one.

The USA overestimated the number and quality of Soviet missiles and began a missile race, resulting in the Atlas missiles being operational by 1958 and the Titan and Minuteman being developed. Greater flexibility was provided by Polaris submarines equipped with missiles.

subheadings.label: Mutually Assured Destruction
facts: The USA shifted its strategic policy to an assumption that Russian attacks on itself or its allies would lead to 'devastating retaliatory strikes' with the capacity to destroy half the Russian population and 80% of its industry. Thus, war would mean 'mutually assured destruction'.

As a response, the USSR developed more sophisticated weaponry capable of pre-emptive strikes in a much more targeted way. The MIRV (multiple independently targeted re-entry vehicles) warheads from 1964 set off a further race, as these more exact weapons would target US missile silos.

The USA developed its own MIRVs and also defence systems. The arms race centred on: increasing the destructive capacity of missile warheads; increasing the accuracy of missiles to attack specific targets; developing systems to intercept missiles and to allow missiles to evade interception.

subheadings.label: Star Wars — the new arms race after 1980
facts: After 1980, the arms race started again. The new Republican administration of Ronald Reagan was suspicious of the USSR and concerned about the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and also the expansion of naval forces.
There was also fear of the power of the Soviet SS-20 missiles (in operation from 1978), which had multiple warheads. The USSR was concerned about better relations between the USA and China.

The USA developed Pershing and Cruise missiles, which it stationed in Europe, and most significant of all, it developed the Strategic Defence Initiative (also known as 'Star Wars'), because of its advanced laser and space-based programmes.

This went against the 1972 agreements to limit defensive systems. It was immensely costly and technologically demanding and put the USSR under a lot of pressure to compete, which was one of the factors that led to its downfall after 1989.

Able Archer 83: a NATO exercise simulating a nuclear war that was so realistic the USSR went on actual nuclear alert. Soviet forces genuinely believed war was about to begin — the most dangerous moment of the new Cold War.

subheadings.label: The unstoppable arms race
facts: The arms race perpetuated the Cold War but prevented it from developing into a direct conflict. It did, however, create a dangerous environment for world politics.
It led directly to a crisis over Cuba in 1962, which came close to escalating into nuclear war. Efforts to end the race came from peace movements in the West and also from summits and talks.

The pressure from technological developments and the mutual suspicion on both sides prevented these from being very effective. The arms race changed its character but did not really subside during the period.

subheadings.label: Debate: Did the arms race make the Cold War more or less stable?
facts: MORE STABLE: MAD made direct superpower confrontation irrational — nuclear deterrence kept Europe at peace for 45 years.
MORE STABLE: Both sides' knowledge of each other's capabilities (via intelligence) reduced risk of miscalculation.
MORE STABLE: Cuban Missile Crisis showed both sides would choose restraint when nuclear war was genuinely imminent.
MORE STABLE: Arms race drove arms control — SALT I (1972), INF Treaty (1987) were products of the race, not despite it.
MORE STABLE: Nuclear umbrella meant West Germany didn't need to develop its own weapons — reduced proliferation risk.
LESS STABLE: Cuban Missile Crisis — Soviet submarine nearly launched nuclear torpedo; averted by one officer's veto.
LESS STABLE: MIRV (1964) — one missile hitting multiple targets meant any first strike could eliminate retaliatory capacity.
LESS STABLE: Able Archer 83 — NATO exercise so realistic the USSR went on actual nuclear alert.
LESS STABLE: Massive Retaliation (1954) — threatened nuclear response to any Soviet conventional aggression.
LESS STABLE: SDI (1983) threatened to make Soviet ICBMs obsolete — could have incentivised a pre-emptive first strike.

subheadings.label: Sputnik 1957
facts: Despite a lot of research, it was not the USA but the USSR that made the first major advance into space, with the launch of a man-made satellite. The so-called Sputnik circled the Earth once every 90 minutes at a speed of 28,000 miles an hour. The USA became aware of this in October 1957 when the Russians put their achievements on show.

It seemed threatening that a Russian satellite was crossing the USA far in space — what if this were allied to weaponry? It showed that the USSR was technologically far more advanced than had been thought. It showed that Western liberal capitalism had not produced the levels of scientific and technological superiority that many in the USA had assumed.
This started a Space Race in addition to the arms race that was taking place.

subheadings.label: Soviet firsts
facts: In November 1957 the Russians showed their technical advances by putting a dog, Laika, into space. The US navy's Vanguard satellite launch failed in a humiliatingly public way in December 1957, although a more successful launch took place in March 1958.
The USA formed NASA, using the rocket knowledge of German scientist Werner von Braun.

Soviet advances continued: Luna 1 orbited the sun; the Vostok 1 spacecraft with Yuri Gagarin made the first manned orbital flight. John Glenn made a successful voyage in February 1962. The Russians achieved other 'firsts' — Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space (June 1963) and Alexei Leonov made the first spacewalk (March 1965).
Both sides worked on daring projects — the Russians finally achieved an orbiting space station in 1971. In March the same year, a Soviet probe landed on Venus.

subheadings.label: US achievement — the Moon
facts: Huge US resources went into the Apollo programme. This led to US astronauts circling the moon and returning safely in 1968. It produced one of the greatest moments of the century when Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed on the moon in July 1969.
Kennedy made the element of challenge and competition explicit in a speech in September 1962: '[which] we are unwilling to postpone and which we intend to win'.

The considerable resources taken by this Race and the efforts to control the parallel arms race by the SALT talks led to greater cooperation. The first joint US-Soviet space mission — the Apollo-Soyuz Mission — took place in 1975.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was the Space Race more significant as propaganda or as a military competition?
facts: PROPAGANDA MORE SIGNIFICANT: Sputnik's primary impact was psychological — humiliated US scientific confidence.
PROPAGANDA MORE SIGNIFICANT: Gagarin, Tereshkova, Leonov all 'firsts' — each one a Soviet propaganda coup.
PROPAGANDA MORE SIGNIFICANT: Moon landing (1969) restored US confidence after years of Soviet space supremacy.
PROPAGANDA MORE SIGNIFICANT: Apollo-Soyuz (1975) was pure détente theatre — political symbolism, not military.
PROPAGANDA MORE SIGNIFICANT: Kennedy explicitly framed Moon race as a competition for ideological prestige, not security.
MILITARY MORE SIGNIFICANT: Sputnik used the same rocket technology as Soviet ICBMs — the satellite demonstrated delivery capability.
MILITARY MORE SIGNIFICANT: NASA formed partly to develop dual-use rocket technology.
MILITARY MORE SIGNIFICANT: Both superpowers used reconnaissance satellites — Space Race enabled intelligence gathering essential to arms control.
MILITARY MORE SIGNIFICANT: SDI (Star Wars) was a direct extension of Space Race technology into a weapons system.
MILITARY MORE SIGNIFICANT: Soviet SS-20 and US Pershing missiles were direct descendants of the ICBM race that began with Sputnik.

heading: The Czech Crisis 1968 and the Brezhnev Doctrine

subheadings.label: The Prague Spring
facts: In January 1968 in Czechoslovakia, Alexander Dubček, the new Communist Party Secretary, came into office, and in spring of that year he announced reforms that would introduce more democracy. This was firmly within a socialist system. There was no intention to abandon collective agriculture or state-owned industry or to leave the Warsaw Pact.

The idea was that individuals would be able to fulfil themselves through socialism by having more input into decision making. The National Assembly would be able to discuss and decide issues relating to the development of socialism.
A key measure was the ending of censorship in June. The Prague Spring was a different kind of challenge from the open revolt in Hungary (1956), but more dangerous.

Demonstrators in Warsaw shouted 'We want a Polish Dubček'. The DDR leaders feared that Czechoslovakia would create economic links with West Germany. As freedom of expression emerged, there were revelations about the crimes and repression of the Stalin era, which involved Russian officials.

subheadings.label: The dilemma of the USSR
facts: As early as May, the Soviet leadership was contemplating intervention to keep its control over Eastern Europe. It had to balance the acceptance by the West of previous repression and the very limited chance of any help for the Czechs from the West, against the impact of an invasion on détente and on the image of the USSR as essentially peaceful.
Invasion would revive fears and strengthen NATO, but ignoring the situation might lead to the weakening of Moscow's hold.

The USSR faced demands from Romania to pursue an independent foreign policy and the influence of Chinese communism on Albania. Given that there were threats to its control, it became determined to stop further change in Czechoslovakia.

subheadings.label: The invasion (August 1968)
facts: The Soviet leader Brezhnev expressed concern about the emergence of anti-Russian propaganda. Pressure was put on Dubček by talk of 'Czech revisionism' and extending Warsaw Pact manoeuvres in Czechoslovakia from July 1968 to early August. Dubček had agreed to control criticism of the USSR, but visits by the leaders of Yugoslavia (Tito) and Romania (Ceausescu) on 17 August made the Russian leaders fearful of a break-up of the Eastern bloc.

On 20–21 August 1968, 20 divisions from the USSR, Hungary, Poland, the DDR and Bulgaria invaded. The Czech leaders were arrested and taken to Moscow, where Brezhnev threatened them until they agreed to abandon the reforms.

subheadings.label: The Brezhnev Doctrine
facts: This was stated by the Russian leader after the Czech invasion: 'Each Communist party is responsible not only to its own people, but also to all the socialist countries, to the entire Communist movement. Whoever forgets this, in stressing only the independence of the Communist party, becomes one sided... Discharging their internationalist duty toward the fraternal peoples of Czechoslovakia and defending their own socialist gains, the USSR and the other socialist states had to act decisively...' (Leonid Brezhnev, 25 September 1968)
The policy was clear: the USSR and its allies, especially Poland and the DDR, would invade any communist country that deviated from its 'duty' as interpreted by the Moscow leadership.
This ended any hopes of fragmentation or fundamental change, whatever agreements were made about arms or links with the West, and extended the Cold War until the USSR abandoned it in 1989.

subheadings.label: Significance
facts: The Czech Crisis was arguably the most dangerous challenge to the authority of the USSR in the period 1953–68. It did not bring the Cold War any closer to ending but rather helped to extend it.

While the Czech Crisis was much less than the threats offered by Hungary in 1956, the gap between living standards in East and West had widened and the Eastern bloc was much less solid by 1968 than in 1956.

More liberal reforms might have paved the way for better relations with the USSR and might have produced more prosperity and decreased unrest — the Soviet invasion injured its international reputation, caused massive resentments within Czechoslovakia and paved the way for later changes in and after 1989.

Jan Palach, a Czech student, self-immolated in protest in January 1969 — a powerful symbol of resistance that shocked the world. Albania left the Warsaw Pact in protest; Yugoslavia and Romania both condemned the invasion, showing cracks in the Soviet bloc. Nixon's election (November 1968) brought Realpolitik — the USA was too deeply committed in Vietnam to intervene.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was the Brezhnev Doctrine or the Truman Doctrine more significant for the Cold War?
facts: BREZHNEV DOCTRINE MORE SIGNIFICANT: Explicitly stated USSR would invade any socialist state that deviated — extended Cold War until 1989.
BREZHNEV DOCTRINE MORE SIGNIFICANT: Crushed reform from within — prevented the 1989-style revolutions from happening in 1968.
BREZHNEV DOCTRINE MORE SIGNIFICANT: Albania left Warsaw Pact, Romania condemned invasion — showed Doctrine divided, not united, the bloc.
BREZHNEV DOCTRINE MORE SIGNIFICANT: Its abandonment (Sinatra Doctrine, 1988) was the single most important factor enabling the 1989 revolutions.
BREZHNEV DOCTRINE MORE SIGNIFICANT: Applied in 1979 in Afghanistan — contributed directly to USSR's collapse.
TRUMAN DOCTRINE MORE SIGNIFICANT: Committed the USA to opposing communism globally — shaped 45 years of US foreign policy.
TRUMAN DOCTRINE MORE SIGNIFICANT: Created the logic for $400m to Greece/Turkey, Marshall Aid, Korea, Vietnam, Afghanistan.
TRUMAN DOCTRINE MORE SIGNIFICANT: Ended US isolationism permanently — a constitutional shift in how America related to the world.
TRUMAN DOCTRINE MORE SIGNIFICANT: The Brezhnev Doctrine was a response to Western containment pressure — Truman came first.
TRUMAN DOCTRINE MORE SIGNIFICANT: Created NATO and the military alliance architecture that outlasted the Cold War.

subheadings.label: Origins
facts: Economic unrest, including strikes in the Lenin Shipyard in Gdansk in 1980, led the government to recognise the Solidarity movement. Solidarity under Lech Walesa combined trade union demands for better wages with Catholic nationalist identity — unique in the Eastern bloc.

Poland's large Catholic population had deep reservations about communist rule, strengthened by the election of the Polish pope John Paul II in 1978 and his visit to Poland in 1979 which drew millions.

subheadings.label: The crisis
facts: By 1981 Solidarity had 10 million members — one-third of the Polish population. This level of mass organisation was an unprecedented challenge to communist authority.
The USSR was watching anxiously. Brezhnev made clear that the Polish party must maintain socialist control. US President Reagan made clear his opposition to armed Soviet intervention.
General Wojciech Jaruzelski declared martial law on 13 December 1981. Solidarity was banned and its leaders interned. The immediate crisis was resolved without Soviet military intervention.

subheadings.label: Significance
facts: Solidarity was the most successful mass challenge to Soviet-style communism before 1989. Its suppression by martial law rather than Soviet tanks showed the limits of the Brezhnev Doctrine — direct intervention was becoming too costly.
Poland remained part of the Warsaw Pact, but the USSR had accepted a non-Communist government and important constitutional change.

Solidarity's survival underground and its re-emergence in 1989 showed that communist regimes could not permanently suppress popular opposition. The 1989 Round Table Agreements saw Solidarity compete for 35% of Sejm seats — the elections of June 1989 resulted in a Solidarity government with some Communists holding major posts.
Hopes that the Cold War might subside were also reduced when, after unrest in Poland, the USA made clear its opposition to armed intervention by the USSR.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was Solidarity or Gorbachev's Sinatra Doctrine more significant in ending communist rule in Eastern Europe?
facts: SOLIDARITY MORE SIGNIFICANT: First mass movement (10m members = one-third of population) to successfully challenge communist authority.
SOLIDARITY MORE SIGNIFICANT: 1989 Round Table Agreements directly produced Poland's first non-communist government.
SOLIDARITY MORE SIGNIFICANT: Demonstrated communism could not command popular legitimacy even with martial law.
SOLIDARITY MORE SIGNIFICANT: Pope John Paul II's 1979 visit gave Solidarity a spiritual and national dimension communism couldn't suppress.
SOLIDARITY MORE SIGNIFICANT: Poland's 1989 elections triggered the wave of revolutions across the Eastern bloc.
SINATRA DOCTRINE MORE SIGNIFICANT: Without Gorbachev's refusal to use force, Solidarity's 1989 victory would have been crushed like 1981.
SINATRA DOCTRINE MORE SIGNIFICANT: Hungary, Czechoslovakia, DDR, Romania all had revolutions — Solidarity was one factor, Gorbachev's decision was the common factor.
SINATRA DOCTRINE MORE SIGNIFICANT: Solidarity survived 8 years underground before 1989 — timing was determined by Moscow, not Warsaw.
SINATRA DOCTRINE MORE SIGNIFICANT: 1981 showed what happened without the Sinatra Doctrine — martial law worked.
SINATRA DOCTRINE MORE SIGNIFICANT: Gorbachev explicitly told Honecker to make changes — his intervention, not popular pressure, was decisive in the DDR.

subheadings.label: Better relations in the 1960s
facts: 'Détente' is the term used for the period of improved relations between the USA and the USSR from 1969 to 1980.

There had been summit meetings between East and West and some significant treaties: the Partial Test Ban Treaty of August 1963, the Outer Space Treaty 1967 and the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty — signs that communication was open.

subheadings.label: Reasons for détente after 1969
facts: The USSR was spending approximately 40% of its budget on defence by the 1970s while economic growth stalled — making arms reduction an economic necessity, not just a diplomatic choice.

The USSR faced worsening relations with China — serious armed border clashes on the Ussuri River in 1969. The USSR even secretly asked the USA's reaction to a joint attack on China's nuclear installations. The USSR needed to reduce its potential enemies.
When Nixon visited China in 1972 and there was the possibility of better relations between the USA and China, this put even more pressure on the USSR to improve relations with the USA.
The USA also faced problems. The Vietnam War was costly. The sudden rise in oil prices in 1973 as a result of war in the Middle East made a reduction in arms spending seem a sensible policy.
Soviet leaders also faced economic difficulties, slow growth rates and problems in food production. Reduced arms spending would help provide more consumer goods and food.

Another factor was the Ostpolitik followed by West Germany, which saw Brandt sign major treaties with the USSR, Poland, Czechoslovakia and the DDR. Stalin and many of the wartime 'old guard' had given way to more flexible and pragmatic leaders like Leonid Brezhnev.

Since the Cuban adventure in 1962 there had been fear of the effects of nuclear war. The more pragmatic — and possibly less principled — era of Nixon and his foreign policy adviser Kissinger, who based policy on national interest not ideology, replaced the more rigid anti-communism of the Truman-Eisenhower era.

subheadings.label: Détente and SALT
facts: There were more diplomatic contacts, with Brezhnev and Nixon visiting each other's countries and agreeing in 1972 to outlaw biological weapons.

The SALT treaty of 1972 followed talks since 1970 and established a 5-year freeze on constructing missile launchers and a freeze on ICBMs and submarine-launched ballistic missiles and long-range bombers. Both sides agreed to restrict anti-ballistic screens or defence systems to their capital cities and main missile sites.
The USSR and USA agreed the Helsinki Agreements in 1975, increasing contacts between East and West. Also in 1975, there was a joint US-USSR space programme — the Apollo-Soyuz mission.

In 1979 US President Carter and Brezhnev signed SALT II in Vienna. There was further reduction of missile launchers and MIRV warheads, but détente was to fall away and the US Senate refused to ratify the treaty.

subheadings.label: Ostpolitik (Willy Brandt, 1969–74)
facts: A key feature of détente was Ostpolitik (literally 'East Politics') pursued by the West German leader Willy Brandt from 1969.

The FRG Hallstein Doctrine had stated that the Federal Republic would break off diplomatic relations with any state that officially recognised the DDR. Brandt saw that Germany could not be so relentlessly divided and was concerned with the economic costs of maintaining defences.

The key agreement was the Moscow Treaty of August 1970 between Brandt and Brezhnev: neither had any territorial claim against any other state; it recognised the western frontier of Poland; Germany finally accepted the loss of territory of 1945 as 'inviolable'; the Federal Republic abandoned the Hallstein Doctrine and agreed both Germanies would become members of the UN.

In September 1971, it was agreed that there should be no restrictions on travel between the Federal Republic and West Berlin. In December 1972 the Basic Treaty was signed — the FRG agreed to recognise the existence of the DDR as an equal sovereign state.

Brandt had ended possible diplomatic problems involved with the 1955 Hallstein Doctrine. It opened the way for more talks in Helsinki in 1975 about reduction of armaments in Central Europe and human rights.

subheadings.label: Helsinki Accords (1975)
facts: 33 nations signed the Helsinki Accords. Three 'baskets': Basket 1 — European borders inviolable, recognising the post-war territorial settlement; Basket 2 — economic and scientific cooperation between East and West; Basket 3 — human rights to be respected — Soviet bloc accepted this in principle.
Seen as the zenith of détente — the high point of East-West cooperation.

Basket 3 was ignored in practice by the USSR — but gave Eastern European dissidents a legal basis to demand their rights, increasingly important in the 1980s. Charter 77 in Czechoslovakia and Solidarity in Poland directly used Helsinki commitments.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was détente or the arms race more influential in shaping the Cold War 1969–79?
facts: DÉTENTE MORE INFLUENTIAL: SALT I (1972) — first formal arms limitation treaty; halted the exponential growth of arsenals.
DÉTENTE MORE INFLUENTIAL: Helsinki Accords (1975) gave Eastern European dissidents a legal framework — directly fed 1989 revolutions.
DÉTENTE MORE INFLUENTIAL: Ostpolitik normalised Germany's division — removed Berlin as a constant flashpoint.
DÉTENTE MORE INFLUENTIAL: Nixon-China visit created triangular diplomacy — most creative Cold War diplomacy of the era.
DÉTENTE MORE INFLUENTIAL: Apollo-Soyuz mission (1975) — concrete symbol of superpower cooperation.
ARMS RACE MORE INFLUENTIAL: SALT I froze, not reduced, warheads — MIRV warheads continued proliferating.
ARMS RACE MORE INFLUENTIAL: SALT II never ratified — Senate rejected it after Afghanistan, showing détente had shallow domestic roots.
ARMS RACE MORE INFLUENTIAL: Soviet SS-20 missiles (1978) deployed during détente — showed arms race continued regardless.
ARMS RACE MORE INFLUENTIAL: Both sides continued massive military spending — USSR ~40% of budget on defence.
ARMS RACE MORE INFLUENTIAL: Afghanistan invasion (1979) ended détente instantly — it was never a structural transformation, only a tactical pause.

heading: The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and the new Cold War 1979–84

subheadings.label: Background to the invasion
facts: The high point of détente had been seen as the Helsinki Agreements, but these did not prevent further developments in the arms race when the USSR stationed the powerful SS-20 missiles in Central Europe in 1976.

In April 1978, without Moscow's approval, the Afghan communists overthrew the monarch in Afghanistan and began a radical programme of secularisation and reform. This resulted in an opposition movement by Islamic forces with support in the countryside.
The Iranian revolution had inspired the growth of Islamic radicalism and the USSR was vulnerable because of its large Muslim population in the southern republics.

The Afghan communist leader Amin was removed and killed and replaced by Babrak Kemal, a communist loyal to Moscow. In December 1979, 100,000 Soviet forces entered Afghanistan. They faced opposition to Moscow-dominated communist rule inspired by Islamic beliefs and supported by the USA via Pakistan. Soviet troops withdrew in 1989.

subheadings.label: The problems of the war
facts: The nature of the terrain in Afghanistan — which had created problems for European powers trying to control the country since the nineteenth century — led to a sustained guerrilla war.
The experience of USSR forces echoed the US struggle in Vietnam. The opposition fighters had the support of local populations. Their religious convictions made them willing to endure casualties.

The Afghan national army faded away and the forces of the USSR were engaged in a direct conflict with a ruthless enemy with years of experience fighting in the harsh and difficult terrain. The war was fought with increasing brutality and disregard for civilian casualties.
The war damaged the reputation of the USSR not only in the West but also within the Soviet bloc, which saw it as costly — over 38,000 Soviets died or were wounded — and pointless.

subheadings.label: Western reaction
facts: The invasion gave rise to memories of Czechoslovakia and Hungary and seemed to indicate that détente was pointless. There were fears of Russian expansion towards the Persian Gulf and the key oil supplies on which the West depended.
President Carter banned grain supplies, the US Senate refused to ratify the SALT II treaty, and the USA boycotted the 1980 Moscow Olympics.

In addition, the USA supplied the Afghan rebels through its ally Pakistan. By 1986 the level of aid included surface to air missiles. The USA also approved the export of Chinese military technology to the Mujaheeden.

subheadings.label: Changes in leadership in the West
facts: In 1980 Ronald Reagan was elected US president. He was openly hostile to the USSR and its 'evil empire', and saw the concessions in SALT as against US interests and Helsinki as a repeat of the appeasement of Yalta.
In Britain, Margaret Thatcher, one of Britain's most ideologically driven leaders, was elected in 1979, determined to oppose socialism and communism and to support the USA.
The deployment of cruise and Pershing missiles in 1983 and the development of the SDI Star Wars initiatives confirmed that the new Cold War was to be accompanied by a new arms race.

subheadings.label: Why the new Cold War continued
facts: For the Russian leaders Brezhnev (who died in 1982) and his successors Andropov and Chernenko, the Afghan War and the relentless arms race waged by the USA, together with tough opposition to the whole ideology of communism from the West, made ending the new Cold War difficult.

The greater economic and technological resources of the USA, as demonstrated in the Star Wars developments, gave an advantage to the USA. This meant it had little interest in reducing its favourable position by further détente.
In September 1983 a Soviet warplane shot down a South Korean airliner that had strayed into Soviet airspace — there was even a major crisis that threatened to begin a world war.
Afghanistan was a new proxy war. The Cold War was approaching its end game.
The USSR boycotted the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics in retaliation for the US 1980 Moscow boycott. Sport had become a proxy for Cold War confrontation.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was Afghanistan or Reagan's military build-up more responsible for ending détente?
facts: AFGHANISTAN MORE RESPONSIBLE: Invasion directly triggered Carter's grain embargo, SALT II rejection, Olympic boycott.
AFGHANISTAN MORE RESPONSIBLE: Demonstrated Soviet expansionism beyond its agreed sphere — violated the Helsinki spirit.
AFGHANISTAN MORE RESPONSIBLE: Over 38,000 Soviet casualties made the adventure obviously counterproductive.
AFGHANISTAN MORE RESPONSIBLE: Supplied Mujaheeden — USA directly funded a proxy war; détente could not survive this.
AFGHANISTAN MORE RESPONSIBLE: 'New Cold War' was a Soviet provocation — Reagan was responding, not initiating.
REAGAN MORE RESPONSIBLE: SS-20 missiles deployed 1978 under Carter — arms race had already resumed before Afghanistan.
REAGAN MORE RESPONSIBLE: 'Evil empire' rhetoric was ideological, not a response to Afghanistan.
REAGAN MORE RESPONSIBLE: SDI (1983) threatened to make the entire Soviet nuclear arsenal obsolete — existential challenge.
REAGAN MORE RESPONSIBLE: Able Archer 83 — US exercise so realistic the USSR went on nuclear alert; created by Reagan's recklessness.
REAGAN MORE RESPONSIBLE: US Senate had already refused to ratify SALT II before Afghanistan — détente was ending regardless.

heading: Economic and social problems in the USSR and Eastern Europe

subheadings.label: Weaknesses of the system
facts: The end of the Cold War came when the USSR could no longer cope with the demands of global overstretch and a costly arms race with the USA, and so sought to revive détente with the West. An important element in changing policy was the economic and social problems of both the USSR and its Eastern European satellites. These led to changes, which weakened the control of the Communist Party both within the USSR and over the Soviet bloc.

Planning objectives were unrealistic. The quality of goods produced, without the necessary competition between private firms, was poor. There was a lack of motivation in the workforce, as living standards did not improve. There were social problems like alcoholism and absenteeism.
By the mid-1980s the total production of the USSR was only 37% of the gross national product of the USA.

This malaise had spread to the Eastern European countries, which were even more frustrated because they were closer to the more successful capitalist economies of the 1980s that were enjoying the freedom of deregulation from government control.

subheadings.label: Agricultural stagnation
facts: Agriculture suffered from a labour shortage as industrial and urban growth had ended the pool of mass agricultural labour. This had not been countered by better productivity.

Attempts to exploit the land by increasing chemical fertilisation had led to serious soil damage. Heavy investment in irrigation had led to loss of resources — the Aral Sea had dried up, for instance.
Basic food production, for example grain, remained stagnant from the 1960s to the 1980s, making the USSR more dependent on imports.

subheadings.label: Oil shortage
facts: The second problem was a significant fall in oil production in the USSR. The planned economy needed a regular supply of cheap oil. Also, the USSR exported 30% of its oil, mostly to Eastern Europe. In the late 1980s oil production fell by 30%. This hit exports and also damaged relations with the Comecon countries.
Oil had permitted an 8% growth rate in the USSR in the 1960s — by the 1980s this had fallen to 1.8%.

The whole basis of the planned economy was being undermined. The USSR was failing to deliver to consumers, to its allies or to its defences. The infrastructure was outdated and this was dramatically revealed by an accident at the Chernobyl nuclear power station in 1986.
Economic and social unrest became increasingly apparent in the satellites, notably in Poland with the emergence of the radical trade union activity in the shipyards.

The Chernobyl nuclear disaster of 1986 exposed the depth of industrial failure — $18 billion was spent on containment, and the environmental catastrophe was impossible to conceal. This accelerated glasnost and undermined public confidence in the Soviet system.

subheadings.label: Debate: Were internal Soviet problems or Western pressure more responsible for ending the Cold War?
facts: INTERNAL PROBLEMS MORE RESPONSIBLE: USSR GDP only 37% of USA's by mid-1980s — structurally unsustainable.
INTERNAL PROBLEMS MORE RESPONSIBLE: Oil production fell 30% — planned economy failed its most basic function.
INTERNAL PROBLEMS MORE RESPONSIBLE: Chernobyl 1986 exposed industrial failure publicly — $18bn spent on containment.
INTERNAL PROBLEMS MORE RESPONSIBLE: Agricultural stagnation from 1960s to 1980s made USSR dependent on Western grain imports.
INTERNAL PROBLEMS MORE RESPONSIBLE: Gorbachev's own analysis: the USSR needed to change regardless of Western pressure.
WESTERN PRESSURE MORE RESPONSIBLE: SDI threatened to make entire Soviet nuclear arsenal obsolete — forced concessions.
WESTERN PRESSURE MORE RESPONSIBLE: Reagan's military spending ($171bn → $376bn) the USSR simply could not match.
WESTERN PRESSURE MORE RESPONSIBLE: Marshall Aid and West Germany's Wirtschaftswunder provided devastating comparison.
WESTERN PRESSURE MORE RESPONSIBLE: Afghanistan: US Operation Cyclone (CIA/Mujaheeden) turned quagmire into catastrophe.
WESTERN PRESSURE MORE RESPONSIBLE: Helsinki Accords Basket 3 gave dissidents a legal framework — Western ideological pressure worked.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995

heading: Reagan, the arms race and Western pressure

subheadings.label: Western reactions to Afghanistan
facts: The West had largely accepted Soviet actions within its sphere of influence in Europe from 1953 to 1968. The invasion of Afghanistan in December 1979 was against a communist government but was seen as aggression.

The USA protested by boycotting the Olympic Games in Moscow in 1980 and more importantly by supporting guerrilla resistance by the Mujaheeden. This was more pressure than had been applied in Hungary 1956 or Czechoslovakia 1968.
The USA also increased its military spending and extended the arms race, which put pressure on the USSR.

Carter Doctrine (1980): Truman had committed the USA to defending free peoples against communism; Carter now committed the USA to respond strongly to any threat to the Persian Gulf — a direct response to Soviet expansion into Afghanistan marking the formal end of détente.

subheadings.label: Reagan and the new arms race
facts: Reagan rejected the previous restrictions on defence systems. By restricting these, the whole theory of mutual destruction as a deterrent was maintained. However, with the development of highly sophisticated and expensive new laser and space-based systems, there was the possibility that the USA could actually win a future conflict.

With the ramping-up of defence spending by the USA, the USSR was put at a disadvantage as its economy was stagnant and its technology had not kept up with that of the West. The new, if unspoken, concept that a future nuclear war might be 'winnable' gave the West new confidence.

subheadings.label: Limitations of Western influence
facts: Soviet military spending was already high and did not increase in response to this arms race. The problem was that economic growth was falling and there was a shortage of oil. This meant it was difficult to keep up with arms production. It was this rather than just pressure from the West that led to Gorbachev seeking a way to scale back the arms race.

The amount of direct pressure that the USA put on was also limited. Trade continued, as did exports of grain. Western capital was invested in the East. Reagan's belief in free markets and the economic needs of US banks and businesses overrode his ideological hostility to the USSR.

subheadings.label: Wider world
facts: The West put pressure on communist influences in the developing world. Reagan fought off communist influence in Nicaragua and invaded Grenada. These were more an indication of US determination than a major influence on the USSR.
The aid to insurgents in Afghanistan, however, was more serious.

subheadings.label: Détente revives
facts: The new détente of 1985–88 was an indication that the USSR was susceptible to pressure. In April 1985 Gorbachev stopped increasing SS-20 missiles stationed in Eastern Europe and he attempted at a meeting in Iceland to persuade Reagan to give up the SDI developments.
He did succeed, however, in getting the total withdrawal of medium-range missiles in Europe at a conference between the USSR and NATO in Washington in 1987 — the INF Treaty.

These concessions and agreements with the USA were accompanied by attempts to end conflicts with China and to reduce conflict and military spending and to adopt a more flexible attitude to its economy.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was Reagan's arms build-up or Gorbachev's reforms more important in ending the Cold War?
facts: REAGAN MORE IMPORTANT: SDI forced Gorbachev to the negotiating table — USSR couldn't compete technologically.
REAGAN MORE IMPORTANT: Arms spending $171bn → $376bn demonstrated economic dominance USSR couldn't match.
REAGAN MORE IMPORTANT: 'Evil empire' rhetoric changed the moral climate — denied USSR legitimacy.
REAGAN MORE IMPORTANT: Mujaheeden support turned Afghanistan from a short operation into a draining quagmire.
REAGAN MORE IMPORTANT: INF Treaty (1987) was only possible because Reagan's build-up gave him leverage.
GORBACHEV MORE IMPORTANT: Soviet military spending did not increase in response to the arms race — internal stagnation drove change.
GORBACHEV MORE IMPORTANT: Trade continued, grain exported — Reagan's hostility was ideological, not economic.
GORBACHEV MORE IMPORTANT: Sinatra Doctrine (1988) was Gorbachev's unilateral decision — Reagan had no role in it.
GORBACHEV MORE IMPORTANT: Glasnost unleashed forces Gorbachev could have suppressed — he chose not to.
GORBACHEV MORE IMPORTANT: China's Tiananmen Square (1989) showed another path was possible — Gorbachev's choice was decisive.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995

heading: Gorbachev — perestroika and glasnost

subheadings.label: Gorbachev's context
facts: When Gorbachev became leader of the USSR in 1985, there was a widespread understanding in party circles that there were severe economic problems and a need to act to meet the challenge from the West. The two elderly leaders who had followed Brezhnev — Yuri Andropov and Konstantin Chernenko — meant that stagnation had characterised policy at a vital time.
Gorbachev, relatively young at 54 and well-educated, introduced key changes.

subheadings.label: Perestroika and glasnost
facts: 'Perestroika' referred to the restructuring of the economy to relax centralised control and to permit greater economic freedom and initiative. 'Glasnost' was an 'openness' that would allow more discussion of economic and political issues to drive progress.

In 1986 state controls of the media were relaxed and the public learnt about the inefficiencies and corruption that had come to characterise national and local political and economic management. This was to be a prelude to new ideas and reforms to stop decline.

subheadings.label: Political change
facts: In January 1987 Gorbachev spoke openly to the Central Committee of the weaknesses of the system and proposed much greater public participation and making officials more accountable. Multi-candidate elections by secret ballot for the local councils (Soviets) and party organisations were proposed.

In June 1987 private enterprise was allowed in some industries. The changes divided the party. Some hardliners felt that this was a dangerous path when the threat from the USA and China was unresolved. Others wanted more radical reforms.

The hold of the Communist Party began to weaken. New political organisations began to form, like the Democratic Union. Political criticisms in books and pamphlets appeared and more open religious worship once again began to emerge.

In February 1989 there were elections for a new Congress of People's Deputies, which saw the defeat of many of the party establishment. New political leaders from outside the party emerged, including Boris Yeltsin.

subheadings.label: Impact of the changes
facts: The pace and urgency of change were determined by the changing economic context and the external pressures of the new Cold War. There had been pressures for change in the satellites but these had been controlled in Poland.

The existence of a reform movement — Solidarity — paved the way for reform, however. Economic stagnation and corruption had been criticised in Hungary and Bulgaria and these countries were prepared to adopt similar measures to Gorbachev.

In the DDR and Romania, the leadership showed little desire for change. Thus, Eastern Europe was divided over the changes. By 1989, Gorbachev would not bolster unpopular communist regimes that were unwilling to apply the remedies he had introduced in the USSR.
Integral changes in the USSR paved the way for a new détente and meant that instead of pressure for change being dictated by Western pressure, it was coming from the leadership of the USSR itself.
Although not intended to be a parliament, the new Congress came to assume that role. In 1990 the official dominance of the Communist Party in the USSR was ended.

December 1988: Gorbachev's UN speech formally abandoned the Brezhnev Doctrine — satellite states were now free to 'do it their way' (hence 'Sinatra Doctrine'). This single decision — refusing to use force — was the most important factor enabling the 1989 revolutions.

subheadings.label: Debate: Were perestroika and glasnost necessary reforms or the mistakes that destroyed the USSR?
facts: NECESSARY: USSR economy at 37% of US GDP — the system was failing and change was unavoidable.
NECESSARY: Chernobyl 1986 proved publicly that the system could not even manage basic infrastructure safely.
NECESSARY: Without reform, the USSR faced terminal economic decline and eventual collapse anyway.
NECESSARY: Gorbachev's generation understood the depth of failure — the alternative was an even more catastrophic collapse.
NECESSARY: Oil production falling 30% — the planned economy was structurally broken regardless of leadership.
FATAL MISTAKES: Glasnost exposed the regime's crimes and failures — once exposed, the Party's legitimacy was impossible to restore.
FATAL MISTAKES: Perestroika created economic disruption without growth — shortages worsened before any improvement.
FATAL MISTAKES: Multi-candidate elections (1987) gave anti-communist forces a legal platform — Boris Yeltsin emerged.
FATAL MISTAKES: Sinatra Doctrine abandoned the Brezhnev Doctrine — without that threat, the entire Eastern empire collapsed in months.
FATAL MISTAKES: China's path (Tiananmen 1989) showed that reform could be suppressed — Gorbachev chose a different path.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995

heading: The importance of the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in ending the Cold War

subheadings.label: The war
facts: In 1979, 100,000 USSR forces entered Afghanistan and installed a more controllable communist leader. They faced opposition to Moscow-dominated communist rule inspired by Islamic beliefs and supported by the USA via Pakistan. Soviet troops withdrew in 1989.

The nature of the terrain in Afghanistan — which had created problems for European powers trying to control the country since the nineteenth century — led to a sustained guerrilla war. The experience of USSR forces echoed the US struggle in Vietnam. The opposition fighters had the support of local populations.

subheadings.label: The problems of the war
facts: The Afghan national army faded away and the forces of the USSR were engaged in a direct conflict with a ruthless enemy with years of experience fighting in harsh terrain. The war was fought with increasing brutality and disregard for civilian casualties.
The war damaged the reputation of the USSR not only in the West but also within the Soviet bloc, which saw it as costly — over 38,000 Soviets died or were wounded — and pointless.
In September 1985 the execution of a civilian led to a mutiny by Central Asian Muslim troops in northern Afghanistan that resulted in 450 deaths and 500 vehicles being destroyed.

The losses in Afghanistan increased resentment within the USSR from non-Russians, who felt that they were paying the price for involvement in a war that brought little benefit to those outside Russia and its leadership. 'Draft dodging' became common.

Operation Cyclone: the CIA supplied the Mujaheeden via Pakistan. By 1986 the level of aid included surface-to-air missiles that neutralised Soviet air superiority — turning Afghanistan into a genuinely unwinnable war.

subheadings.label: The effects of the war on Soviet confidence
facts: Previously, armed Soviet intervention in satellite states in Europe had been effective and short-lived. There had been limited resistance internally and the West had not acted. This was not true in Afghanistan and thus it eroded the confidence of Soviet leaders in using military intervention.
Thus, military action was not seen as a viable option in 1989 when the Soviet Empire began to disintegrate, and this led to the end of the USSR and the Cold War.

The second effect of the war was it demonstrated the weakness of the Red Army. Its inability to defeat guerrilla forces, the increasing resort to acts of brutality and terror, and the disintegration of discipline and morale, combined to weaken the reputation of the army.
The failures in Afghanistan also changed the perception of the West and made the Cold War more 'winnable'.

subheadings.label: Public awareness and glasnost
facts: It was difficult to impose censorship on the lack of success. When glasnost allowed press freedom, the reporting of the war brought about discontent and a demand for political change.
The veterans of the war — the Afghanisti — provided a lot of criticism of the ruling communist elites and were active in political opposition.
The spiralling costs of the war were another drain on a Russian economy already having to meet heavier defence demands and to import more wheat and oil.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was Afghanistan or economic stagnation more important in bringing down the USSR?
facts: AFGHANISTAN MORE IMPORTANT: Eroded Soviet confidence in military intervention — crucial in 1989 when Gorbachev didn't send tanks.
AFGHANISTAN MORE IMPORTANT: 38,000+ killed — undermined Red Army prestige as the guarantor of communist rule.
AFGHANISTAN MORE IMPORTANT: Glasnost + Afghanistan coverage = unprecedented public criticism of the regime.
AFGHANISTAN MORE IMPORTANT: Draft dodging and ethnic resentment created internal divisions the system couldn't contain.
AFGHANISTAN MORE IMPORTANT: Demonstrated to Gorbachev that military force was no longer a viable tool — changed Soviet strategic thinking.
ECONOMIC STAGNATION MORE IMPORTANT: USSR GDP only 37% of USA's — Afghanistan was a symptom, not the cause.
ECONOMIC STAGNATION MORE IMPORTANT: Oil production fell 30% — the structural failure predated Afghanistan.
ECONOMIC STAGNATION MORE IMPORTANT: Agricultural stagnation since 1960s made USSR dependent on Western grain.
ECONOMIC STAGNATION MORE IMPORTANT: Chernobyl 1986 exposed industrial failure more dramatically than Afghanistan.
ECONOMIC STAGNATION MORE IMPORTANT: SDI arms race cost the USSR could not afford — it was the economic burden, not casualties, that broke the system.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995

heading: The revolutions of 1989 and the fall of the Berlin Wall

subheadings.label: Common elements
facts: In Poland, Hungary and Bulgaria there was internal change with the acceptance of Gorbachev, which ended the communist monopoly of power. This led to the rapid spread of political change in the East. The USSR's control of its satellites paved the way for the end of the USSR itself in 1991.

Common elements in the events of 1989: a build-up of resentment against a background of economic underperformance and rising prices; reforming leaders and groups who were ready to share power; the acceptance by Gorbachev and the Moscow leadership that states outside the USSR should make changes and an unwillingness to use force to maintain the Brezhnev Doctrine; widespread popular support for change; rapid arrangements for free elections.

subheadings.label: Poland
facts: Economic unrest, including strikes in the shipyards of Gdansk in 1988, led the government to recognise the Solidarity movement. In April 1989 the Round Table Agreements saw Solidarity recognised as a political party.

There was a new constitution, with Solidarity allowed to compete with the Communist Party for 35% of the seats in a lower house of parliament. There would be free elections for the second chamber and both houses would elect a president. The elections of June resulted in a Solidarity government with some Communists holding major posts.

The existing leader, Jaruzelski, remained president, and Communists held key posts in the new government. Poland remained part of the Warsaw Pact, but the USSR had accepted a non-Communist government and important constitutional change.

subheadings.label: Hungary
facts: Unrest in 1988 resulted in the replacement of Kadar by a reforming communist, Grosz, who planned in 1989 to introduce a multi-party system.
It was agreed with opposition groups to hold free elections in 1990.
Hungary opened its borders with Austria in August 1989. This made it possible for 150,000 East Germans to leave for the West via this route.

subheadings.label: The DDR and the Berlin Wall
facts: Hungary opening its borders provided 150,000 East Germans a route to the West. There were demonstrations in Leipzig in September and October 1989 calling for change. The East German leader Honecker could not count on Gorbachev, who advised him to make changes.

Crowds were growing in major cities, with half a million in East Berlin demanding reform and freedom to travel. The government allowed free exit from 10 November 1989, but as soon as this was announced on the 9th the border guards opened up crossing points from East to West Berlin, effectively opening the Berlin Wall.
The Wall was subsequently torn down by crowds.

subheadings.label: Czechoslovakia, Romania, Bulgaria
facts: News from Berlin led to large-scale demonstrations for political changes in Czechoslovakia. Opposition groups, including the famous Charter 77 group led by the dramatist Vaclav Havel, formed an organisation called Civic Forum and demanded change.

They formed a coalition government in December in which the Communists were only a minority, and Havel was made president. The so-called 'Velvet Revolution' led to the end of communism and the formation of two states, Slovakia and the Czech Republic, in 1992.

In Romania, demonstrations against President Ceausescu began in November 1989, influenced by events in Hungary, and then spread. Ceausescu and his wife fled but were captured and executed on 25 December 1989 — the only leaders to suffer this fate.

In Bulgaria, the veteran communist leader Zhivkov was removed from power in November 1989 by the reforming foreign minister Mladenov. Talks were held with opposition groups for free elections in 1990.

The Velvet Divorce (1 January 1993): Czechoslovakia peacefully split into the Czech Republic and Slovakia — agreed without a referendum, demonstrating the durability of the 1989 peaceful transition model.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was Gorbachev's Sinatra Doctrine or the popular revolutions more responsible for 1989?
facts: SINATRA DOCTRINE MORE RESPONSIBLE: Without Gorbachev's refusal to intervene, Soviet tanks would have crushed the movements as in 1956 and 1968.
SINATRA DOCTRINE MORE RESPONSIBLE: Hungary, DDR, Czechoslovakia, Romania, Bulgaria all happened — Gorbachev's decision was the common enabling factor.
SINATRA DOCTRINE MORE RESPONSIBLE: Gorbachev personally told Honecker to make changes — Soviet signal, not popular pressure, broke the DDR.
SINATRA DOCTRINE MORE RESPONSIBLE: The revolutions happened within weeks of each other — Gorbachev's decision created a simultaneous opening.
SINATRA DOCTRINE MORE RESPONSIBLE: China's Tiananmen Square (June 1989) showed the alternative was available — Gorbachev chose differently.
POPULAR REVOLUTIONS MORE RESPONSIBLE: 40 years of accumulated resentment could not be indefinitely contained.
POPULAR REVOLUTIONS MORE RESPONSIBLE: Solidarity (Poland), Charter 77 (Czechoslovakia), Civic Forum — pre-existing movements that needed only an opening.
POPULAR REVOLUTIONS MORE RESPONSIBLE: Economic failure made communist regimes illegitimate — populations knew Western living standards.
POPULAR REVOLUTIONS MORE RESPONSIBLE: Romania: no Sinatra Doctrine moment — Ceausescu executed by his own people. Internal revolution.
POPULAR REVOLUTIONS MORE RESPONSIBLE: Helsinki Accords Basket 3 gave dissidents a legal framework they used over decades.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995

heading: German reunification

subheadings.label: Change in the DDR
facts: The events of 1989 and the end of the Wall and travel restrictions between East and West Berlin opened the way for reunification. The withdrawal of support for the DDR from the USSR was a key factor.

The DDR accepted multi-party free elections, which ended communist rule. These returned a coalition led by a CDU politician, Lothar de Maiziere, in March 1990. Rapid reunification was driven by the economic collapse in the East and the devaluation of the currency.

subheadings.label: The stages of reunification
facts: The first step was a social, economic and monetary union in May 1990. To allow the DDR to function, the Federal Deutschmark became the official currency. That necessitated that West German laws should also apply in the East.

The East German parliament voted for accession to the West. The Reunification Treaty of 31 August 1990 saw the five states of the former Germany — Brandenburg, Mecklenburg Vorpommen, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia — join the Federal Republic.

Legally, Berlin was still under the control of the Allied Control Council set up after 1945. The 'Two Plus Four Treaty' — the two Germanys together with the four occupying powers — formalised that Berlin should be part of the Federal Republic.

In November 1990, the enlarged Germany signed a treaty with Poland guaranteeing that the frontiers of 1945 would not be revised. The new Germany became part of NATO — urged by the USA — and the last vestiges of the Cold War ended with the withdrawal of the last allied troops in 1994.

Gorbachev agreed to German NATO membership in exchange for assurances that NATO would not expand eastwards — a commitment that became the most contested legacy of the Cold War's end in subsequent decades.

subheadings.label: International reactions
facts: The end of the Cold War re-awakened fears of Germany. The Poles were anxious about the possible revision of their western frontier. The British leader Thatcher and the French president Mitterrand both expressed opposition and concern. Israel condemned reunification outright.

It might have been expected that the USSR would be the country most opposed after its terrible experiences, but Gorbachev did not oppose it. The acceptance in Europe of a major change in the balance of power was remarkable.
Cooperation in NATO and the European Economic Community, together with US support for reunification, paved the way.

subheadings.label: The importance of reunification
facts: The Cold War had ensured that Germany had not been able to dominate Central Europe, change the boundaries of 1945 or attempt to dominate its neighbours, as it had done in 1914 and 1939. It had prevented the rise of right-wing nationalism and tied Germany to different forms of democracy.

The West put in $2 trillion to the East but this could not prevent continuing inequalities. Unemployment remained much higher in the East and living standards lower. It proved more difficult than expected to reconcile the differences between the two.
The reunification was an important result of the end of the Cold War. For the people of Germany there was a painful period of readjustment.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was German reunification or the collapse of the USSR the more significant outcome of the Cold War's end?
facts: REUNIFICATION MORE SIGNIFICANT: Reversed the most visible and enduring physical division of the Cold War — 28 years of the Wall.
REUNIFICATION MORE SIGNIFICANT: Created the most powerful economy in Europe — transformed the continental balance.
REUNIFICATION MORE SIGNIFICANT: Gorbachev's acceptance of German NATO membership was the most strategically consequential decision of 1990.
REUNIFICATION MORE SIGNIFICANT: NATO expansion promise (1990) became the most contested legacy issue of post-Cold War Europe.
REUNIFICATION MORE SIGNIFICANT: Demonstrated the Cold War's end was not just an ideological shift but a territorial revolution.
USSR COLLAPSE MORE SIGNIFICANT: Created 15 independent states and ended the world's largest empire.
USSR COLLAPSE MORE SIGNIFICANT: Russia inherited nuclear arsenal — the most dangerous Cold War inheritance.
USSR COLLAPSE MORE SIGNIFICANT: Ended the 74-year communist experiment — the most consequential political experiment of the 20th century.
USSR COLLAPSE MORE SIGNIFICANT: USA became sole global superpower — transformed world order more fundamentally than German reunification.
USSR COLLAPSE MORE SIGNIFICANT: Russia's post-Soviet trajectory (Putin, Ukraine) shows the USSR collapse's consequences are still unresolved.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995

heading: The coup of 1991, the collapse of the USSR and Russia under Yeltsin

subheadings.label: The coup (August 1991)
facts: The rapid changes since 1989 had built up opposition from conservative elements in the Communist Party and from some of the leading figures in government, the army and the KGB. A proposal to reform the Soviet Union by a New Union Treaty led to an attempted takeover of the state, beginning on 19 August.
Troops took control of the TV and radio stations in Moscow and moved into the capital. Gorbachev was detained in the Crimea and cut off from all links with Moscow.

Had the coup succeeded then resistance from the Baltic states might well have been met with considerable armed force, with the Communist Party reinforced and considerable repression of opinion imposed within the USSR. The Cold War might have restarted.

US President Bush pleaded directly with the plotters. The opposition of President Boris Yeltsin, a popular figure in Moscow, was a key element in the failure of the coup. Yeltsin made an emotional appeal, jumping on a tank. The tide had turned by 21 August and the troops were withdrawn. Gorbachev was restored and the plotters, condemned by parliament, fled.

subheadings.label: Aftermath of the coup
facts: The détente with the West had been preserved but the aftermath of the coup confirmed the end of the Cold War because it led to significant developments that weakened the former USSR.

Gorbachev was discredited and Yeltsin became the dominant leader. Unstable and with poor judgement, Yeltsin saw off the Communist Party, banning it from political activities in November 1991, and accepted the break-up and formal demise of the USSR.

The Baltic republics took advantage of the coup to leave the union. Yeltsin, apparently in a state of intoxication, accepted the withdrawal of Russia, Belarus and Ukraine in December 1991. In effect, the largest state had seceded from the union and the controlling, unifying influence of the Communist Party was removed.

subheadings.label: Russia under Yeltsin — economic change
