facts: Yeltsin launched a sudden transformation to a capitalist, individualistic culture. State controls and welfare were removed. Trade was liberalised, state industries were privatised in ways that benefited a small number of powerful businessmen — the oligarchs.

'Shock therapy' (January 1992): price controls removed overnight, causing hyperinflation that wiped out savings and threw those on fixed incomes into poverty. GDP halved. The effects were devastating and far exceeded what the reformers had expected.

There was also a catastrophic decline in production and state services. Many workers received no wages for months. Life expectancy fell sharply in the 1990s — the human cost of the transition was enormous.

subheadings.label: Social and political problems under Yeltsin
facts: Socially, there were disturbing signs of crime, alcoholism, inequality of wealth and lack of confidence or hope.

Politically, the changes led to Yeltsin's unpopularity and the growth of ultra-nationalist and communist opposition. A low point was the tank attack on the Russian White House in 1993. Pro-communist army leaders brought tanks up to the Russian parliament building. The deputies, however, refused to accept the president's dissolution of parliament and openly defied the show of force, Yeltsin himself climbing up on a tank to make a defiant speech.
A new constitution gave Yeltsin greater powers in 1993, but the brutal war against Chechen separatism that began in 1994 indicated old attitudes remained.

subheadings.label: End of the Cold War
facts: Russia's newfound capitalism and adoption of Western economic values was seen as the final end to the Cold War because the underlying ideological split that had emerged in 1917 was now clearly over.

The Cold War was described by Gromyko as starting as a 'secret Cold War' with the delay in the second front in 1944. It ended when the USSR collapsed in 1991 — 47 years of ideological confrontation over.

subheadings.label: Debate: Did the Cold War end in 1989, 1991 or never?
facts: 1989: Berlin Wall's fall — the physical symbol of the Cold War's division removed.
1989: Sinatra Doctrine abandoned Brezhnev Doctrine — the defining Cold War tool of Soviet control ended.
1989: Eastern European revolutions ended the satellite system — the Cold War's European geography transformed.
1991: USSR formally dissolved Christmas Day — the state that sustained the Cold War ceased to exist.
1991: Communist Party banned November 1991 — institutional basis of Cold War ideology removed.
1991: Russia adopted capitalism — the ideological split that began in 1917 was formally declared over.
NEVER ENDED: Russia retained nuclear arsenal and permanent UNSC seat — the power asymmetry survived.
NEVER ENDED: NATO expansion eastwards continued — Cold War structures persist in new form.
NEVER ENDED: Putin's Russia (invasion of Ukraine 2022) suggests the underlying tensions never resolved.
NEVER ENDED: The promise not to expand NATO (Gorbachev, 1990) became the most contested issue of post-Cold War Europe — the Cold War's unfinished business.

unit: Chapter 4 – The End of the Cold War 1984–1995

heading: The collapse of Yugoslavia

subheadings.label: Yugoslavia's unique position
facts: Yugoslavia had been the key area of Eastern Europe not dominated by the USSR. It had broken away from the Soviet sphere in 1948 under its leader, the wartime communist resistance chief Tito.
The communist regime was a unifying factor in the country, but Tito kept Yugoslavia neutral in the Cold War. It became a member of the Non-Aligned Movement in 1961.
Thus the end of the Cold War meant that its influence declined, as did its importance to the West.

subheadings.label: Existing divisions
facts: There was a history of violent hostility between the different national groups that made up the country. Yugoslavia was an artificial construction of the post-World War I treaties. Former territories of the Austrian Empire, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Slovenia and Croatia were joined to Serbia, whose king ruled the new state.

Occupied by the Germans during World War II, anti-Serbian groups, especially the Croats, fought a bloodthirsty civil war against the Serb resistance to the Germans. The country was divided not only on ethnic but also on religious grounds, with a large Muslim minority.

subheadings.label: The impact of changes in Europe after 1989
facts: Tito managed to unite the country until his death in 1980. In 1989, changes threatened the hard-won stability. The USA was less committed to supporting Yugoslavia economically now that it was no longer needed as a counterweight to the Soviet bloc, which had collapsed.

The ending of the power and influence of the USSR in the East removed a key element that had kept the different elements in Yugoslavia together — the fear of Russia. The unification of Germany and the break-away of the Baltic states, together with the growth of nationalism in other areas of the former Soviet Empire, encouraged nationalism.

subheadings.label: Nationalism and break-up
facts: In Serbia, Slobodan Milošević, who became president in 1989, rose to prominence by promoting Serbian nationalism. His personal ambitions led to Serbia ending the autonomous status of the provinces of Vojvodina and Kosovo.

Elections in Slovenia and Croatia led to separatist demands for an end to the federal state. Slovenia voted for independence in late 1990 and Croatia in May 1991. Both declared independence on 25 June 1991.
There was a substantial Serb minority in Croatia who wanted to join Serbia. Civil war broke out, with Milošević using the federal army to support the Croatian Serbs.

In Bosnia-Herzegovina there was a referendum, which resulted in a call for independence being boycotted by the Serbs who lived there. Ethnic conflicts united with religious divisions. Despite international recognition of the separate states, bloody conflict broke out and there was some of the most brutal fighting and ethnic cleansing by the Serbs seen in Europe since 1945.

subheadings.label: International intervention
facts: This led to international intervention, which proved ineffective in protecting Muslim civilians. The Srebrenica massacre of 1995 — in which Serbian forces murdered 8,000 Bosnian Muslim men and boys — was the worst atrocity in Europe since World War II. NATO bombing in 1995 forced the Dayton Peace Agreement, ending the Bosnian War.
Only intervention by Russia brought Milošević to accept the withdrawal of Serb forces.

subheadings.label: Debate: Was Yugoslavia's collapse a Cold War consequence or the result of deeper ethnic tensions?
facts: COLD WAR CONSEQUENCE: Tito's Yugoslavia only held together as a Western counter-balance to the Soviet bloc.
COLD WAR CONSEQUENCE: Loss of Soviet threat removed the 'fear of Russia' that had united Yugoslavia's factions.
COLD WAR CONSEQUENCE: German reunification and Baltic independence emboldened Slovenian and Croatian nationalists.
COLD WAR CONSEQUENCE: USA reduced economic support — Yugoslavia no longer strategically vital.
COLD WAR CONSEQUENCE: Gorbachev's reforms delegitimised communism — the ideology that had suppressed nationalism.
DEEPER ETHNIC TENSIONS: Ethnic and religious divisions predated communism by centuries.
DEEPER ETHNIC TENSIONS: WW2 Ustasha-Serb atrocities left wounds communism had only papered over.
DEEPER ETHNIC TENSIONS: Tito's death in 1980 removed the key unifying figure — 9 years before 1989.
DEEPER ETHNIC TENSIONS: Srebrenica massacre (8,000 killed) was driven by ethnic hatred, not Cold War politics.
DEEPER ETHNIC TENSIONS: Milošević's nationalism was the immediate trigger — he would have pursued it in any geopolitical context.
